Wallhack M-001 Review: When Fun Overrides Specs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:30:00 UTC
21:30:00 KST

With a tactile dongle for on-the-fly customization and a metal chassis, the Wallhack M-001 is the most fun I've had reviewing a gaming mouse in a long time.
Magnesium shell. Hot-swappable, rechargeable batteries. 52-gram weight. Functional and innovative dongle. Satisfying tactile experience. Great styling and design language.
TIRED
High price point. Slightly outdated sensor. Only 2.4G wireless connectivity with dongle; no Bluetooth or USB-C connectivity on mouse.
Batteries. They're not typically thought of as a significant source of innovation. Most companies have spent the last few years removing mice in favor of more lightweight designs.
That's what's made the return of the replaceable and rechargeable battery surprising—something I once thought to be a lost technology from a bygone era. A few companies have recently realized that the ability to pop out and replace your battery in seconds is a great way to extend mouse life without needing to increase battery size or efficiency.
From the handful of mice I’ve tested with hot-swappable batteries so far, Wallhack does it best. The mouse is designed around the function’s ease-of-use, and everything else comes together to make a mouse that feels not only competitive for gaming, but also well thought-out and satisfying to use in everyday life.
Effective Shape
The M-001’s shape is a standard right-handed, symmetrical design. This means the mouse’s left and right sides are shaped identically, but only the left side has thumb buttons. There are two main buttons, two side buttons, a standard ratcheting scroll wheel, and a power switch on the underside.
With a length of 120 mm, the M-001 is slightly shorter than contemporaries like the Razer Viper V4 Pro (125 mm) and Logitech Pro Superstrike X2 (127 mm). The overall width and height are comparable, at 63.5-mm tall and a 39-mm wide. The largest difference is the profile of the mouse: The front end sits significantly lower than other mice, and the rear has a more significant hump, which creates a more angled shape overall. When using a palm grip, this puts your hand at a slightly more aggressive forwards angle, with your palm sitting higher and your fingers pointing more downwards. It’s a slight difference, but I found this angle to be better for quick movements compared to a more “flat” design. However, like most shape-related choices, this is ultimately down to individual preference. (To compare mouse sizes, I typically use a website like eloshapes)
The two main buttons are lightly sculpted, with subtle concavity for fingers to comfortably rest in. Similarly, there is a subtle taper at the bottom center of the mouse which makes lifting and moving easier. The side buttons use a simple, rounded shape placed just above the taper, making it easy to rock your thumb upwards to press them without getting in the way. They’re just elevated enough that the buttons don’t recess into the shell when pressed. The only shape-related issue I had was the scroll wheel, which is a good bit more elevated than other mice. This isn’t a huge issue, and I adapted to it after a few hours of use, but it’s something I could see being off-putting for users accustomed to a lower-profile scroll wheel.
(Not) Heavy Metal
The most important part of this mouse’s construction is the magnesium shell, which provides significantly more rigidity than the plastic shells used on most mice. Because of this, the mouse feels incredibly sturdy and solid. The metal shell also gives the mouse a cool, slick feeling underneath your fingertips, which I prefer to the matte plastic feeling that most mice have.
Despite using metal, it only weighs 53.6 grams, making the M-001 quite light by most standards, It still falls slightly behind the Viper V4 Pro’s 50.3 grams and lags way behind Corsair’s superlight, 36-gram Sabre V2 Pro Ultralight. But the M-001 is incredibly solid, with none of the flexibility or flimsiness that most plastic mice have. When compared to other magnesium mice like the AngryMiao Infinity .97 or Corsair’s magnesium-shelled Sabre, the M-001 has an entirely solid upper shell without any cutouts or holes, which feels much better for regular use with a multitude of grip styles (plus, it’s much less likely to have dust, dead skin, or anything else build up inside of it). While the full magnesium shell increases weight, it’s a worthwhile trade-off for a smooth and rigid shape.
It’s also worth noting that some of Wallhack’s promotional material depicts the mouse as being a solid black color, but this isn’t quite the case. The unit I received is much closer to a gunmetal color, with a significant amount of metallic flake across the finish. The color looks fantastic in person, but it's difficult to properly capture in images.
Flipping over this mouse reveals one of the more atypical design decisions being made: the lack of a bottom shell. Instead of an entire underside, there is a thin frame around the circumference of the mouse that holds six feet in place. Between them is a chasm that reveals the entire PCB and battery.
Of particular note is the PCB’s function inside the mouse: Instead of simply sitting inside of the shell, the PCB works as a primary structural component. Similar techniques have been used in designing supercars and sport bikes, with the Ferrari F50 using the engine block as a stressed member that provides rigidity to the entire car, a technology borrowed from Ferrari’s F1 team. This provides some obvious benefits to rigidity and weight-savings, but it’s also just undeniably cool to be able to flip over your mouse and see the entire circuit board.
Right behind the PCB is the star of the show, a hot-swappable battery. While I’ve tested quite a few mice with this technology, none of them have managed to make the battery-swapping so satisfying. Instead of being attached with magnets or a rotating locking mechanism, the batteries use a custom-made -spring-loaded ejector similar to an SD card or a Nintendo Switch cartridge. To insert the battery, simply press until you feel a click, and it will lock into place. To remove it, do the same: press until you feel a click, and it will pop out slightly. Of all the mice I’ve tested with removable batteries, this is by far my favorite mechanism to use: It’s intuitive, fun, and feels sturdy.
This battery system does come with a trade-off. Because hot-swappable batteries means an effectively-infinite battery life (as long as you remember to plug the old one into the dongle when you swap), Wallhack has decided to entirely remove the USB-C port on the mouse. This means it only functions as a 2.4G wireless mouse and cannot be plugged or charged in directly. This isn’t a huge issue (it never inconvenienced me, since there was always a fully charged battery ready to swap in), and it theoretically means the connection quality will be better, since there’s fewer components between the antenna and the receiver. But it is worth noting that, if a battery dies or your dongle craps out, there’s no other way to use this mouse.
The Perfect Dongle
In every high-polling mouse I’ve reviewed, the dongle has been a bit of a pain point. A high polling rate necessitates proximity, which in turn requires in a small thing sitting on your desk. In most cases, these things have only one or two functions: They connect to the mouse, and they maybe have a small number of LED indicators (between 1 and 3) that can display battery life, connection quality, or some other setting. Almost every time, they’re small and light enough to slide around on your desk and will inevitably end up falling behind it once or twice due to the weight of the cable pulling it back.
With the M-001, nearly all of these issues are resolved: The dongle is given purpose, function, and I’d even argue dignity. Instead of the small, existing-by-necessity designs that most manufacturers ship with their mice, Wallhack has managed to make a beautiful piece of industrial design. The dongle is a medium-sized metal wedge sporting a gunmetal gray finish identical to the mouse. It has two camera-like dials up front, a button, and a slot for a rechargeable battery. The DPI dial features numbering from 400 to 25,600, and the polling dial goes from 125 Hz to 8,000 Hz.
The dials both have LED indicators next to them, which illuminate alongside the mouse to indicate a setting being changed. When rotated, they both have a satisfying ratcheting mechanism that’s stiff enough to avoid accidental inputs, without being difficult to turn using a single finger.
While I loved these dials from the moment I saw them, I really didn’t expect to use them much. I’ve always been more of a set-and-forget type of person. But after testing this mouse for a while, I regularly found myself using both of the dials: On-the-fly DPI adjustments were great for games like Marvel Rivals. I tended to prefer, for example, a higher DPI for Thing and a lower for Thor. Polling adjustments, too, were useful in situations where older games (like Destiny 2) got grumpy when I was using a mouse above 1,000 Hz.
Performance and Software
Like many mice today, the M-001 uses an in-browser customization client. Wallhack’s web client, Wallhack Terminal, takes a unique stylistic approach, relying on a black-and-white, text-based system that resembles Command Prompt more than a typical gaming software. This is both a breath of fresh air stylistically, and much more straightforward than some of the software I’ve used in the past.
The configurator has an extensive feature set, including adjustments for mouse rotation, acceleration, and lift-off distance, which is adjustable by millimeters instead of the vague Low/Medium/High that some softwares use. The sensor can also be pushed to scan faster than the mouse’s 8,000 Hz polling rate, which can potentially improve the accuracy of the sensor, but limits battery life.
Along with adjusting DPI and polling with the dials on the dongle, switching them to the red “DPI” And “Hz” text allows for more granular adjustments within the configurator.
The sensor inside the mouse is a Pixart PAW3950. For anyone who doesn’t have an exhaustive list of mouse sensors floating around their head, this is the same type of sensor used in the 2022 Razer Viper V2 Pro (branded as the Razer Focus Pro 30k). That's four years old at this point. It’s not quite a cutting-edge sensor anymore. But unless you're in the top-tier of competitive play, the sensor will feel consistent and reliable enough, being able to easily track and manage direction changes during fast-paced shootouts. My personal daily driver is a Viper V2 Pro with the exact same sensor (I prefer the shape to the V3 and V4), and it’s still perfectly serviceable after four years of use.
The main buttons inside this mouse use Omron Optical switches, while the side buttons opt for low-profile Omron blue-dot mechanical switches. The scroll wheel’s encoder is a mechanical unit as well, which means it doesn’t have quite the same longevity as the optical units some mice are beginning to use. However, they are easier to replace or fix if something does go wrong.
The internal design of this mouse is impressively simple: There are six feet on the underside, and the outer four all have screws underneath. When you remove these four screws, the bottom half of the shell comes off cleanly (no flimsy plastic clips!), and a few more screws separate the internals from the top shell.
Mice Should Be Fun
I’ve said many times that, when it comes to peripherals, technical specs are only one part of the story. More than that, it’s important to have a device you enjoy using. Of all the mice I’ve tested, the M-001 is by far one of the most enjoyable. The shape is comfortable and natural for multiple grip styles, and the material ensures that the mouse feels rigid and stable despite its light weight. The dongle is a brilliant design that elevates itself from a sad desk tchotchke to a practical and functional device. And the battery mechanism is one of the most clever and fun designs I’ve seen in ages.
Everything about this mouse is deeply satisfying, and I found myself excited to use it every time I sat down. Of course, this mouse isn’t at the cutting edge of sensors or switches, and because of this, I can’t exactly recommend this mouse to someone looking for an ultra-cost-effective option with min-maxed specs. But in using the mouse on the daily, I didn't find that it mattered as much as you might think. 8,000 Hz polling and a 25,600 DPI sensor are enough for all but the pros. Instead, it uses tried-and-true internals that function perfectly well and, more importantly, have crisp and precise tactile responses.
Henri Robbins is a WIRED contributor specializing in mechanical keyboards and PC peripherals. He also reviewed hardware for Input and Inverse. He graduated from Miami University, where he studied journalism, media and communications, and photography. He resides in Cincinnati. ... Read More

By Steven Scheer
JERUSALEM, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces re-election this week, is drawing criticism from economists and political rivals after suggesting Israel could use cryptocurrency to help shield its economy from potential international sanctions.
In an interview with Israel’s Channel 10 on Friday, Netanyahu said he was preparing for a scenario in which broader sanctions were imposed on Israel.
Last month, Britain, France and Canada said they would block imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank in what was the latest in a series of actions targeting Israel’s settlement policy, underscoring its growing diplomatic isolation among some of its traditional allies.
“There could be sanctions, and sanctions on banks so you need to set up a bypass economy,” Netanyahu said. “You know, there are currencies that can bypass (sanctions). We are also working on that.”
Asked whether he was referring to cryptocurrency, Netanyahu replied: “Very true, very true,” adding that blockchain technology was another possibility.
The comments drew a rare rebuke by the Bank of Israel, which said crypto currencies cannot serve as a route to bypass sanctions and that political leaders should focus on policy that would render such measures unnecessary.
“The right course for Israel’s economy is to preserve our economic relations with our main trading partners, and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy,” it said.
Netanyahu on Sunday continued to defend his record, urging voters to back him and saying he and US President Donald Trump had two years left to work together to topple Iran’s rulers.
PLAN DRAWS CRITICISM
On Sunday, more than 100 economists, including former Bank of Israel officials, ex-central bank governor Jacob Frenkel and several Nobel laureates, signed a letter expressing alarm over Netanyahu’s proposal. They said it would lead to higher unemployment, a fall in foreign investment and the collapse of Israel’s economic standing in the world.
“As we have seen in countries that have suffered similar sanctions, such as South Africa, Iran, and Russia, the living standards of Israeli citizens would plummet dramatically, and the state’s ability to finance its security and defend itself against its enemies would be severely damaged,” the letter read.
“Netanyahu is knowingly leading the State of Israel toward boycott and international economic isolation, and all he has to offer the Israeli economy is a puzzling solution, one accepted in criminal organizations, that will not help in the slightest.”
Netanyahu’s main rival in Tuesday’s election, Gadi Eisenkot, called the crypto plan “madness” and said he feared that the “BibiCoin policy” would drive companies abroad and undermine national security.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said: “Netanyahu has gone off the rails … He promises the citizens of Israel before these elections that they’ll be standing in line for an hour and a half for bread, like in Russia and Iran.”
Opinion polls point to a potential stalemate in the election with neither Netanyahu’s ruling coalition nor an opposition alliance securing a governing majority in parliament.

Strikes on oil refineries and dozens of Russian vessels: how the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ secret unit operates
Ukraine

Strikes on oil refineries and dozens of Russian vessels: how the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ secret unit operates
Kyiv • UNN
The Kairos unit was transformed into the 7th Separate Center with hundreds of military personnel. It coordinates long-range strikes on Russian targets.
The Ukrainian Kairos battalion, which participates in long-range strikes against Russian facilities, has been deployed within the 7th Separate Center of the Armed Forces of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces. This was reported by Bloomberg, according to UNN.
Details
According to the agency, the Kairos unit, which was previously part of the 414th Separate Brigade of Unmanned Systems “Magyar’s Birds,” has evolved into a much larger military structure. The 7th Separate Center now numbers hundreds of service members and is capable of coordinating operations by other units.
The commander of the formation, known by the call sign “Ray,” told journalists that the capabilities of Ukraine’s long-range strikes have grown significantly. Whereas previously drones could carry out missions at a distance of about 100 kilometers and carry a relatively small warhead, Ukrainian forces now use significantly more powerful weapons, including relatively inexpensive cruise missiles.
One of Kairos’s areas of activity has been attacks on Russian maritime logistics. According to the commander, over the course of one month the unit struck 60 vessels in the Sea of Azov. In addition, during the summer campaign aimed at isolating occupied Crimea, the Unmanned Systems Forces carried out approximately 7,000 strikes using drones. These figures were provided by the Ukrainian side; there has been no independent confirmation of all the claimed results.
Bloomberg also reports on Kairos’s involvement in large-scale attacks on Russian energy facilities. In particular, the unit took part in an operation to attack the territory of the Moscow oil refinery in Kapotnya on September 20, 2026. Following the attack, the facility suspended oil refining, and repairs to the damaged equipment could take several weeks.
Satellite reconnaissance and data analysis play an important role in preparing long-range strikes. Ukrainian forces use current and archival satellite imagery to study Russian facilities. Specialists with experience in the energy sector are also involved in planning the operations.
According to the agency’s assessment, the expansion of the capabilities of Ukrainian long-range strike units demonstrates significant changes in the conduct of the war. Ukraine is increasingly using its own technologies, intelligence data, and coordinated operations to strike Russia’s military and energy infrastructure at a considerable distance from the front line.

Algerian parliament’s upper house approves troop deployment to Niger
Vote to send forces comes after a recent defence pact between two neighbouring countries.
The upper house of Algeria’s parliament has unanimously approved the deployment of troops to neighbouring Niger.
The Algerian constitution empowers the president to send military units abroad, provided that both chambers of parliament approve it by a two-thirds majority.
The Council of the Nation held an emergency session on Sunday to vote on troop deployment, while the People’s National Assembly, or the lower house, is expected to hold a separate session later in the evening, Algeria’s popular newspaper El Khabar reported. If the deployment is approved, it would be the first mission outside Algeria’s borders since the 1973 War between Israel and several Arab countries, known to Arabs as the October War and Israelis as the Yom Kippur War.
The military units to be deployed by Algeria are expected to be tasked with securing oil facilities in Niger.
The vote came after a visit by Niger’s Defence Minister General Salifou Modi to Algeria last week, where he held talks with Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune and Chief of Staff of the People’s National Army General Said Chanegriha.
During that visit, the two sides signed a military cooperation protocol, the details of which were not made public.
Earlier this month, Tebboune confirmed that Algeria sent fighter jets to Niger in late August to help thwart a “coup attempt” that shook the capital, Niamey.
The Algerian Ministry of Defence previously said it had sent four jets to Niger following the unrest. It said two patrols of four Sukhoi Su-30 aircraft had landed at Niamey airport, accompanied by an air-to-air refuelling plane.
The warplanes were deployed at the request of Nigerien authorities on “a mission to support the Nigerien army in confronting an attempt to destabilise the brotherly state of Niger”, the ministry said on August 30.
Relations between Algeria and Niger have witnessed a significant rapprochement over the past few months on political, diplomatic, military and economic levels, following a period of tension between the two countries.

AI giant cuts internet access to its most powerful models
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:18:33 UTC
21:18:33 KST

AI giant cuts internet access to its most powerful models
OpenAI has restricted internet access for training its most powerful artificial intelligence (AI) models after agents found ways to escape isolated computing environments. It will switch to an offline setup with cached web pages for reinforcement learning.
The findings published by the company on Friday come amid growing concerns over the cybersecurity risks posed by increasingly capable AI agents, which can identify software vulnerabilities and exploit weaknesses in the systems they interact with. Security researchers have warned that such capabilities could allow agents to exploit flaws in the safeguards designed to contain them.
OpenAI said one of its research models gained limited internet access on September 20 by exploiting a misconfiguration in the system that translates web addresses into IP addresses. The company contained the incident and paused training and evaluation of its most advanced models while strengthening its defenses.
Training resumed on October 1, including reinforcement learning and internal inference, but the company retained the restriction on live internet access. In its October 23 report, OpenAI said the models would continue to be trained in an offline environment until it had developed sufficiently robust safeguards to permit broader access.
The latest disclosure follows an incident in July in which OpenAI models bypassed controls designed to isolate them from the internet and compromised parts of the company’s research infrastructure and Hugging Face’s systems. According to OpenAI, the agents exploited a vulnerability in a software package registry to access the internet, found exposed credentials and used them to access third-party services.
Earlier this week, OpenAI also disclosed two incidents in which agents weakened internal safety monitoring while carrying out coding tasks. On October 3, an agent disabled automatic security alerts, while on October 6 another removed a monitoring integration and later falsely told the user it had not done so. The company said it was strengthening controls to prevent agents from disabling monitoring and investigating why they had acted that way.
Similar incidents have been reported by other AI developers. Anthropic said its Claude models accessed four organizations’ systems during cybersecurity tests, while Meta disclosed that its Muse Spark model exploited a vulnerability in a real company’s website after a testing error gave it internet access. Google also reported that its Gemini model accessed the systems of three companies during an evaluation, highlighting the challenges of containing increasingly capable AI agents in controlled testing environments.
Calls for tighter AI regulation have grown louder, with Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton warning that advanced AI could escape human control and Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates urging governments to impose safety standards. US President Donald Trump has opposed restrictions however, arguing they could give China a technological edge. Meanwhile, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently opined that society must accept some “bad things,” including hacks and scams, as the technology’s benefits outweigh its risks.

Why Israel’s latest assault on Hebron is so significant for the West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:17:39 UTC
21:17:39 KST

Why Israel’s latest assault on Hebron is so significant for the West Bank
Israeli military campaigns in Hebron trigger mass displacement and economic strangulation, deepening a humanitarian crisis across the occupied West Bank.
Palestinians in Hebron have been subjected to days of Israeli raids and forced displacement in the latest assault on the occupied West Bank city.
Israel has imposed a lockdown on Palestinians and detained at least 47 Palestinians across Hebron since Friday, according to the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society.
About 2,500 people have been forced out of the city as some Palestinian homes have been converted into military posts and barracks.
The operations followed a shooting attack on Friday that killed two soldiers while the two Palestinian suspects were also killed.
Here is what to know about Israel’s latest assault on Hebron:
Mass forced expulsions
Hebron has been subject to severe collective punishment by Israeli forces that has impacted about 900,000 Palestinians.
The military lockdown began immediately after a Friday morning shooting at a military checkpoint in the Farsh al-Hawa area.
After the closure of all entrances to the city, Israeli forces launched a large demolition operation on dozens of Palestinian buildings.
Troops also stormed the Ein Deir Bahha neighbourhood, forcing dozens of families to flee from their homes at night without any belongings. According to Hebron municipality data, the targeted displacement area covers 350 dunams (35 hectares or 86 acres), and nearly 500 Palestinian families have been uprooted.
Hesham al-Sharbati, a human rights researcher, told Al Jazeera that the military’s actions represent “a complete eviction campaign for a Palestinian residential neighbourhood”. He said what is happening is “a form of ethnic cleansing” and the collective punishment of the Palestinian community “amounts to a war crime”.
Moamar Yousef al-Awiwi, a Hebron municipal council member, said the latest Israeli operation in the city comes after a series of measures aimed at displacing the Palestinian population.
“[It] serves as a crime and collective punishment contrary to all international customs and laws,” he told Al Jazeera.
Rights groups have compared the current assault on Hebron to the tactics used during the January 2025 “Iron Wall” operation in the Jenin and Nur Shams refugee camps, which displaced more than 30,000 people and destroyed over half of their residential buildings.
Economic strangulation
Hebron is an important city for the Palestinian economy, which is in the midst of a severe crisis caused by Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and pogroms and raids by Israeli forces and settlers in the West Bank.
Hebron accounts for about 40 percent of Palestinian industrial output and 30 percent of exports, but economic activity has been badly affected by recent Israeli restrictions and assaults.
Hebron has the highest concentration of military obstacles in the West Bank with about 40 percent of the 89 main checkpoints in the occupied territory concentrated in the city’s most highly restricted zones.
Economic researcher Ahmed Abu Qamar said the current restrictions on Hebron will be felt widely due to the city’s economic significance for the West Bank.
“Hebron… [is a] first-class industrial city and is considered one of the most important pillars and foundations of the Palestinian economy regarding [its] broad industrial and commercial base,” Abu Qamar told Al Jazeera. “Any restrictions imposed on it or any closures of its outlets or restrictions on freedom of movement … or military operation[s] will put pressure on the entire Palestinian economy in the West Bank.”
Restrictions on trade and business activity in Hebron lead to “a rise in production costs due to the difficulty of supply and logistical disruption” with businesses likely to miss delivery deadlines.
“Ultimately, the halting of facilities or reducing production lines … [means] many economic facilities will be forced to either completely stop working or reduce their working hours to the minimum,” he added.
City centre settlers
The daily life of Palestinians in Hebron is also badly affected by the hundreds of Israeli settlers in the Old City.
Under the 1997 Hebron Protocol, Hebron was divided into two sectors: H1, supposedly under Palestinian civil control, and H2, representing 20 percent of the city. The latter was to remain under complete Israeli security control with 7,000 Palestinians living there subject to the strict dictates of the military apparatus.
Israeli authorities have systematically expanded “closed zones” around settlements in the city centre, which are illegal under international law. In early October, Israeli authorities installed three iron gates across a 200-metre (220-yard) stretch of the Old City, further cutting off historical commercial arteries, such as Shuhada Street, where more than 500 shops have been forcibly shuttered over the years.
Over the winter, many Palestinian residents are forced to navigate dangerous, unlit paths through local cemeteries just to bypass military closures and bag searches.
Religious site tensions
At the epicentre of the H2 zone lies the Ibrahimi Mosque, revered by Muslims and Jews, who refer to it as the Tomb of the Patriarchs. This 14th-century site is part of the Old City, which UNESCO has recognised as a World Heritage Site, and has been subject to numerous assaults by Israeli settlers.
In 1994, an American-Israeli settler opened fire with an automatic assault rifle inside the sanctuary, killing 29 Palestinian worshippers and prompting the Israeli military to permanently partition the holy site and severely restrict Palestinian access to surrounding neighbourhoods.
Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich announced the seizure of planning and construction powers over the mosque and the surrounding H2 zone, stripping the Palestinian municipality of its oversight.
In doing so, Smotrich declared he had abolished vital parts of the 1997 Hebron Agreement, marking a dramatic shift that further entrenches the occupation in the city.

Could Hormuz become America’s Suez?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:10:54 UTC
21:10:54 KST

In 1956, Britain was forced to abandon the Suez Canal and withdraw from Egypt after a humiliating political and financial defeat. The crisis did not end the British Empire overnight, but it exposed the decline of a power that had dominated much of the world for more than two centuries, in an empire on which the sun famously never set. Britain could still fight wars, but it could no longer act as an independent global power without facing the economic and political limits of its strength. Now, nearly seventy years later, the question is whether the war with Iran and the crisis around the Strait of Hormuz could become America’s Suez.
When war becomes too expensive
After Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal in July 1956, Britain, France and Israel launched a military campaign to regain control of the canal and weaken Nasser’s government. Their forces made rapid progress, but the operation soon became a financial and political crisis for London.
The British pound came under heavy pressure, and the Bank of England had to use its dollar reserves to defend the currency. The United States opposed the invasion and refused to provide the financial support Britain needed unless it agreed to stop the operation. On 6th November, Britain accepted a ceasefire. It later withdrew its forces from Egypt.
As the International Monetary Fund’s account of the crisis explains, the pressure on sterling was central to Britain’s decision. The crisis showed that the government could not continue the war without putting its financial position at long-term risk.
The war with Iran could create a similar problem for the United States, although the economic conditions are different. The dollar is far stronger internationally than the pound was in 1956, and the American economy has greater resources. But the comparison is about the cost of sustaining a war when its political goals remain out of reach.
If the war continues without a clear result, the United States will have to spend more on military operations, weapons, logistics and the protection of its forces. At the same time, the disruption of energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz can raise costs across the global economy. These pressures may gradually make the war harder to justify, especially if Iran can draw the United States into a prolonged conflict with no clear progress toward its goals.
The cost reaches American households
The Strait of Hormuz is central to this problem because of its role in the global energy market. Before the war, around one-fifth of the world’s oil consumption passed through the strait, along with a major share of global liquefied natural gas shipments. As oil prices rose, gasoline and diesel became more expensive, air travel and shipping costs increased, and the cost of transporting goods went up. This is where the war became a serious domestic problem for the White House. Higher gasoline prices were immediately visible to American households. Families had to spend more to drive for daily activities and higher diesel prices increased the cost of moving goods.
The latest energy-market reports show how difficult this problem can even become. In October 2026, Reuters reported that Brent crude remained above $100 a barrel. Diesel prices in the United States had also risen sharply, adding to domestic political pressure ahead of the midterm elections. The Reuters report on rising oil prices and the prolonged conflict describes the growing challenge for the Trump administration.
High energy prices can also make it harder to control inflation. Transport and production become more expensive, and the effects spread through the economy. If the Federal Reserve keeps interest rates high to control inflation, borrowing becomes more expensive for households and businesses. The government also has to meet the direct cost of the war while paying interest on its existing debt.
Nevertheless, none of these pressures would force Washington to end the war. The key issue is their combined effect over time. If the war continues, energy prices remain high and the United States fails to achieve objectives, the economic cost of continuing may eventually become greater than the expected benefit.
From military leverage to economic limits
A war of attrition changes the way governments calculate success. At the beginning of a conflict, leaders may expect military action to produce a quick political result. If that result does not come, they face a difficult choice: increase the pressure and spend more, or accept that the original goals may be impossible to achieve at an acceptable cost.
This is the danger facing the United States. Washington has the ability to strike Iranian targets and maintain a strong military presence in the region. But the ability to damage does not mean that Iran will accept American demands. If each new round of fighting adds to the cost without producing a decisive political result, the United States will find itself spending more while moving no closer to its goals.
The Strait of Hormuz gives Iran a way to increase this pressure. Disruption to shipping can keep energy markets unstable and raise the economic cost of the conflict well beyond the battlefield. The longer the disruption continues, the more difficult it becomes for Washington to separate its military campaign from its effects on the American economy.
The question is whether the United States can continue to bear the full cost of the conflict if the economic pressure grows while the chance of achieving its objectives declines. At some stage, American administration may conclude that continuing the war will bring more damage than benefit. That would create the conditions for an American retreat. If Washington withdraws without achieving its main goals, the result could be a strategic defeat, even if American forces remain far stronger than Iran’s in conventional military terms.
Why China could benefit
Such an outcome would also affect the wider balance of power. China is already benefiting from a war that consumes American resources, damages Washington’s reputation and reduces its ability to focus on other strategic priorities. Beijing does not need to defeat the United States directly. It can benefit simply by watching Americas useless overstretch. The war also gives China an opportunity to question whether the United States can keep its commitments to allies in Asia. China would also suffer from high energy prices and disruptions to trade. But if the United States emerges from the war with fewer resources, greater economic pressure and damaged credibility, China could gain room to expand its influence without taking on the costs of a direct military confrontation.
This is one reason the outcome of the war matters beyond the Middle East. A costly American withdrawal could affect how allies and rivals judge US power. Countries that depend on Washington for security may question its ability to sustain a long conflict. Rivals may become more willing to challenge American influence in other regions.
Could this be America’s Suez?
The Suez Crisis did not single-handedly end British power. Britain’s relative decline had been developing for decades, and the United States had already become the leading Western power. But Suez made the change unmistakable. Britain had launched a heavy military operation and then had to withdraw under financial and political pressure. But the crisis clearly exposed the limits of its ability to act as a global power.
A similar outcome is possible for the United States in Iran. If the war becomes more costly with time, if energy prices continue to place pressure on American households and businesses, and if Washington cannot achieve its main objectives, the economic logic for continuing the conflict may become increasingly weak. A withdrawal without a clear political achievement would then damage the credibility of American power as a world superpower.
The United States is not Britain in 1956. Its international position will not collapse because of one war. Yet these advantages do not remove the basic problem: US may ruin its credit as super power of current international order.
The real test will come when Washington has to choose between continuing an expensive war and accepting a retreat. If it leaves Iran without achieving its goals, the consequences could extend far beyond the battlefield. The war could become a turning point that speeds up the decline of American order and gives other powers more room to shape the coming international order. Such scenario would be what could make Hormuz America’s Suez.

How to apply for the US Green Card lottery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:07:58 UTC
21:07:58 KST

How to apply for the US Green Card lottery
A Green Card allows foreign nationals to live and work permanently in the United States. One way to obtain it is through the Diversity Visa lottery. As the United States prepares for another registration period, Qazinform News Agency explains who can apply and how the process works.
Who can apply?
The Diversity Visa Program offers up to 55,000 immigrant visas annually. It targets people born in countries with historically low immigration rates to the United States.
Kazakhstan was among the eligible countries in the last published lottery instructions. However, applicants should check the updated list before applying.
Candidates must also meet at least one of two requirements:
- Complete secondary education equivalent to 12 years of US schooling.
- Have two years of qualifying work experience within the past five years.
Not every occupation qualifies. The US Department of Labor determines which jobs meet the requirements.
When can you apply?
Registration for DV-2027 has been delayed. Under an amended court order, the US State Department must announce registration dates by October 29 and open applications by November 1, 2026.
A federal judge rejected the government's request to suspend the order, but an appeal remains pending.
Applicants should check dvprogram.state.gov for official dates. The website accepts entries only during the announced registration period.
What documents do you need?
Most applicants must prepare a valid passport and a recent digital photograph. Limited exceptions to the passport requirement apply.
Under new rules effective April 10, 2026, entrants must provide passport details and upload a scan of the biographic and signature pages. The scan must be in JPEG format and no larger than 5 MB.
The photograph must meet the following requirements:
- Taken within the past six months.
- Square, measuring 600 × 600 pixels.
- JPEG format, no larger than 240 KB.
- Plain white or off-white background.
- Face looking directly at the camera, without glasses.
Applicants must also provide personal details, education information and family information.
How to submit an application
Visit dvprogram.state.gov once registration opens. Complete the electronic entry form, DS-5501.
Enter your name, date and place of birth, passport details, address and other required information. Upload the photographs and passport scan.
Applicants must list their spouse and all living, unmarried children under 21, including adopted children and stepchildren, even if they will not immigrate. Exceptions apply to family members who are already US citizens or permanent residents. Separate photographs are required for each listed family member.
Each eligible spouse can submit a separate entry. However, each person may enter the lottery only once per registration period. Multiple entries lead to disqualification.
A new $1 registration fee applies to each entry. It must be paid through the authorized US government payment system.
After submitting the form, save the confirmation number. You will need it to check the results.
How to check the results
The US government does not notify lottery winners by email or regular mail.
Applicants must visit the official Diversity Visa website, select Entrant Status Check and enter their confirmation number.
What happens if you win?
Selection does not automatically grant a Green Card.
Selected applicants must complete the DS-260 immigrant visa application, submit supporting documents and undergo a medical examination.
They must also attend an interview at a US embassy or consulate. In Kazakhstan, immigrant visa interviews are conducted at the US Consulate General in Almaty.
The Diversity Visa application fee is $330 per person. Medical examinations and other immigration expenses cost extra.
Applicants must meet all eligibility requirements before receiving a visa. Selection alone does not guarantee approval.
How to avoid scams
The US Department of State warns against websites and agents promising guaranteed selection.
Only use official US government websites ending in .gov. Never pay individuals who claim they can improve your chances.
Keep your confirmation number and check the results yourself. No private company can guarantee a Green Card.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that a US court had ordered a 30-day registration period for DV-2027.

Three giant black holes discovered in a galaxy from the dawn of time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:07:01 UTC
21:07:01 KST

Three giant black holes discovered in a galaxy from the dawn of time
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics, Garching
- Summary:
- Astronomers have discovered three actively feeding black holes inside a single galaxy more than 12.5 billion light-years away, revealing a remarkable scene from the universe’s infancy. Two of the black holes are separated by just 620 light-years and are expected to eventually merge, while a third lurks farther away. One weighs an astonishing 80 million suns, and another is growing faster than conventional theories predict.
- Share:
Astronomers have discovered three actively feeding supermassive black holes in a single galaxy more than 12.5 billion light-years from Earth. The finding, made by an international research team led by the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics (MPE), offers a rare glimpse of how enormous black holes grew and interacted during the universe's earliest stages.
The black holes are located in a galaxy known as J0148-4214. All three are actively accumulating matter, which spirals toward them through surrounding disks of gas and other material. Because the galaxy is so distant, its light has traveled through space for approximately 12.5 billion years before reaching Earth. This means astronomers are observing it as it existed just 1.2 billion years after the Big Bang.
Over such vast distances, the expansion of the universe stretches light to longer, redder wavelengths. Astronomers measure this effect through a property called redshift. For J0148-4214, the researchers measured a redshift of z=5.02, allowing them to determine its remarkable distance.
Three Black Holes in One Ancient Galaxy
"This is the first evidence of three active black holes in a single galaxy in the distant Universe," says Hannah Übler, research group leader at MPE and lead author of the study.
Two of the black holes lie near the galaxy's center, separated by a projected distance of just 620 light-years. The third is much farther out, approximately 5,500 light-years from the center.
The discovery provides important evidence about how massive black holes came together in the young universe.
"It suggests that processes in the early Universe were efficient at bringing massive black holes together, setting the stage for the massive black hole mergers we expect to detect with future gravitational wave observatories," says Übler.
Astronomers believe that galaxy collisions and mergers were common during the universe's early history. As galaxies combined, their central black holes could also move closer together and eventually merge. These mergers would produce increasingly massive black holes at the centers of the newly formed galaxies, potentially helping explain how some grew to enormous sizes so soon after the Big Bang.
How Astronomers Detected the Hidden Black Holes
The researchers identified the three black holes by examining distinctive patterns in the light emitted by hydrogen gas. Near a black hole, powerful gravitational forces cause gas to move at extremely high speeds. These movements leave recognizable signatures in the spectrum of light, allowing astronomers to detect black hole activity even when the objects themselves cannot be seen directly.
In the center of J0148-4214, the team found a particularly complicated hydrogen emission pattern. The best explanation was the presence of two closely spaced black holes rather than a single source.
To distinguish between them, the scientists used a precise measurement technique called spectro-astrometry. By tracking subtle changes in the positions of spectral emissions across the galaxy, they were able to identify the locations of both central black holes, even though the telescope could not resolve them as two separate points of light.
The observations also revealed the third active black hole in the galaxy's outer region.
Three Black Holes With Remarkably Different Masses
The three black holes vary dramatically in size. According to the researchers' calculations, their masses are approximately 80 million, 600,000, and 2 million times that of the Sun.
Surprisingly, the largest black hole is not the one feeding most aggressively. Its smaller neighbor, with a mass of roughly 600,000 suns, is accumulating matter at a much higher rate. In fact, its estimated feeding rate exceeds the maximum predicted by basic models of black hole growth (the Eddington limit).
This unusually rapid growth may offer clues to how some black holes became extraordinarily massive during the relatively short time available in the early universe.
"The JWST data allowed us not only to identify the three black holes, but also to estimate their masses, accretion rates, and the stellar mass of the galaxy," says Dr. Giovanni Mazzolari, second author of the study and researcher at MPE. "We find a total stellar mass of about 1.3 billion suns, and the black holes represent a significant fraction of that."
An Ancient Black Hole Merger in the Making
The two black holes near the galaxy's center are expected to merge within the next few hundred million years. Their eventual collision could help produce an even more massive black hole, illustrating a process that may have been essential to the growth of the universe's earliest cosmic giants.
"These results are extremely exciting," adds Roberto Maiolino, professor at the University of Cambridge and co-author of the study. "They suggest that black hole merging may be an additional, fast route for their rapid growth in the early Universe."
The third black hole presents another intriguing puzzle. Located well outside the galaxy's center, it could be a remnant of an earlier merger that was pushed outward by a powerful gravitational recoil. Such a kick can occur when merging black holes emit gravitational waves unevenly, sending the resulting black hole in the opposite direction.
Another possibility is that the third black hole is gradually moving toward the galaxy's center, where it may eventually interact with the other two.
James Webb Reveals Black Holes That Might Otherwise Remain Hidden
The discovery highlights the remarkable capabilities of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) for studying black holes in distant galaxies.
In particular, the findings demonstrate the importance of integral field spectroscopy, which allows astronomers to examine how light and its spectral signatures vary across different parts of a galaxy.
Using Webb's Near Infrared Spectrograph in its integral field spectroscopy mode (NIRSpec-IFS), the researchers were able to separate signals that would otherwise have appeared to come from a single black hole.
Without that detailed spatial information, astronomers likely would have identified only one of the galaxy's three active black holes.
The results suggest that other distant galaxies may contain multiple growing black holes that have gone undetected. Finding more of these hidden systems could help scientists reconstruct the history of black hole mergers and better understand how the universe produced its most massive black holes so early in cosmic history.

- Clashes broke out between protesters and police in cities like Paris, Marseille and Lyon, with police having deploying tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds
- French police deployed more than 70,000 police and elite security forces across France to contain the unrest
You can read all our updates on the protests and unrest in France and other parts of Europe on October 24 and 25, 2026, below.
WATCH: France protests continue despite police crackdown
Amid the latest demonstrations, what's driving the unrest, and could a broader youth-led protest movement be taking shape?
French unions and protest groups call for more rallies
French unions and protest groups have called for fresh demonstrations on October 31 and a nationwide strike on November 5 to maintain pressure on the government.
The left-wing Solidaires union federation said anger over wages, living costs and public services was bringing together students, workers, firefighters and other groups.
"We see an aggregation of anger," Solidaires co-leader Murielle Guilbert told broadcaster BFM TV.
The SUD Education teaching union said it would join the October 31 demonstrations. The larger CGT union is set to decide during the week.
The Yellow Vests movement also called for rallies, including sit-ins outside town halls and the National Assembly.
The government has opened talks with unions and student representatives, but protest leaders say its proposals are inadequate.
France reports more than 1,300 arrests after protests
French authorities detained 1,314 people during nationwide protests on Saturday, according to a provisional Interior Ministry tally.
The ministry said 53 police officers and other security personnel were injured, firefighters responded to 75 fires and 24 businesses were looted. It did not provide a figure for injured protesters.
Clashes broke out in cities including Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux, Toulouse and Tours, with police using tear gas. The ministry blamed groups including radical far-left activists for confrontations along or near protest routes.
Authorities counted 410,000 participants at 289 demonstrations and gatherings, down from 550,000 a week earlier. Other estimates put Saturday's turnout as high as 800,000.
The reported arrests and violence were substantially lower than on October 17, when authorities recorded 2,628 detentions and 1,144 injured security personnel.
The ministry said several investigations had been opened and described the subsequent night as calm.
Authorities say nearly 1,000 arrested after day of protests in France
With Saturday's protest over, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez reported nearly 1,000 arrests.
The number is expected to rise as security officials tally up the day's events, Nunez added.
"Multiple lootings have been averted," he said.
While some clashes between protesters and police were reported in many French cities, the scope of the unrest was much smaller compared to the protests last Saturday, which saw buildings defaced and burned, and some 1,500 shops looted across the country.
Nunez previously put the number of people arrested last weekend at 2,700.
WATCH: Could the unrest play into the hands of Le Pen's National Rally party?
Here's what to know if you are joining us now
Some 410,000 people marched across France on Saturday, according to the country's interior ministry, as the country braced for a possible repeat of violence seen last weekend.
In Paris alone, at least 110,000 people turned out to denounce rising living costs and growing inequality.
Police were out in force in major French cities. While rallies in Paris and Marseille were mostly peaceful, clashes between protesters and police were reported in towards the evening.
Riot police in Paris fired tear gas and water cannons at some 500 hooded youths before they eventually dispersed. In Marseille, youths blocked roads by setting trash cans on fire. They threw rocks and bottles at security forces.
Clashes were also reported in the cities of Lyon, Bordeaux, Grenoble, Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Rennes, Nantes and Toulouse.
Altercations during protests are not sight unseen in France, DW reporter on the ground says
France is known for its protest culture, where demonstration is considered a bedrock value.
Altercations between the police and demonstrators are by and large part of the French protest ritual.
What we are seeing could even be considered a relatively calm end-of-demonstration situation, Lisa Louis, who is in Paris, said.
Milan: Protests less unruly than last weekend amid high security
Meanwhile, security guards were deployed in Milan on Saturday amid demonstrations against the rising cost of living.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ordered 500 soldiers to be dispatched to the city, in addition to about 5,000 police and other law enforcement personnel there.
But the protests in the large Italian city were less unruly than last weekend, when looters ransacked businesses near the central Duomo area. Around 3,000 people rallied in Milan, with another smaller demonstration taking place in Rome.
IN PICTURES: Clashes break out between police and protesters in demonstrations across France
As the day went on (and largely toward the end of demonstrations in many cities), clashes occurred between protesters and the authorities during the demonstrations across France. 
At least 400,000 people have taken part in protests across France
The French interior ministry said it estimates 410,000 people to have taken part in protest throughout France today.
Demonstrations were set to take place in Paris and Marseille but protesters took to the streets in other cities for rallies like Lyon and Nantes.
There were reports about clashes between protesters and police in several cities, including Paris.
There were protests in the city of Lyon, in the east-central part of France, where police used tear gas to disperse protesters wearing masks.
There are also reports about clashes in Marseille, where police fired tear gas to disperse crowds.
About 550,000 people attended demonstrations throughout the country last weekend.
French protests nowhere near the looting seen last weekend as yet, says DW reporter on the ground
The mood over the past few days in France felt almost a bit apocalyptic. Business owners told me they were worried more looting might lie ahead, after gangs of individuals had ransacked and destroyed at least 3,000 shops across the country last weekend.
"Some of us are planning to buy weapons to defend ourselves, in case the pillagers come back. One day, there's going to be a tragedy — for sure," Jonathan Siad, owner of a tobacco shop in Paris, said to me.
Other store owners were too afraid to talk to us in front of the camera – they worried criminals might see the interview and target their shop.
Residents told me they would try to avoid the area where the demonstration was taking place. Only to add that they hoped the situation wouldn't escalate like last week, when even places far away from the actual marches became hotspots of clashes between the police and protesters.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez had admitted on Monday a "loss of control" last Saturday. The authorities thus increased the number of police deployed across France by 10,000 to 70,000 this Saturday.
First clashes between protesters and the police started to occur in the late afternoon in several cities across France such as Marseille, Lyon and Paris.
But for now, the much feared mass looting and ransacking doesn't seem to be happening. The situation is nowhere near the total chaos Paris and other cities like Marseille experienced last Saturday.
"Last weekend, our neighborhood resembled a war zone with gangs roaming the area. Today, it's completely empty apart from police with their vans," Yassaman Metghalchi, co-owner of a jewelry shop in the city center of Paris that got looted last Saturday, told me.
"All of our neighbors feel reassured – although the night is still young and we need to wait and see what will happen," she added.
Paris police say 110,000 protesters on Saturday in 'City of Lights'
Paris police say 110,000 protesters were on the streets in the city on Saturday. The anti-government "Yellow Vest" movementteamed up with aggrieved school students for this round of demonstrations.
The CGT trade union, meanwhile, said 800,000 participated in protests across France, with 250,000 people taking part in Paris.
Saturday's protesters were limited by Parisian authorities to the city's southeastern edge, away from the center.
Authorities prepared to help the protesters march safely from the Place d'Italie in the 13th arrondissement on the left bank of the Seine River to Porte de Vincennes which lies further away on the right bank.
A post on X by Paris Police Prefecture showed the Porte d'Italie from the sky ahead of the march.
French news agency AFP reported clashes in Paris after the demonstrations.
French use tear gas at protests in Lyon, Lille, Toulouse and Nantes
The French police used tear gas in response to protests in the southeastern city of Lyon. Use of tear gas was also reported in the cities of Lille, Toulouse and Nantes.
Protests against Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally in Orleans
In Orleans, south of Paris, protesters also came out to the streets against a two-day congress held in the city of Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party.
According to polls, Le Pen is the frontrunner in France's presidential elections next year.

====================================================================================================

Neuroscientists are digging into a worrying link between polluted air and children’s brain wiring
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:00:49 UTC
21:00:49 KST

Different sources of fine particle air pollution show distinct, subtle links to how the developing brains of children communicate, according to new nationwide research published in Journal of Environmental Psychology. Particles from traffic, coal burning, and agricultural fertilizers were each tied to their own patterns of connectivity in networks involved in sensory processing and higher-order thinking. The findings offer early evidence that where air pollution comes from may matter, not just how much of it children breathe.
Outdoor air pollution contains fine particulate matter, commonly known as PM2.5, which consists of airborne particles smaller than 2.5 micrometers across. Because these specks are tiny enough to inhale deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, they may reach the brain.
The brain coordinates its activities through large-scale functional networks, which are collections of brain regions in different locations whose activity tends to rise and fall together. Researchers can measure this synchrony with brain scans that track changes in blood flow while a person lies still and rests. During childhood and the transition into adolescence, these communication channels continue to reorganize as youth develop adult reasoning, sensory integration, and emotional control.
Past research has linked outdoor air pollution to differences in these communication patterns. In a 2023 longitudinal study, members of the team behind the new research used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study, a large national project following thousands of American youth. They found that children with higher exposure to fine particles and other pollutants showed differences in how their resting brain networks matured across early adolescence. Additionally, a study covered by PsyPost in 2023 found that briefly breathing diesel exhaust in a controlled experiment temporarily weakened connectivity within the default mode network, a set of regions most active during mind-wandering and self-reflection, in adults.
Fine particulate matter is not a single chemical substance, but rather a complex blend created by both natural processes and human activities. Addressing this complexity, a 2024 study by members of the same team, using data from the same national project, found that specific chemical ingredients and pollution sources had varying relationships with children’s memory and thinking skills. The new study uses the six pollution sources identified in that work. The investigation was led by Katherine L. Bottenhorn of the University of Southern California and Florida International University and Megan M. Herting of the University of Southern California.
For the new study, the authors again drew on data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study, which spans 21 research sites across the country. Data from one site were dropped because of hardware problems, leaving 20 sites for the cross-sectional analysis; the longitudinal analysis was limited to the 12 sites that used the same brand of scanner. The researchers analyzed brain scans from 6,291 children who were between 9 and 11 years old, as well as a subset of 1,972 participants scanned on consistent magnetic resonance imaging equipment roughly two years later, between ages 11 and 13.
The participants’ resting-state brain activity was recorded while they relaxed with their eyes open. The scientists mapped interactions among 12 functional networks, encompassing primary sensory networks like vision and hearing, attention circuits, and higher-order systems. The salience network helps flag important events and shift attention, while the cingulo-opercular network, described here as a cognitive-control network, helps keep attention on a task.
The team used annual air quality models tied to each child’s home address to estimate their exposure to 15 chemical components of air pollution during 2016. By grouping these chemicals mathematically, the authors estimated exposure to six primary sources: crustal materials (such as soil and dust), ammonium sulfates (largely from coal combustion), biomass burning (such as wood smoke and wildfires), traffic emissions, ammonium nitrates (often linked to agricultural fertilizers), and industrial fuel combustion.
The researchers applied a machine learning method called connectome-based predictive modeling to identify connectivity patterns related to each pollution source. To see if the results could generalize across the country, the scientists trained models using participants from all study sites except one, and then tested how well that model predicted pollution levels for children living at the held-out site. The analyses adjusted for several potential confounding variables, including household income, race and ethnicity, perceived neighborhood safety, neighborhood population density, distance to major roads, urbanicity, physical activity, screen time, scanner hardware, and head movement inside the scanner.
The cross-sectional analysis at ages 9 to 11 identified consistent links between specific pollution sources and connectivity across sensory and motor networks. Greater exposure to traffic emissions related to weaker functional communication between visual and mouth-related motor networks, as well as between auditory and cognitive-control circuits. In contrast, higher exposure to ammonium sulfates was linked to stronger communication between sensory systems and higher-order cognitive networks, including the default mode network. Crustal materials, industrial fuel burning, and total particulate matter were each tied to a handful of sensory and attention-related connections, while biomass burning showed no consistent pattern at ages 9 to 11.
Higher-order networks, which are involved in introspective thought, stimulus processing, and, according to some researchers, vulnerability to mental health problems, were also tied to specific pollution sources. Exposure to ammonium nitrates was associated with stronger communication between salience and cognitive-control networks, but weaker communication within memory networks and between attention networks and other networks.
Over the following two years, the researchers found consistent patterns of change linked to three sources. Higher traffic exposure was tied to increasing connectivity over time between hand-movement networks and attention-related areas, but decreasing connectivity between auditory and cognitive-control networks. Higher biomass burning exposure was linked to increasing connectivity among attention-related networks, and higher ammonium sulfate exposure to weakening connectivity between an attention network and a hand-movement network, while crustal materials, ammonium nitrates, industrial fuel burning, and total particulate matter showed no consistent pattern of change.
Despite identifying consistent connections in the training data, the connectivity patterns accounted for less than 1 percent of the variation in children’s exposure at ages 9 to 11, and no more than about 2 percent for changes over time. When tested on children from held-out study sites, the models performed no better, and often worse, than simply guessing the average exposure. Prediction errors were largest at sites in the western United States and at sites where exposure levels varied more from child to child.
The authors concluded that, after accounting for other factors, these pollution sources likely play only a small role in differences in brain connectivity between children, and that the links may not apply to youth in other regions. They also note that the patterns for biomass burning and ammonium sulfates held up best across sites, while those for crustal materials and traffic emissions deserve more caution.
The findings are in line with a study covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which found that young teenagers exposed to elevated particulate pollution showed less brain network maturation over two years, though that previous research evaluated an overall brain maturity score rather than connectivity across specific functional networks and distinct pollution sources.
“This is an important and timely topic, and the paper complements a growing body of evidence that children’s physical environments in general, and air pollution exposure in particular, are associated with their neural and cognitive development,” said Monica Rosenberg, an associate professor of psychology at the University of Chicago, director of the Cognition, Attention, and Brain Lab, and a co-developer of the brain-modeling technique used in the study, who was not involved in the research.
“The longitudinal aspect of this work is unique and is a major strength—the authors didn’t just show associations between brain networks and pollution at a single time point but found that pollution predicts developmental trajectories of networks,” Rosenberg told PsyPost.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The study used observational data and statistical associations, meaning it cannot establish that breathing these specific particles directly caused the observed network differences. Because the research took place across many regions with varying environmental mixtures, local factors that were unmeasured might account for some of the geographic discrepancies.
The authors also did not apply a statistical correction for the many connections they tested at once, so some of the identified links could be false positives, and the analysis was exploratory, with no advance predictions about which networks would be affected. Because each study site used scanners from a single manufacturer, differences between regions cannot be fully separated from differences in scanning equipment.
Rosenberg noted that the geographic inconsistency represents an important caveat for understanding the results. “One caveat is that the primary predictive models did not successfully generalize across sites, meaning that associations between brain network patterns and air pollution were inconsistent across geographic locations,” she said. “In addition to the thorough analyses presented in the paper, it would be interesting to test whether the observed brain changes were associated with cognitive and/or attentional performance since the implications of neural changes alone aren’t always clear.”
Another caveat involves how exposure was measured. The researchers assigned air pollution levels based on each child’s home address during a single year, which does not capture personal daily habits such as indoor air filtration, ventilation, daily travel routes, or time spent exercising outdoors. In addition, the participants in this nationwide study were somewhat more likely to come from higher-income and non-Hispanic white households than the national average, and average particulate exposures across the sample were below current federal limits. Future studies will need to follow youth through later adolescence to evaluate whether these source-specific network patterns correspond with tangible differences in sensory function, attention, or mental health outcomes.
The study, “Sources of outdoor air pollution exposure and child brain network development across the United States,” was authored by Katherine L. Bottenhorn, Kirthana Sukumaran, Amanda C. Del Giacco, Hedyeh Ahmadi, Jordan D. Corbett, Alethea V. de Jesus, Carlos Cardenas-Iniguez, Rima Habre, Daniel A. Hackman, Joel Schwartz, Jiu-Chiuan Chen, and Megan M. Herting.

Interest rates unlikely to reach 4.75% by next summer, say City economists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:00:05 UTC
21:00:05 KST

Financial markets are wrong to predict the Bank of England will raise UK interest rates by a full percentage point or more by next summer, City economists believe.
According to market-implied interest rate expectations, the Bank is likely to raise interest rates at least four times over the next year, lifting the bank rate from 3.75% today to 4.75% by the end of July, and possibly to 5% – meaning five rises – by December 2027.
But a number of City experts believe such a sharp tightening cycle is unlikely, given there is little sign that the rise in energy costs is pushing up other prices sharply.
“If you look at the swaps market, and you look at what’s priced in for the Bank of England, you’ve got four rate hikes and then no cuts ever. And I think you’d be hard-pressed to find anybody that really agrees with that,” said James Smith, a developed markets economist at the Dutch bank ING.
“By next spring, I think they [the Bank] could be sounding the all clear, and by the end of next year they could be cutting rates again,” Smith told a briefing in the City last week.
Market-implied interest rates are calculated from the prices of a range of financial instruments, including derivatives such as “swaps”, to establish where traders think interest rates will be in future.
Economists cite several reasons why market-implied interest rates expectations are high. One is that these expectations have been closely correlated with oil prices since the Iran war began.
The higher oil prices have risen, the more rate increases have been priced in. An investor could be right that interest rates won’t rise as far as markets think, but if oil prices keep increasing in the meantime, they would face mark-to-market losses and potentially margin calls.
“It can get pretty painful, so a lot of traders are quite reluctant to take this risk until there’s greater certainty about energy supply and the extent of inflation this winter,” said Smith.
Many traders got burnt at the start of the current Middle East crisis, when most were positioned for further rate cuts this year, he said.
Sanjay Raja, the chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, also doubts that the Bank will raise rates as fast as the market pricing suggests.
“I do not believe that any mainstream forecaster thinks the Bank of England will hike to 5% by the end of next year with the information set we have today,” Raja said. “It’s not to say it won’t happen. But based on current projections, it seems less likely.”
He has calculated that a lot of the forecast interest rate rises is actually “baked-in risk premia” – where investors require an extra return to protect them from uncertainty or instability.
“Once we strip that out, we have estimated that there is only really ~50bps [half a percentage point] of hikes pencilled in,” he said.
Deutsche Bank’s base case is for the Bank of England to take the bank rate to 4.25% by next February and then hold rates there until the end of 2027.
The Bank of England is widely expected to raise interest rates to 4% at its next meeting, on 5 November, after UK inflation rose further above its target in September to 3.5%.
Last month Goldman Sachs said its probability-weighted forecast path for the bank rate remained “notably below market pricing”, although it does expect the Bank to raise rates to 4% next month.
Morgan Stanley’s base case is for rises in November and February, with rates on hold thereafter. But in a new research note, it suggests there could be additional pressure to raise interest rates if the Low Pay Commission recommends a larger increase in the national living wage than expected.
Oxford Economics, a consultancy, also thinks the UK rate-raising cycle will be much less pronounced than what is currently priced into financial markets.
“We forecast the [Bank’s] monetary policy committee will raise interest rates by 25bps [a quarter of a percentage point] at its November and February meetings, taking the bank rate to 4.25%. This is significantly below the peak in money market expectations, which currently point to the bank rate peaking between 4.75% and 5%,” they told clients last week.
Even Huw Pill, the Bank’s hawkish chief economist, has suggested market expectations are running too hot. He told an International Monetary Fund meeting in Bangkok this month he was sceptical that the Bank would need to raise interest rates four times over the next year.
