This comedian jokes about deportation from Ireland … but it is happening for real
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

Jaishree Malik bounds on to the Cheeky Monkey comedy club stage and brandishes an envelope – it is a letter from the Irish government. Would the audience like to hear what’s in the letter?
“Yeah,” the first rows reply. She repeats the question, prompting a louder response. “Yeah!”
Malik extracts typed A4 pages and begins to read. “I wish to advise you that under section 3 of the immigration act 1999, the minister for justice, home affairs and migration is proposing to make a deportation order in your case.”
A nervous laugh ripples across the audience, then there’s a pause. “Oh,” says someone.
Malik beams. “Don’t worry, it’s not for you.” She resumes reading. “The reason for this is because you have remained in the state without permission […] you are therefore a person whose deportation would, in the minister’s opinion, be conducive to the common good.”
For the audience in the basement of the International bar in central Dublin, the penny drops: the letter is real. Malik, 25, is facing deportation to her native India.
“Did you know you were friends with a criminal?” she asks. “I’m sorry you had to find out this way.” She cracks a few more jokes, then: “In case you can’t tell, I’m fucking furious about this.” She concludes her set to whoops and applause.
Malik may be the only immigrant in Ireland to turn her own deportation order into comedy but plenty of others share her anger at a system they say has become harsh and arbitrary.
The Irish government has toughened border enforcement and rules on migration, asylum and naturalisation amid a housing shortage and strain on public services partly attributed to immigration. Placards at anti-immigration protests declare that “Ireland is full”.
The justice minister, Jim O’Callaghan, has said the authorities wish to curb population growth that is seven times the EU average. Critics say the welcome mat has been withdrawn unfairly from deserving cases, including students from Gaza denied visas despite scholarship offers from Irish universities.
Others, such as Malik, have had visa renewal and extension requests delayed and denied despite job offers. “It’s Kafkaesque. Why would I read The Trial? I’m living it,” she said in an interview, referencing the novel about a protagonist pitted against unreasoning bureaucracy.
From Gurgaon, near Dehli, Malik moved to Ireland in 2022 on a student visa to pursue an M.Phil (Master of Philosophy) in literature at Trinity College Dublin. She had a job on campus during her studies advising prospective and current students. After graduating she obtained a visa that let her stay and work for two years through the Third Level Graduate Scheme and continued working at Trinity with international exchange students.
She moved to another job in Trinity and applied to the department of justice to extend her visa, pending confirmation of a new one, but a delay in processing the application led to Malik losing that job in February and entering legal limbo. The department told her she had no right to work while the application was being processed.
She submitted additional information to bolster her case and, while awaiting a ruling, subsisted on savings and channelled her anxiety at open mic comedy nights. Malik had dabbled in comedy at Trinity but never previously performed around the city.
“Your best material comes when your life is falling apart. But the first time I was so scared. I was reading bits from my phone. It wasn’t landing very well, I didn’t know where to pause. But I got a lot of good feedback. All the comedians were absolutely lovely.”
Malik refined her act and incorporated her exasperation when the department of public works offered a job that she could not accept because of the visa imbroglio. “It’s so absurd. I’m being offered a job by the government that I can’t take because of the government.”
Some audiences think she is playing a character, she said. “They come up to me and say, ‘Oh, that’s so funny’. Then I explain and they’re like, ‘Oh wait, it’s actually real?’”
Ivana Bacik, a legislator and leader of the Labour party, said Malik’s case reflected a hardening of immigration policy. “It’s impacting on lots of people and indeed lots of employers because they’re losing good people.”
The department of justice was using “spurious reasons” to deny visas to Gaza students, said Bacik. “I believe there’s much more compassion and warmth towards inward migration among Irish communities and it’s not reflected in the ministry’s approach.”
A group that represents the Gaza students said the “breakdown” started this summer. “We were refused for documents we were never asked to provide, such as a bank statement and proof of intention to return,” it said in an emailed statement. “We were then told to appeal with original documents by post, and as you know, Gaza is destroyed and there is no postal service.” The students have taken test cases to Ireland’s high court.
A department of justice spokesperson said he could not comment on the court cases but that screening and verification were integral to the immigration system and that there had been no change in policy towards Palestinian students. “Each visa application is assessed on its own merits.”
For Malik, the battle to remain in Ireland ended with the deportation letter sent on 5 October. She will leave next month but continue performing until the end.
“I am very angry but when I get up on stage and I make people laugh, it sort of disarms the anger and the political stuff. If I can go up there and make you laugh about something so powerful it makes it less powerful and it becomes the joke. That is the jester’s privilege.”
Ireland is not immune to xenophobia and racism but audiences have been supportive, said Malik. “I’m talking about visas, yes, but under this I am still a person. I’ve made a lot of Irish friends who are basically family and they’re all outraged on my behalf.”
She has not fully absorbed the fact she must leave, she said. “I don’t think it’ll hit me until I’m on the plane.” She is bracing for “reverse culture shock” once back in India.
In the meantime, Malik is preparing to shed her possessions, close her bank account and pack before heading in the early hours of 14 November to Dublin airport. “My flatmate drives and she’s offered to take me even though it’s a very inconvenient time. That’s a very good flatmate. Shout out to the flatmate.”

They wallow in Trump gunk 24/7. They say it’s necessary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

For a couple of journalists who spend such an inordinate amount of time sloshing around the putrid inner recesses of Donald Trump’s mind, they come across as remarkably chipper.
Michael Wolff, chronicler of the 45th and 47th president, and Joanna Coles, chief creative and content officer of the Daily Beast, are just about to record the 168th episode of their runaway podcast, Inside Trump’s Head. Now in its 15th month, the thrice-weekly show is attracting an expanding audience as it digs down into Trump’s unique blend of megalomania, narcissism and insatiable lust for fame.
We are sitting in Coles’s office on the fifth floor of the IAC building, the shiplike Frank Gehry structure in Manhattan where the Daily Beast is headquartered. Coles, dressed sharply as you would expect from a former mentor on Project Runway in snakeskin shoes, jeans and white jacket, is having her trademark shock of white hair groomed for camera.
Wolff, who has styled himself more in the mould of a country gentleman in sumptuous brown corduroy suit (of which more later), seizes on the hair arranging to unleash his own trademark: the Wolff monologue.
“I don’t have any hair,” he laments. “I used to. You should see the author photo of my first book – I looked like a 70s porn star, heavy moustache and heavy hair. All gone now …”
The pair are fond of ending each other’s sentences. And they bicker a lot, like those long-married couples in When Harry Met Sally. “Do be quiet!” Coles snaps at him in a mock schoolma’am’s voice. “She really was a kind of pest,” he snipes back, recalling the early days of their friendship.
Underneath the crotchety patina, though, it’s clear they adore each other.
In the fickle world of Trump-focused media, the Daily Beast’s podcast seems to be enjoying an enduring appeal. Since its launch in August 2025, its audience in audio form has tripled to 1.5m downloads a month, while it now exceeds 5m monthly full-episode views on YouTube. The lion’s share of its supporters are in the US, but it also has a healthy following in Canada, the UK and Australia.
Part cod psychology, part celebrity gossip, part Shakespearean tragedy, the podcast leads us to places that more traditional Trump reporting rarely goes. The title is indicative. As Coles puts it, “we go deep into the dark matter inside Trump’s head”.
The 168th episode, whose recording I attend, takes in Trump’s belligerent UN general assembly speech happening that day and his later fawning reception of China’s President Xi Jinping. But it is fair to say that fans of the podcast don’t come to it for geopolitical analysis.
An average episode will delve into such matters as: the defenestration of senior women in his administration, including the short-lived press secretary Katie Zacharia and ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle; Trump’s weight (they call him the “all-you-can-eat president”); Melania’s mysterious disappearing act (Wolff and the first lady have form, having locked horns in a long-running legal dispute); and the outsized role of executive assistant Natalie Harp, whom Wolff flagged as an issue well before the White House correspondents’ pack.
They have also tackled the portentous question: does the president wear diapers? “There was no odor that surrounded him,” Wolff revealed in one show, drawing on his olfactory reporting skills from when he trailed after Trump during the 2024 presidential campaign.
There is no mincing of words in the pod, no on-the-one-hand-this-on-the-other-hand-that. Coles brings the sharpness of her Fleet Street training to bear in analysing Trump, as well as her skills as a forensic interviewer well-versed in the seamier side of celebrity lifestyles. Wolff can inject the observations of a book and magazine writer and the knowledge he gained from the extraordinary access given to him at the start of the era, when he was invited to spend weeks inside the first Trump White House.
His language on the podcast is spicy. Wolff has variously described Trump on air as “that fat fucker” and a “fucking asshole”, while Coles likes to highlight what she is convinced is the president’s declining mental faculties.
Trump’s top team returns fire with equal gusto. Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, has on umpteen occasions slammed Wolff as “a lying sack of shit” and a “fraud”, while Coles is a “retard” and a “blithering idiot”.
Faced with such blowback, the duo are unapologetic about their choice of subjects or words, dismissing Cheung’s attacks as “performative”. “We talk how people talk, about their friends, about their bosses,” Coles says. “We are not trying to put a glass wall between us and politicians, we’re trying to understand them as people.”
Trump has often claimed that he has made a fortune for the “fake news” media, and such bragging would appear fair comment when it comes to Inside Trump’s Head. Coles estimates that a third of the Daily Beast’s content and traffic is entirely dependent on him.
As for Wolff, Trump has been a veritable cash cow. According to Forbes, Wolff made $13m just in the first year of Fire and Fury. Will he say exactly how much he has profited from all four books?
He hesitates, then says, “No.”
Coles, true to form, finishes his sentence. “Well, you have made a lot of money,” she says. “There’s your 18th-century mansion in Amagansett.”
“It’s 19th-century,” he retorts. “And it’s a farmhouse.”
“What about your hand-sewn Savile Row suit, it’s Anderson & Sheppard isn’t it?” she presses, referring to that sumptuous brown corduroy affair he is sporting.
Wolff silently concurs. A bespoke Anderson & Sheppard suit, as worn by King Charles and Daniel Craig, can easily set you back $9,000.
The podcast’s unashamed technique of examining Trump in the round, with all his personal flaws and foibles, is not without its critics. The New York Times columnist Frank Bruni last month wrote an opinion piece that berated media outlets that focus on Trump’s appearance rather than on the damage he is doing to the world. Though he didn’t mention the podcast, Bruni did mention “cankles”, a Daily Beast favourite.
When I raise the Bruni argument – that what matters is Trump’s anti-democratic actions not his inner psychology – it sparks off another Wolff monologue.
“Trump is the most unique politician anyone has come across,” he says. “He’s so unique no political reporter can cover him. That’s our conceit: to probe what the traditional media is not covering. They cover Trump as they would an ordinary politician, and his politics as an ordinary function of cause and effect. But Trump is completely outside of the familiar ecosystem of the presidency.”
He’s only half done. “You can analyse Trump’s policies all you like, but what he is doing has nothing to do with policy. It has everything to do with himself, with his self-aggrandizement. To understand him, you have to look at his character, how this guy thinks, what are his fundamental motivations.”
The seeds of Inside Trump’s Head can be traced back to the start of Wolff’s decade-long engagement with its subject. The two men had some contact in the early 2000s when Wolff was writing a media column for New York magazine, but it was not until May 2016 that he and Trump went head-to-head.
In the course of an interview during Trump’s first White House bid, Wolff asked him why he was running for president. Trump replied: “To be the most famous man in the world.”
Wolff recalls: “I thought at that moment, my God! This is going to be a trip.”
Ever since that exchange Wolff has been on an epic voyage of discovery to get to the bottom of Trump’s bottomless desire for fame. “It’s not just a character flaw that he craves all this attention. It has become Trump’s strategy. ‘How do I stay the most famous person in the world?’ That is literally the question he asks himself when he wakes up every day.”
Trump’s attention-seeking is one of the central themes of the four books that Wolff has written about him – starting with the bestseller Fire and Fury that took readers into the chaos of Trump 1.0, and most recently last year’s All or Nothing that marked his return to office. It is also what inspired Coles to create Inside Trump’s Head as part of her plan to reinvigorate the Daily Beast after Barry Diller, the billionaire chairof IAC, invited her and Ben Sherwood to take over its helm in 2024.
Coles and Wolff have been friends for 25 years, after she left her West Yorkshire roots and relocated as a Guardian reporter from London to New York. It was Wolff who gave her a leg up into American media, helping her leave the Times of London to which she had defected and secure an editing job at New York magazine.
(This seems a reasonable moment to make a full personal disclosure. I have been friends with Coles since we worked together in the Guardian newsroom in London in the 1990s. I have also known Wolff since I myself moved to New York for the Guardian in 2006, and I have on occasion written about him. The last time I did so I reported on the Trump-related interviews he conducted with Jeffrey Epstein, during which Wolff gave the convicted sex offender PR advice on how to handle the scandal spiraling around him. Wolff emailed me having read the piece. “Jesus, Ed, you’re a nitwit,” he said.)
The Coles-Wolff friendship hasn’t always been easy. They’ve had intermittent feuds along the way, in which they have avoided speaking to each other for a couple of years, though neither can remember why. “I feud with a lot of people,” Wolff concedes.
I wonder what price the two of them are paying for what they are doing. There are many journalists who have covered Trump for the past 10 years, myself included, who know only too well the toll it takes on one’s mental health, repeatedly grappling with his lies and darkness. But few have devoted themselves to the task as round-the-clock as they have. In one podcast, Wolff admits: “There are very few conversations I ever have that are not about Donald Trump.”
What’s the collateral damage of all that wallowing in Trump gunk?
“Good question,” Wolff says. “I would fall back on that, as a writer, to get this story, to get this character, is once in a lifetime. You have the opportunity to have a voice in history. You don’t walk away from this so readily.”
“I’m British, so I don’t even think about my mental health,” Coles quips in that schoolma’am’s voice. She carries on: “We are at a pivotal moment for the global world order. Growing up in Europe, in the shadow of the second world war, you had tremendous confidence in America as an ally. All that is changing because of one man. I would feel depressed if I weren’t trying to understand this as much as I can.”
With the midterm elections fast approaching, the tone and focus of the podcast is inevitably shifting towards Lame Duck Trump. Aren’t they worried that we are nearing the end of this extraordinary epoch, of the “government of one” as they like to frame it, and the journalistic riches it brings?
Coles puts on a brave face. “We are interested in people and power. Whatever comes next will be interesting, because Trump has blown off the doors and allowed us to see inside the mechanics of power, and you can’t put the doors back on.”
The last question I direct to Wolff. Having sacrificed (at great personal gain) 10 years of his life to Trump, can he see the US, the world, ever recovering from this trauma? Will we ever be post-Trump?
“We’re going to get to the other side of this, yes,” he says, beginning his final monologue. “I absolutely believe that the unique Donald Trump will not come again. When he leaves, everyone is going to sigh with relief, even the Republicans.”
He’s not done yet.
“It’s a fascinating thing. Nobody, except his fanbase, likes this guy. I mean, Trump is a fat fuck, even to those closest to him.”

U-turn on EV policy could stall UK’s take-up of EVs | Fiona Harvey and Jasper Jolly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

Electric cars make people happy. More than nine in 10 EV drivers – 94% in a recent poll – are saving money, and a similar number would stick with electric for their next purchase, and recommend them to family and friends. Sales are soaring: more than half of the new cars sold in the UK last month were electric, if hybrids are taken into account, and about 28% of new car sales overall were electric only.
This is hardly surprising, given that soaring petrol and diesel costs have pushed up the price of a full tank to about £120. EV drivers are paying about 2.4p a mile.
Why then is the government considering a major U-turn on electric vehicle policy that, if followed through, could stall the take-up of EVs, help to close off a route to lower living costs, and dent the UK’s ability to meet its carbon targets?
Andy Burnham, the prime minister, wrote in the Guardian this week that he would push ahead with the target of reaching net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Despite the go-ahead for the Jackdaw gasfield this week, sources in government also hinted to the Guardian that another large project, the Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland, was less likely to be greenlighted.
However, analysis from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) thinktank, seen by the Guardian, shows that the looming decision on the future of electric vehicles could also have a major impact on net zero and carbon budgets, though it has received far less attention.
Under the zero emissions vehicle mandate, all new cars and vans sold from 2035 must be fully electric, with interim targets for 80% of new cars and 70% of new vans to be ZEVs by 2030.
The end goal of 2035 is likely to remain, but under a consultation that ended on Friday, the 2030 targets could be weakened to 70% or even as low as 50% of new cars. Taken with previous watering down of the policy to allow more sales of hybrid cars – which use both electric and combustion engines – that change would lead to emissions greater than burning all the gas in the Jackdaw field, according to the ECIU.
If the mandate were cut more drastically to require only 50% of sales to be EVs by 2030, this could mean an additional 147 megatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, which would equate to about 58% of the likely emissions from burning the oil produced by the Rosebank field.
Jess Ralston, an analyst at the ECIU, said weakening the target would not solve the problems for manufacturers, who are already facing intensified competition from China as increasing numbers of people opt for EVs. It would also not benefit the public because EVs can be £1,750 a year cheaper to run, and potentially more with oil prices rising.
“With climate concern high among the public after extreme heat and persisting drought, and public support for net zero up above two-thirds, a decision to U-turn could look very odd,” Ralston said. “Ministers have talked about getting families off the fossil fuel rollercoaster – this would be the opposite, locking in higher driving costs, more air pollution and higher carbon emissions.”
Burnham faces a further complication: in 2024, the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese EVs, and now wants to limit public subsidies to vehicles made in Europe, under pressure from European carmakers. If Burnham wants closer integration with the EU, and more favourable trade terms, he may be forced to slap matching tariffs on Chinese imports to the UK. This would raise the cost of EVs in the UK and cut off one route to lower living costs.
If fully implemented as originally planned, the ZEV mandate could be the largest single carbon-saving measure the government has yet proposed, according to previous research. But after intensive lobbying from carmakers for a weakening, Labour MPs are deeply divided.
Car manufacturers in the UK have been slow to retool their plants to EVs, and some have pursued hybrid vehicles instead. Many analysts consider hybrids, which combine a polluting petrol engine and a smaller battery, a technological dead end. By contrast, China has rapidly ramped up its EV manufacturing, and now dominates the global market, producing about three-quarters of all EVs. Sales of EVs have soared, now making up about a quarter of all new car sales around the world.
Some Labour MPs in constituencies with car plants side with the manufacturers, while others argue that with petrol prices soaring and unlikely to abate, EVs are a way to lower the cost of living and get Britain off the fossil fuel hook.
Chris Hinchliff, Labour MP for North East Hertfordshire, told the Guardian: “Weakening the EV target would be another nail in the coffin of a livable future.”
Barry Gardiner, Labour MP for Brent West and former environment minister, said a U-turn would hurt forward-looking companies and favour laggards. “Watering down the mandate means that good companies, who moved straight away to comply, feel they have been unfairly burdened with additional costs while their lazy competitors have sneaked an advantage,” he said. “Government flip-flops are a huge problem for business. State the regulation clearly and then stick to it. Business will then adapt and do what it does best because it knows it has a level playing field.”
A government spokesperson said: “We are reviewing the ZEV mandate to ensure it continues to support British industry and investment, and no decisions have been taken. Crucially, the end goal has not changed – we will phase out all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and be fully zero emission by 2035, and remain committed to our legally binding net zero targets.”
Consumer research shows the 2 million people currently driving EVs in the UK tend to like them: polling by the Electric Vehicle Association found 94% of EV drivers reported they were saving money compared with petrol or diesel cars. A similar number would stay electric for their next car, and recommend an EV to friends or family.

As a young man, magazines were my window to the world. That wonder will be lost when all the shops have gone | John Harris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

Towards the end of the 1970s, the brief but spectacular career of those punk rockers and folk devils the Sex Pistols was followed by The Great Rock’n’Roll Swindle, a rather tawdry drama-documentary. It recast their rise and fall as a huge scam, summed up by a slogan on a T-shirt worn by their former manager Malcolm McLaren: “Cash from Chaos”.
Back then, that motto was a neat representation of his personal brand of cultural mischief. But the culture always takes unexpected twists and turns – and 50 years on, an almost-identical maxim seems to be defining the fate of an increasing chunk of the British retail economy. While Andy Burnham pledges to restore life to town centres, a private equity outfit is busy buying up national retail chains and then shutting down scores of their outlets, while seemingly operating in line with its boss’s most celebrated quotation: “Where there’s chaos, there’s opportunity.”
Those words came from Jamie Constable, the owner of a set of businesses that includes Modella Capital, which specialises in “distressed investing” and “aggressive restructuring”. In 2024, Modella bought the craft supplies chain Hobbycraft – insisting on its “real commitment to bricks-and-mortar retail”, but then shutting 18 shops and triggering 600 job losses, while leaving redundancy costs to the taxpayer. Months later, it acquired the discount outlets branded as The Original Factory Shop, only for the entire chain to collapse. But its most ambitious move was its recent purchase of the 480 high-street shops that previously traded as WH Smith, rebranded by Modella as TG Jones (a completely made-up name, which it said would “keep that sense of a family business”), and the rapidly announced closure of up to 150 of them.
In September, 19 branches breathed their last, in such varied locations as Bath, Southend, Cardigan, Redhill and the Essex new town of Basildon. This month, the shutters are permanently falling in – among 23 places – Pinner, Truro, Inverness and Leek in Staffordshire. Thanks to their shortsighted folding into previous WH Smith premises, the closure plan will inevitably mean the loss of many local post offices: by early 2027, 70 will have gone. It will inevitably accelerate the decline of printed newspapers. But for me and many others, the key tragedy in this story is all about magazines, those gloriously tactile creations that played a crucial role in making many of us who we are.
I say that as someone who fell in love with this form of publishing as a child, via a weekly educational magazine called Look and Learn – stuffed, as I recall, with comic-strip versions of Dickens stories, and stuff about space exploration. By my early teens, I was an avid reader of Sounds, the Melody Maker and NME, the so-called weekly music papers that were really magazines whose ink came off on your fingers. Much to my amazement, between my 19th and 26th birthdays, I ended up successively working for all three – until, in 1995, I joined the now defunct company Emap Metro, which set enormous store by its mastery of glossy fortnightlies and monthlies.
Some of these names may mean precious little to younger readers, but spark a Proustian rush among older ones: Q, Smash Hits, Select (which I edited for three years), Sky, the metal and hard rock title Kerrang!, Big, Neon, FHM. Most have now closed, but three of the old stable are still standing, under different ownership: Kerrang!, which mostly lives online; the film bible Empire; and Mojo, the lovingly produced music magazine that I am thrilled to still write for.
Thirty years ago, we all knew that there was no better medium for in-depth interviews, or high-end photography. The management constantly asked us who our intended reader was, and what the future was likely to entail. Even the smallest cover-lines were pored over, as if the mere mention of Placebo or DJ Shadow might attract scores of newbies. And though a lot of us didn’t listen, we were told to never, ever put our magazines in sealed plastic bags (which, in line with a longstanding convention, would contain “free gifts”), for fear of losing the kind of punter who liked to browse before they bought.
And therein lies the TG Jones tragedy. The business has rightly acquired an utterly grim reputation, but is – or was – one reliable place to still find shelves full of printed content worthy of endless curiosity. And now? The culturally omnivorous twentysomething in Rickmansworth will no longer chance upon the latest edition of the cutting-edge music monthly the Wire, and thereby be inducted into a world of esoteric electronica and contemporary avant-garde jazz. The student-age customer in Ormskirk tiring of production-line pop may know nothing of the more substantial music covered by Mojo’s excellent competitor Uncut.
Would-be radicals will be unable to browse the printed iteration of Tribune; film freaks may be completely unaware of the in-depth, art-house wonders of Sight and Sound. Publishers will fall over themselves to alert us to subscription offers, but for a lot of people, they will be prohibitively expensive.
As George Orwell once put it, the UK is “a nation of stamp-collectors, pigeon-fanciers, amateur carpenters, coupon-snippers, darts-players, crossword-puzzle fans”. Products that reflect that enduring aspect of our national character are still at the core of magazine publishing, and why some titles still sell enviably: at the last count, for example, BBC Gardeners’ World sold a monthly average of 164,807 copies, while Country Living shifted 107,596. The broad women’s and fashion sector is also still here. It isn’t all over, by any means.
Still, one can easily imagine a Mark Zuckerberg-esque voice scoffing at all this as so much stone-age nonsense, and claiming that what printed magazines deliver can easily be either replicated or superseded on the internet. Experience often suggests otherwise: witness the fate of the once-independent online music magazine Pitchfork, bought out by the corporate publisher Condé Nast in 2015 and bizarrely folded into the workings of the men’s title GQ nine years later: a classic case of what we now know as enshittification. But there is an even bigger point here about how we now engage with the things we like and love, summarised in a forthcoming book titled Circulation: How Culture Moves in the Age of Algorithm by the Nashville-based US music insider David Macias, with a foreword written by Dan Clancy, the CEO of the livestreaming platform Twitch.
His argument is about music, but its logic applies across the cultural, recreational and sporting board. “The algorithm is great at finding me new music in the limited style I listen to,” he writes. “But it is really bad at showing me something new and different. My listening has become homogeneous, even though I can pick any album ever created.” This is the tedious prospect that the demise of the magazine will only accelerate – so after the high-street chaos has died down, we could be faced with an awful silence, broken only by the leakage from headphones playing the same things over and over again. And to speak the language of the insatiable capitalist, where will anyone find money in that?
- John Harris is a Guardian columnist

What is the £100k income ‘cliff-edge’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

Believe it or not, there are downsides to earning more than £100,000 a year – particularly if you have small children.
“It’s the ambition of many people to reach an income of £100,000, but it does come with an unexpected sting in the tail,” says Sean McCann, a chartered financial planner at NFU Mutual.
Those who make it into six figures face a 60% tax bill on some income. That is because the tax-free personal allowance starts to be taken away once you earn more than £100,000.
For every £2 of income over that, you lose £1 of the £12,570 annual tax-free personal allowance.
“This means that any earnings between £100,000 and £125,140 are effectively taxed at 60%,” says McCann. “When you add on the 2% national insurance payable, that means you only keep £38 of every £100 earned.”
An estimated 800,000 people are in this position, according to a freedom of information request by NFU Mutual.
In England, high earners also lose access to government childcare subsidies once a parent has an adjusted net income of more than £100,000 for a tax year.
As a result, a family with two young children loses roughly £30,000 of financial support if either parent earns even £1 more than the threshold, according to the investment platform AJ Bell.
There are three components to this: tax-free childcare; free hours’ childcare; and child benefit.
AJ Bell’s maths is for a family with a nine-month-old baby and a two-year-old, and puts a value of £4,000, £23,872, and £2,337 on the respective elements.
Sarah Coles, the platform’s head of personal finance, says parents “lose a big chunk” of support as soon as they hit the earnings limit: “It isn’t tapered away gradually, hence the ‘cliff-edge’ moniker.”
All entitlement to tax-free childcare (worth up to £2,000 a child a year) goes, Coles explains.
You also forgo the 30 hours funded term-time childcare for children aged nine months old to three years old, and half the 30 hours for children aged between three and four.
And at this level, all the family’s child benefit entitlement (currently £27.05 a week for your eldest or only child, and £17.90 for each additional child) is clawed back by the high-income child benefit charge (a tax “penalty” that kicks in when someone’s income exceeds £60,000).
So how many missed out on funded childcare because a parent exceeded the income threshold?
Official government data suggests that between 50,500 and 99,000 children in 2025-26. That is according to a freedom of information figures obtained by the wealth management firm Quilter. That is up sharply on just two years earlier, when it was estimated at between 15,600 and 30,800.
Zoe Wood

Scientists Trapped an Antimatter Particle for Months to Study Its Secrets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Antimatter is not known for being easy to get ahold of. That’s part of why these particles remain so cryptic. But recently, a team of physicists at Northwestern University managed to trap a single antimatter particle for months. Cooling it to temperatures near absolute zero, they could control its quantum states with great precision without even touching it. The experiment, published in Physical Review Letters, represents a breakthrough in our understanding of one of the great mysteries of physics.
In theory, antimatter should be everywhere. Mathematics predicts that every particle of matter has an equivalent antiparticle, a fact that scientists have verified experimentally. The universe should therefore contain similar amounts of both, but almost everything we observe is made up of ordinary matter, and we still don’t know why.
It is possible to produce antimatter particles in laboratories, but studying them is still incredibly difficult. When an antiparticle comes into contact with ordinary matter, the two annihilate each other and release energy. To prevent research facilities from exploding, scientists use vacuum chambers and electromagnetic fields that suspend the antiparticles in isolation. But this only partially solves the problem. Studying these particles, especially experimenting with their behavior on a quantum scale, remains challenging.
For this experiment, researchers at Northwestern trapped a positron, the antimatter counterpart of electrons. The team, led by Gerald Gabrielse, developed a device known as a single-positron quantum cyclotron, which used electric and magnetic fields to hold the positron in a vacuum at a temperature close to absolute zero. This means the antimatter particle was at its lowest energy state, allowing the researchers to induce controlled changes in its quantum behavior. Unlike other methods in particle physics, this approach didn’t destroy the particle. The researchers were therefore able to keep the single antiparticle trapped for months, allowing them to repeat measurements.
So what can taming antimatter particles actually teach us? Scientists know that matter and antimatter have very similar properties. For example, an electron and a positron have exactly the same mass, although their electric charges are opposite. However, questions still remain about exactly how similar these two forms of matter are and whether there are small differences that have gone unnoticed in experiments conducted to date.
To this end, researchers want to compare the magnetic properties of both particles. Physicists have already made very precise measurements with electrons, but achieving the same level of precision with positrons has proven more difficult. According to the American Physical Society, the new device could enable measurements of antimatter particles about 30 times more precise than scientists were capable of before.
So far, the experiment has not revealed any unexpected differences between the two particles. What the researchers have achieved is an improvement in their ability to detect these differences in antimatter particles. If future measurements find that a positron responds to magnetic fields differently than an electron, scientists would have to revise some of the laws they use to explain the behavior of matter and antimatter.
This story originally appeared in WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

‘Trump Is Cooked’: Republicans Clash Over Ukraine as Midterms Loom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:55:00 UTC
20:55:00 KST

“I think Trump is cooked in the midterms, unless literally every poll is disgustingly wrong.”
This assessment came from a Republican-adjacent Washington source speaking to Kyiv Post on condition of anonymity as US President Donald Trump’s handling of Russia’s war against Ukraine draws unusually public criticism from his own party.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I don’t think [Trump’s] efforts to scapegoat Ukraine will make that worse, but he’s also not getting away with it,” the source added. The latest sentiment comes on the heels of Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff traveling to St. Petersburg to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin for a new round of negotiations, during which he referred to Putin as a “humanitarian”. Meanwhile, Russian forces continued attacking Ukrainian cities and Kyiv reported restricted access to satellite communications essential to frontline operations and intercepting Russian drones.
For Republican commentators and politicians who had spent months pushing the Trump administration to increase pressure on Moscow, this was an unpleasant sight. They found themselves watching the US offer Russia economic relief while pressing Ukraine for concessions and restricting its defense capabilities.
Beyond immediate moral discomfort and questions on Washington’s foreign policy priorities, there’s also the practical aspect as they seek re-election during the Nov. 3 midterms. With all 435 House seats and roughly a third of the Senate contested, the Republican party’s chances of preserving a majority in both chambers risks slipping away as Trump’s approval rating continues to plunge.
Russia Open to US-Ukraine Trilateral Talks After Nov. 4
The undone MAGA momentum
In late July, conservative MAGA commentator Laura Loomer made headlines. Formerly a fierce critic of Ukraine, she traveled to Kyiv to interview President Volodymyr Zelensky, publicly acknowledging that she had repeated Russian propaganda before realizing Moscow’s support for Iran in its confrontation with Israel and the US – a circumstance that helped change her position.
This is how she became part of an emerging pro-Ukraine conservative camp alongside figures such as Ben Shapiro, who had also interviewed Zelensky, as well as Mark Levin and other prominent Trump-adjacent commentators.
For a country often presented to some Republican audiences as a burden on American taxpayers, this was a significant opening and a promising one as well, since the renewed enthusiasm reinforced the case for the sanctions championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. The logic was that if Russia would not agree to a ceasefire or a negotiated end to the war, it should face a heavier economic cost for continuing the invasion.
The momentum bore fruit: Congress passed the bill, and Trump signed it into law on Sept. 18. Key provisions were due to take effect by Oct. 18, although the legislation also gave the president broad waiver powers.
Yet what appeared to be a breakthrough soon became a full-fledged retreat.
Instead of imposing those additional penalties, Trump abruptly announced his diesel agreement with Moscow on Oct. 9.
A week later, he waived major new sanctions and duties under the Graham legislation (though leaving existing sanctions in place) and launched what Susan B. Glasser of The New Yorker coined as a pre-election campaign against Zelensky, toward whom his antipathy is long documented.
Trump blamed Ukraine’s refinery attacks for aggravating fuel shortages and suggested that a settlement would require different Ukrainian leadership, while thanking Putin for presumably being “the reasonable one” in the illegal war he started.
This time, however, the pressure went beyond personal attacks: intelligence sharing, satellite access and weapons deliveries had become part of the dispute, accompanied by a considerably more Moscow-friendly rhetoric than in spring when the US resorted to similar ways of pressuring the victim of Russia’s aggression.
Republicans push back
Glasser’s description of Trump’s actions might be easy for his supporters to dismiss as criticism from a familiar opponent. The reaction from Republicans themselves, however, was harder to explain away with freshly-converted Loomer saying: “Buying Russian oil puts money back into the coffers of the Islamic regime of Iran that chants Death to America. We know this.”
While disagreements with Zelensky, including concerns about corruption and oversight, were not unusual for many Republicans, restricting Ukraine’s ability to defend itself while offering economic relief to Russia was another.
“What is interesting is that his recent, unveiled support for Putin has finally seen some anger from Congressional Republicans,” the source told Kyiv Post, warning that some of them “are leaving office.”
Reacting to Witkoff’s salute to Putin in St. Petersburg as a “humanitarian” for releasing American detainee Stephen Hubbard, another Republican-adjacent source privately told Kyiv Post: “I so hate Witkoff.”
The anger, however, was not limited to private conversations. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis responded in very strong terms to Witkoff’s flattery, asking:: “WTF, Steve?” Separately, Sen. John Cornyn described Putin as a “stone cold killer.”
Hours after the meeting, Russia launched another attack on Kyiv.
The backlash followed strong objections to the privately-struck diesel deal. Tillis, Susan Collins and Mitch McConnell joined a bipartisan letter urging Trump to reverse the agreement, arguing that it would offer limited relief to American consumers while supplying revenue to Moscow.
Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, standing for reelection in Pennsylvania’s 1st Congressional District pursued legislation to block Russian energy purchases. European governments also rejected following Washington’s lead on sanctions relief.
Then came the reports of restrictions on intelligence and satellite communications that only served to intensify the tensions on Capitol Hill.
Zelensky said on Oct. 20 that US intelligence sharing had resumed. Satellite access took longer to improve: restrictions on SpaceX’s Starlink and defense-tailored Starshield services had disrupted connections on fast-moving equipment, including Ukrainian drones.
On Oct. 24, Ukrainian defense specialists reported that terminals were operating above the previous 161 km/h limit. Later that morning, Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara reported stable connections above 400 km/h.
But Patriot interceptor deliveries remained delayed, according to Zelensky’s remarks reported that day. Restored intelligence and communications did not resolve the shortage of missiles needed to intercept Russian attacks.
For Republicans seeking re-election, these developments leave an awkward question to answer: what has Washington attained by this and how it does affect them?
Trump vs. American voters
Despite the existing notion among some that the Republicans are Russia-friendly, the evidence paints a different picture.
Earlier Pew polling found that 47% of Republicans regarded Russia as an enemy. Across Americans, 83% viewed Russia unfavorably.
The real partisan Ukraine disagreement lies in two distinct domains: US budgetary and culture wars. The former comes down to the idea of spending and how it affects the average person’s ability to fulfill the basic American idea of buying a home, which, unlike today, used to be a largely affordable endeavor.
The latter is more poignantly about which way American society should be heading: toward a more secular group with the progressive agenda dominating the mainstream view, or the opposite.
Ukraine got trapped in both as it needs money from an already heavily indebted society and the idea, often spread by Russian propagandists and other malign agents, that it’s a Democratic stronghold of progressive thought.
Both affect the Republican stance toward Kyiv, even if they view Ukraine’s resistance as a legitimate fight at large, which is reflected in the Republican polling ahead of the looming midterms.
University of Maryland surveys, conducted between July 21 and Aug. 17, found Republican majorities supporting continued military assistance to Ukraine in 31 of 39 battleground states and congressional districts surveyed.
The question covered equipment, ammunition, training and intelligence — including capabilities subsequently drawn into October’s disputes.
To understand what that means practically for Republicans, beyond the question of why deal with Putin in the first place, requires consideration of what House members must do when they return to their districts: explain not only why they supported or opposed a particular bill, but also the direction of their party’s policies.
The risk? A backlash.
This is what happened to Ukraine-born Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz who encountered an angry crowd at a March 2025 town hall in Indiana, where questions about Ukraine accompanied criticism of federal spending cuts and other Trump policies.
Republican lawmakers thus face a two-sided task. On the one hand, attacking their party’s leader risks alienating his supporters. On the other hand, defending him without qualification means explaining policies that some of their own constituents oppose – including what Kyiv Post’s source described as “unveiled support for Putin.”
Nor can they simply rely on the “Trump effect,” hoping his endorsement will improve their prospects: A New York Times/Siena survey released on Oct. 21 put Trump’s approval at 36%, against 59% disapproval. Approval of his handling of the cost of living stood at 29%; on gas prices, it was 24%.
Even if candidates can persuade their core supporters that the diesel deal, admittedly, supported by over 50% of the Republican voters, was necessary, winning a competitive election requires more than securing the loyalty of the core base.
The independents the Republicans need
In majoritarian systems, which operate on the “winner takes it all” principle, candidates also need voters who are not reliably behind their party. That includes swing voters and independents, although the two groups are not interchangeable.
Here is where Republicans face less encouraging news.
Independents opposed the diesel deal by 71% to 10%, while opposition among all respondents stood at 63%.
“The diesel fuel deal does almost nothing to help diesel prices, but it does damage Republicans politically. Trump needs Independents to vote Republican,” Steven Moore recently wrote.
Moore is a former Republican congressional chief of staff and founder of the Ukraine Freedom Project, which has worked to build conservative support for Kyiv.
Depending on how much weight these voters give foreign policy, their dissatisfaction could help Democratic candidates or weaken Republican turnout. The survey does not measure whether the deal will change their votes, but the gap between Republican and independent opinion is substantial and cannot be ignored.
They could still vote Republican for other reasons, from economic policy to cultural issues.
Or, they could opt for a Democrat if they choose to show at the polling stations at all, given that fewer than half of eligible Americans voted in recent midterms.
What if the Democrats win?
If there’s anything to learn from Trump’s handling of electoral defeats, it’s that he strongly rules out such possibilities per se. This is why the recent actions aimed at preparing to contest the outcome if they’re not favorable to the Republican Party should be taken into consideration – even if they do not result in substantial practical and societal repercussions.
Yet any hope in Kyiv, or in some European capitals, that a Democratic victory would automatically restore generous and predictable funding, would be misplaced.
Ukraine appears to have a difficult time navigating the American political landscape and how to approach it – an impression stemming from Zelensky’s former right-hand man Andriy Yermak’s confession that he does not wish to understand Washington’s political ins and outs. He’s resigned due to alleged involvement in a large-scale corruption scandal.
The former US Ambassador Oksana Markarova’s perceived Democratic sympathies coupled with the corruption allegations involving her recently-resigned successor Olha Stefanishyna and today’s absence of a newly-appointed ambassador further complicate Kyiv’s positions on Capitol Hill, which bears little resemblance to its 2022 version when both the Democrats and the Republicans voted in favor of providing aid to Ukraine.
What would change more immediately if the Democrats take over is the political pressure on the administration.
If Democrats take the House, they would be positioned to replace Mike Johnson as speaker, control committees and pursue investigations. Ukraine would almost certainly feature in that confrontation, as Kyiv Post’s source predicts: “Democrats with both houses will be launching a salvo of investigations and even impeachment hearings. Trump’s nonsense toward Ukraine will definitely be part of that.”
In fact, the scrutiny of the administration’s decisions is already underway.
On Oct. 22, Sen. Richard Blumenthal announced an inquiry into restrictions on Starlink and Starshield, seeking information from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Musk about who authorized the changes and how they were implemented.
The inquiry also examines the Pentagon’s dependence on SpaceX and whether US forces could face similar disruptions. Restoring Ukraine’s access does not settle who restricted it or why.
A Democratic House would give those investigations greater institutional backing, including control over hearing agendas and the pursuit of documents and testimony. The sanctions waivers and diesel agreement would offer further subjects for scrutiny.
But scrutiny and the reversal of current aid-absent policy aren’t identical endeavors.
Some Democrats, like Ilhan Omar voted against Graham’s sanctions, and even if Democrats initiate another Ukraine aid package, or if Fitzpatrick-initiate bipartisan Ukraine Support Act, which passed the House on June 4 and proposed additional assistance for Kyiv alongside sanctions against Russia, appears on the Senate floor with enough “yays,” it would still need Trump’s signature.
Little suggests that the man who thanks Putin, has his envoy call him a humanitarian, and floats 200% tariffs on both Ukraine and Russia to force them into a peace deal, will do just that.

‘The emotions don’t disappear’: Inside the IDF clinic where soldiers learn to sleep and live again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:54:02 UTC
20:54:02 KST

The Tel Aviv building housing the IDF Medical Corps' Taatzumot center looks like any other residential or office building in the heart of the city. There are no prominent military markings on its facade, and nothing prepares visitors for the reality waiting beyond the door. But behind its ordinary appearance, a daily encounter takes place with one of the heaviest and least visible costs of war: the psychological wounds that combat soldiers bring home from the battlefield.
Here, far from the front lines, a different kind of battle is taking place: the struggle to function again. The soldiers who arrive at the center carry with them what their service has left behind: traumatic events, fallen friends, feelings of guilt, constant alertness and sleepless nights, all of which have become part of their everyday lives. For some, the road to recovery begins at the moment they admit they need help.
In the room where the group meets, uniforms are left outside, and so are names. The center maintains strict confidentiality, and in some sessions, even combat experience and the events themselves remain beyond the door. What remains is a circle of people who need no explanations. Here, no one has to explain what anxiety feels like, why a particular sound makes them jump or why returning home has not brought the peace they expected.
Women also receive treatment at Taatzumot, most of them, according to staff, from military intelligence and mixed-gender battalions. On the day we visited the center, a female combat soldier was sitting in the circle. She did not speak, and no one asked her to explain why. Sometimes, simply sitting in a room alongside people who understand without words is already part of the journey back to life.
The gap between the image of a combat soldier who keeps going under any circumstances and the realization that even they can reach a breaking point is one of the recurring themes in these meetings. While seeking help from a military mental health officer was once seen by some soldiers as embarrassing or a sign of weakness, the center is trying to replace that perception with the understanding that treatment is part of coping with the psychological cost of military service.
At home, one soldier in the group says, everyone worries about him, wants to know what he is going through and tries to help. But sometimes that concern turns into endless questions, while what he really needs is quiet and space to process what he has experienced.
At Taatzumot, he says, they understand that need. Meeting people who have gone through similar experiences allows him to feel that he does not have to explain himself at every moment, and that his difficulties do not make him different from everyone else. "I understand that they worry," he says of his family, "but they need to understand that things have to be done differently."
A new group every Sunday
The Taatzumot center was established about two and a half years ago to provide treatment for soldiers experiencing significant psychological distress and impaired functioning.
Lt. Col. Dr. Michal Lifshitz, head of the Taatzumot branch, explains that the model developed at the center combines intensive treatment with a broad support system that addresses not only symptoms, but also everyday life, military structure and the ability to function again.
"Every Sunday, a new group of 10 to 12 patients begins treatment," she says. "The group is led by a commander, sometimes someone who has served in significant combat roles. Some are commanders from the Duvdevan commando unit who now serve in the reserves, and for about a month, that person serves as the group's commander in every sense."
At first glance, one might assume that someone seeking treatment needs, above all, distance from the military system. But the IDF has found that for some soldiers, the military framework itself is an essential part of recovery.
"Before the center was established, some soldiers dropped out of previous treatment programs. Treatment alone was not always enough to ensure they stayed," Lifshitz explains. "The presence of a commander who makes sure the soldiers arrive every day, sometimes in uniform, maintains a sense of belonging and commitment and helps prevent them from dropping out."
Alongside the commander, she emphasizes, two facilitators accompany the group and are responsible for opening and closing each day.
Throughout the day, patients participate in workshops on emotional regulation and coping with post-traumatic stress symptoms, alongside activities designed to gradually restore their sense of control over their lives. One of the main areas of focus is sleep: sleep hygiene, techniques for falling asleep and coping with sleep disorders. That emphasis is no coincidence.
For those who have become accustomed to long periods of operational alertness, the body does not always know when it is safe to relax. Heightened arousal, adrenaline and a constant sense of needing to be prepared for any scenario can persist long after the immediate danger has passed. The night, which should be a time for rest, becomes another battlefield for some soldiers.
Beyond sleep, mind-body activities play a central role, including boxing, surfing and climbing. These are intended to help patients find different ways to regulate their emotions and establish coping routines they can maintain over time.
The idea is not to offer everyone the same treatment, but to allow patients to try different tools and discover what works for them. For one person, it may be physical exercise; for another, an outdoor activity; and for a third, a personal conversation.
Gradually, the group evolves from a treatment framework into a genuine source of support. Patients form relationships, go out together and sometimes even take trips on weekends. Within the group, a kind of trust develops that is difficult to find outside it. No one has to explain why an anxiety attack disrupts their day, why an innocent question can trigger distress or why someone sometimes needs distance from the people closest to them.
Treatment, however, does not end with conversations and activities. Some patients also struggle with everyday tasks they once took for granted. Occupational therapists assess their cognitive and daily functioning and help them rebuild basic habits and abilities. Some need assistance even with getting organized in the morning or performing simple tasks such as brushing their teeth.
These are the moments that reveal just how deeply psychological injuries can affect a person's life. They are not limited to painful memories or feelings of fear. They can seep into everyday routines and undermine the ability to perform even the simplest tasks.
Only about 5% return to combat roles
So far, more than 1,600 soldiers have received treatment at the center. According to figures provided by the branch, about 95% are combat soldiers and roughly 90% are men. Approximately 70% of those who come to the center remain in military service, most of them reassigned to meaningful noncombat roles, including firearms instruction, camouflage, the IDF Education Corps and the IDF Spokesperson's Unit.
Only about 5% return to combat roles. These figures illustrate one of the model's central goals: not necessarily to return every soldier to where they were before the traumatic event, but to help them stabilize, regain their ability to function and find a new place within the military system, whenever possible and appropriate to their condition.
The process is not supposed to stop once treatment at the center ends. Soldiers who are discharged are referred for continued care through the military's Combat Stress Reaction Unit or the Defense Ministry's Rehabilitation Department, with the aim of maintaining continuity of care and preventing a situation in which the transition from military to civilian life leaves patients without a clear source of support.
The branch reports a steady average of about 10 new referrals each week, or roughly 40 new patients per month.
When do most people come to you? At the height of the fighting?
"Not necessarily," Lifshitz says. "Often, the symptoms begin to surface דווקא after soldiers return home or take leave. During operational activity, the soldier is focused on the mission. They are required to function, make decisions and react quickly. Even when difficult events occur, there is not always time or an opportunity to stop and understand what has happened."
"When the operational pressure eases and the soldier returns to a civilian environment, the body and mind begin responding to everything that was pushed aside. In that sense, returning home is not always the end of the battle. Sometimes it is precisely the moment when the internal struggle begins, and the war continues at home."
An abnormal way of life
The path to Taatzumot begins with a referral, followed by assignment to the IDF's RM2 medical support framework and a two- to three-week assessment period, during which the soldier's condition is evaluated and an appropriate treatment plan is determined.
"The clinic provides treatment for soldiers who have experienced a breakdown in their ability to function following deeply distressing events, leading either them or their commanders to recognize that they are struggling," says Alon Mashraki, a reserve military mental health officer. "This manifests itself in post-traumatic stress symptoms, depression, communication difficulties and an inability to return to combat."
In the intensive core treatment program, patients attend the clinic four days a week, for seven to eight hours each day. The program combines professional support, farm-based therapy, yoga, breathing exercises and workshops. A central part of the process involves looking inward, trying to understand the source of the symptoms and how the events they experienced continue to affect them. One issue that comes up repeatedly is guilt over friends who were killed.
For some combat soldiers, the fact that they themselves returned does not necessarily bring relief. Memories, questions about what they could have done differently and the lingering sense of responsibility toward those who will never return continue to accompany them long after they have left the battlefield.
After the core phase, patients move into an outpatient rehabilitation stage that includes three days of treatment per week, activities such as surfing and individual therapy sessions. Later, their military medical fitness classification is reassessed and they are considered for reassignment to a noncombat role, with continued support from a military mental health officer.
What do you say to a soldier who is convinced that these reactions are a sign of weakness?
"War is an abnormal way of life," Mashraki says. "During combat, soldiers learn to push aside emotions such as fear, anger and guilt so they can continue functioning. At the time, that ability can be essential. But the emotions do not disappear. Sometimes they surface later, in dreams, everyday encounters or situations that seem meaningless to those around them."
"There is no reason to be ashamed of seeking help. Anyone who has experienced difficult events deserves professional treatment, the chance to process what they have been through and an opportunity to rebuild their life, not only as a combat soldier, but also as a civilian, a partner and a parent."
The work at the center represents an attempt by the military to address psychological injuries while soldiers are still serving, before they return to civilian life. But the very success of establishing a structured treatment framework highlights a broader question: What will happen to all those who continue to struggle with the consequences of war after they take off their uniforms?
Within the military, there is a framework, commanders, a mental health system and a clear place to turn for help. In civilian life, the systems are different, rehabilitation can be a lengthy process and the burden of coping often falls on family members.
The question, then, is not only how many discharged soldiers will receive treatment, but whether they will have continuous, accessible and appropriate support over time, at home, at work, in their relationships and within a society that is itself trying to recover from years of upheaval.
This is where the greatest concern lies: that psychological injuries will become a silent war, one that Israeli society will struggle to recognize precisely because it has no clearly defined front line, no uniforms and no single moment that can be identified with certainty as the point where it all began.
The Taatzumot center offers one response to that challenge: coping tools, a framework patients can rely on and fellow soldiers who understand their experiences without demanding explanations. But it cannot carry the weight of a national problem on its own.
Three years of fighting have demonstrated how difficult it remains for the state to address the scale of psychological injuries among combat soldiers. The IDF and rehabilitation systems are still learning the extent of the problem and the most effective ways to treat it. Not everyone knows how to ask for help, not everyone receives it in time, and not everyone who needs it manages to enter the system.
The real test, therefore, will not be the number of soldiers the IDF has brought into treatment, the percentage who remain in service or the number of centers established. It will be the ability of the state and Israeli society to identify those at risk in time, reach them before it is too late and ensure that no one is left alone with the war that followed them home.

Bulgaria votes to elect President and Vice President
In Melbourne, one of Australia's most cosmopolitan cities and an important hub for the Bulgarian diaspora on the continent, election day is proceeding calmly and in an orderly manner. This was told to Radio Bulgaria by Mancho Manev, deputy chair of the local precinct election commission. An hour before the polls closed, 77 Bulgarians had cast their ballots in Melbourne. This proves that when people are motivated, there are no excuses or obstacles that should prevent them from exercising their right to vote. For him, elections are a celebration. He was happy that, once again, his vote mattered and that, even at what is figuratively the other side of the world, Bulgaria had made it possible for him to exercise his right to choose.

As a full member of the European Union, Bulgaria should have a significant place on the world map, rather than being spoken of only as the poorest member of the European community.”

Xinhua Headlines: Retracing an odyssey: Why people walk China's Long March 90 years later
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
19:53:27 CST
20:53:27 KST

* This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March.
* People from China and abroad continue to retrace the Long March, some covering the entire route and others exploring sections by car or on foot.
* For many, the journey offers a way to learn about the Red Army's history, understand the CPC and see how China has changed over the decades.
BEIJING, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- One man, one horse and more than a year on the road.
In 2017, Luo Jianhua set out on horseback from Ruijin in east China to retrace the historic Long March. His wife, Ding Qimei, followed in a support vehicle.
Together, they crossed 81 counties and districts across 11 provincial-level regions before reaching Wuqi in northwest China, completing the journey in one year and nine days.
In 2024, Luo and Ding took to the road again with their daughter and grandniece, this time tracing the route of the Red Army's West Route Army.
Born into a farming family in southwest China's Guizhou Province, Luo grew up hearing stories of the Red Army from his elders. One saying stayed with him: "When life gets tough, think of the Red Army's 12,500-kilometer Long March."
Luo left school at 17 to make a living, later running businesses ranging from a coal-washing plant and a pig farm to an organic rice cultivation company.
While the stories he had heard as a child sustained him through difficult times, Luo long harbored a desire to experience firsthand what the Red Army had endured.
STEPPING INTO HISTORY
Hailed by American journalist Edgar Snow as "an odyssey unequaled in modern times," the Long March took place at a time when China was beset by foreign aggression, social turmoil and destitution.
Facing encirclement by overwhelming and much better-armed Kuomintang forces, the Communist Party of China (CPC)-led Red Army embarked on the epic military trek from 1934 to 1936.
During the march, the troops crossed nearly 100 rivers, traversed vast grasslands once known as a "death trap," and climbed over more than 40 mountains, including more than 20 snow-capped mountains rising above 4,000 meters.
This military maneuver gave the CPC a new foothold in northwest China, from which it built up its strength, fought back against invading Japanese troops and eventually toppled the corrupt Kuomintang regime, leading to the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949.
For Luo, retracing the route made the Red Army's hardships that he had read about far more tangible.
In northwest Sichuan Province, he and his horse once sank into a marsh. As he struggled to free the animal, he thought about the soldiers who had crossed similar terrain decades earlier.
"I felt for them. They had so little food and equipment, yet they had to keep going through wind and hail. Some fell and never got up again," he said.
Luo is not alone. People from China and abroad continue to retrace the Long March, some covering the entire route and others exploring sections by car or on foot. For many, the journey offers a way to learn about the Red Army's history, understand the CPC and see how China has changed over the decades.
The Long March's reach has extended beyond China. First published in Britain in 1937, Snow's "Red Star Over China" introduced the Chinese revolution to international readers. Decades later, Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Harrison Salisbury retraced the route and described the Long March as "a great human epic."
That appeal continues today. Dutch sinologist Elsbeth van Paridon, who joined a group retracing the route this summer, said walking the route gave her a feeling similar to looking out over the beaches of Normandy and realizing what had happened there.
She noted that the former revolutionary sites along the route now also serve as ecological parks, becoming part of a broader tourism economy that supports local development.
"That is how you see the spirit of the Long March live on," she said.
William N. Brown, a U.S. professor at Xiamen University who has lived in China for nearly 40 years, has retraced part of the route and witnessed the country's transformation firsthand.
He first traveled to Guizhou in 1994, when unpaved roads and limited river crossings left mountain communities isolated. Pointing to a towering bridge spanning a valley in Qinggangpo Village, Brown highlighted the region's staggering leap in connectivity.
"The most important change is invisible: people have gained confidence and self-respect," he said. "Thirty years ago, many thought prosperity would take 50 years to achieve -- they never expected to see it in their own lifetime."
THE SAME ROAD, A TRANSFORMED CHINA
The changes are also visible in the country's infrastructure. Roads now cut through mountains that Red Army soldiers once crossed on foot, while bridges span valleys and rivers that once posed major obstacles.
China's operational high-speed rail network has surpassed 50,000 kilometers, accounting for over 70 percent of the world's total. Its expressway network extends to nearly 200,000 kilometers, the largest in the world.
The transformation is particularly visible in Guizhou, where rugged karst terrain long made travel difficult. More than 32,000 bridges have been completed or are under construction in the province, including the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge, the world's highest bridge.
Communities along the historic route have also changed. In Guangxi's Quanzhou, Guanyang and Xing'an counties, where the Battle of the Xiangjiang River was fought, more than 100 formerly impoverished villages have been lifted out of poverty through targeted poverty alleviation efforts.
Despite China's profound transformation over recent decades, new challenges remain on its path toward Chinese modernization.
Wan Laizhi, a scholar of CPC history at Guangxi Normal University, said retracing the Long March route helps people appreciate how earlier generations faced adversity and held to their convictions, drawing strength and inspiration from their example to overcome challenges facing China today.
Chen Lipeng, a professor at Renmin University of China, said retracing the route can also help promote tourism in former revolutionary areas and support rural revitalization.
Interest in revolutionary heritage sites is growing, particularly among younger visitors. In the first half of 2026, interest in booking tickets for such attractions rose 86 percent year on year, while bookings by people aged 18 to 35 accounted for more than half of the total, according to industry data.
Luo and Ding, for their part, have worked to keep that history alive. Back home in Zunyi City, they compiled their experiences into books and began visiting schools to share what they had learned.
Earlier this year, they opened a homestay in their village, employing more than 10 local residents. Luo plans to turn part of it into a small educational site displaying materials collected during their journeys.
"Young people today may not face the hardships people endured in the past, but everyone encounters difficulties in life," he said. "I want them to know that there is always a way forward. That is what the Long March spirit means to me."
(Reporting by Cheng Lu, Bai Xu, Wang Jian, Rong Jiaojiao, Li Jingya, Shi Qiangui and Guo Yifan; Video reporters: Liu Qinbing, Zhao Yingbo and Yao Youming; Video editors: Hong Ling, Zhang Mocheng and Zheng Xin.) ■

CHANGSHA, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Zhang Xue, founder of Chinese motorcycle manufacturer ZXMOTO, set a Guinness World Record on Sunday by riding a modified motorcycle 40.74 kilometers across open water in his hometown of Mayang Miao Autonomous County in central China's Hunan Province.
Riding a specially modified ZXMOTO MX450, Zhang made several back-and-forth runs across a river to set the record for the longest distance traveled on open water by a modified motorcycle.
"I have strong faith that I can make it happen. Even if I fail, I will pursue it without hesitation. I really enjoy the process," Zhang said.
The achievement marked the culmination of a pursuit stretching back to 2009, when Zhang first attempted to ride a motorcycle across water using rudimentary modifications. On that occasion, he fell into the water four times and managed a maximum distance of just 20 meters.
For Sunday's attempt, the MX450 was fitted with amphibious skis, an enlarged fuel tank and additional waterproofing.
The motorcycle builds up speed on land before skimming across the water, with a front ski providing steering and the rear tire pushing water backward to generate propulsion.
Zhang said staging the record attempt in his hometown gave the achievement added significance.
"The spirit of perseverance comes from this land," he said. "By bringing this challenge to my hometown, I also wanted to fulfill a dream here and let the world see Mayang." ■

“Strasbourg Calling”: Europe must produce the right things, not simply more

Author
