Interview
German MEP from the Greens Danie Freund:
“Strasbourg Calling”: Europe must produce the right things, not simply more
Interview with MEP Daniel Freund
Sunday 25 October 2026 13:06
Sunday, 25 October 2026, 13:06
MEP Daniel Freund
PHOTO Irina Nedeva
Font size
At its Strasbourg session this week, the European Parliament discussed the conclusions of last week's European Council meeting. However, the major issue of the EU's long-term budget for 2028-2034 remains unresolved. Europe wants to become a geopolitical power, rearm, compete with China and maintain its climate targets. But who will pay for it all?
German Green MEP Daniel Freund, the Greens' coordinator on the Committee on Budgetary Control, warns that Europe cannot take on more responsibilities with less money and must not abandon its climate targets.
Speaking on BNR's special  broadcast from Strasbourg, he said:
“Europe still has a great deal to do in terms of defence, support for Ukraine and competition with China. I see our chancellor, as well as members of my own party, calling for substantial budget cuts. Fuel prices keep rising, driven by our dependence on fossil fuels and the problems involving Iran.
I think we are currently seeing some of the highest prices ever at petrol pumps and filling stations. At the same time, we are seeing a major increase in electric vehicle use. In Denmark, for example, electric vehicles already account for 80% of new car sales, while in Germany the figure is 30%. So I think we need to move in that direction.”
MEP Daniel Freund and BNR's Irina Nedeva in the Radio Studios complex at the European Parliament in Strasbourg (21 October 2026)
PHOTO Rositsa Petkova
Italy, Greece, Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia are preparing a petition calling for a further postponement or weakening of the emissions trading scheme. Europe must nevertheless maintain its climate targets, the politician insisted in an interview with BNR Horizon's programme “Strasbourg Calling”:
“We do not want to keep spending billions to support petrol producers, these huge companies, and in doing so also support dictators. We want to put an end to that! We want to continue transforming our economies and making them increasingly green. This summer, we saw 32,000 Europeans lose their lives during heatwaves. And yet it was the coolest summer compared with those forecast to come. So we certainly need to keep moving in this direction.”
Daniel Freund argued that decarbonisation is not incompatible with industrial competitiveness:
“We can already see what is happening in China. The Chinese market has stopped buying cars with internal combustion engines from us, and only electric vehicles are being used. The same applies to other products. So if we want to remain competitive, we need to offer the right products. For example, companies that use electric trucks and renewable energy are not currently being affected by the fuel crisis.”
Europe must strengthen its defence industry, but even defence is becoming greener, he noted:
“Even if we look at the battlefield in Ukraine, we can see that this war is being fought, to some extent, using renewable energy. A large number of drones are being deployed, and they operate on batteries. What we must do is stand together in defending Ukraine, because in doing so we are fighting for our shared values and our own survival.”
The Greens will support the European Parliament resolution aimed at strengthening security in the Black Sea in response to Russian threats, he added:
“I think we will support the resolution. We stand with Bulgaria, Romania and every country that falls victim to such Russian attacks.”

New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- Yale University
- Summary:
- Millions of years after animals first conquered land, some took an extraordinary evolutionary U-turn and returned to the water. Using machine learning and thousands of fossil measurements, Yale scientists have uncovered surprising clues about which prehistoric creatures truly became aquatic. Their findings suggest that Spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater, while some ancient marine reptiles previously thought to be fully aquatic actually spent considerable time on land.
- Share:
For millions of years, evolution helped animals make the transition from life in the ocean to life on land. But the journey did not always move in one direction. Many species eventually returned to the water, developing new adaptations that allowed them to thrive in aquatic environments.
Dozens of major groups of mammals and reptiles made this remarkable evolutionary reversal. Now, a new study from Yale University is shedding light on when and how these transitions occurred, as well as which ancient animals became fully aquatic and which continued to depend on land.
The findings were published in the journal Current Biology.
"These secondarily aquatic groups adapted in strikingly similar ways to their new aquatic home -- evolving flippers and a suite of other features that made them better swimmers," said lead author Caleb Gordon, who completed his doctorate at Yale's Graduate School of Arts and Sciences (GSAS) earlier this year and is now a postdoctoral researcher at the Florida Museum of Natural History. "As a result, they've become textbook examples of convergent evolution, which can tell us a lot about the processes driving and constraining adaptive change in response to similar environmental cues."
Using Ancient Fossils and AI to Reconstruct Evolution
To investigate these evolutionary changes, the researchers examined hundreds of fossil and modern specimens housed at the Yale Peabody Museum and dozens of other institutions worldwide. They collected extensive new data, including measurements (more than 11,000), photographs, and CT scans.
The team combined traditional paleontological techniques with machine learning models that account for evolutionary relationships. They also incorporated a statistical approach originally used by naval forces during World War II. Together, these methods offered a new way to investigate one of the most remarkable transitions in vertebrate evolution.
"Reconstructing the lives of extinct life forms in a scientifically rigorous way, as opposed to just telling stories, is a precise and delicate undertaking," said Bhart-Anjan Bhullar, senior author of the study. Bhullar is an associate professor of Earth and planetary sciences in Yale's Faculty of Arts and Sciences (FAS) and an associate curator of vertebrate paleontology and vertebrate zoology at the Peabody Museum.
"It requires a careful interweaving of data from modern organisms, of which our understanding is necessarily far deeper, and knowledge of these living organisms' genealogy relative to fossil forms," he said. "Caleb's work accomplishes all of this and more, and on a massive evolutionary scale."
For decades, scientists have disagreed about when particular groups of prehistoric animals became fully adapted to life underwater. The fossil record often provides incomplete or conflicting clues, making it difficult to determine whether an extinct species primarily lived on land, in water, or in both environments.
Some skeletal features may indicate an aquatic lifestyle, while others suggest that the same animal remained capable of moving and feeding on land. These contradictions have led researchers to different conclusions about how ancient species behaved.
"In these cases, paleontologists are often stuck, as different lines of evidence disagree about what the ancient animal was like," Gordon said.
To address this uncertainty, Gordon developed a method using relatively simple but effective machine learning models trained on living animals. By identifying relationships between skeletal proportions and known lifestyles, the models can estimate how extinct species used aquatic environments. They can also predict soft tissue adaptations, including swimming structures that rarely survive in fossils.
Spinosaurus May Have Spent Most of Its Life Underwater
One of the most striking findings concerns Spinosaurus, a giant prehistoric dinosaur whose relationship with water has generated considerable controversy.
Spinosaurus lived approximately 113 million to 94 million years ago in what is now northern Africa. Although scientists generally agree that it was associated with aquatic environments, exactly how it moved, hunted, and spent its time remains a subject of debate.
Some evidence points to an animal that frequently submerged itself and pursued prey underwater, much like seals or penguins. Other findings suggest a lifestyle closer to that of a modern heron, with Spinosaurus walking and searching for food along shorelines and in shallow water.
The Yale team's analysis provides new support for the more aquatic interpretation.
"Our results shed new light on how much time Spinosaurus spent submerged, which could support the underwater hunting view," Gordon said. "We confidently recovered highly aquatic habits for Spinosaurus, indicating that it spent the vast majority of its time submerged in the water."
Although the findings do not settle every question about how Spinosaurus hunted, they strengthen the case that this enormous predator spent much more of its life underwater than on land.
Ancient Marine Reptiles That Never Fully Left Land
The researchers reached a different conclusion about mesosaurs, small marine reptiles that lived between 290 million and 274 million years ago in regions now forming parts of South Africa and eastern South America.
Mesosaurs have long interested paleontologists because they gave birth to live young, a characteristic some researchers have interpreted as evidence of a fully aquatic existence. However, the new analysis suggests that their limbs were not adapted for a life spent entirely in water.
Instead, their skeletal proportions indicate that mesosaurs regularly moved between aquatic and terrestrial environments.
"They spent a lot of time on land, like a modern-day alligator or platypus does," Gordon said. "Mesosaurs didn't completely leave the land behind."
The findings also suggest a broader pattern among the earliest marine reptiles. According to the researchers, all Paleozoic marine reptiles (all marine reptiles around before the dinosaurs appeared) continued to return to land regularly. None appeared to have evolved a completely aquatic lifestyle, with even the most water adapted species remaining amphibious.
The researchers found that forelimb proportions were particularly useful for distinguishing these lifestyles. Using this information, their models could predict with more than 90% accuracy whether an animal possessed soft tissue flippers and whether it had highly or fully aquatic habits.
A World War II Technique Helps Solve an Evolutionary Mystery
An especially unusual part of the research involved adapting a statistical method developed during the 1940s.
"Caleb resurrected a statistical technique from a bygone era," said co-author Jacques Gauthier, a professor of Earth and planetary sciences at Yale and curator-in-charge for vertebrate paleontology at the Peabody Museum. "It was developed during WWII to estimate the probability that an approaching blip on the radar screen was an enemy plane. Caleb cleverly used it to get at whether or not an extinct animal had limbs modified for swimming."
By repurposing this approach, the researchers could assess the likelihood that an extinct species possessed specialized swimming adaptations, even when direct evidence of those features was missing.
The method could eventually help scientists investigate other major changes in evolutionary history. Potential applications include studying when human ancestors developed the ability to walk on two legs and how the dinosaur ancestors of birds evolved the ability to fly.
A New Way to Understand Extinct Animals
Because most prehistoric vertebrates are known primarily through their fossilized skeletons, reconstructing their behavior is one of paleontology's greatest challenges. Bones preserve valuable information, but they rarely provide a complete picture of how an animal lived.
Traditionally, scientists have interpreted particular skeletal features to make arguments about the lifestyles of extinct species. Those interpretations can differ significantly, especially when fossils are incomplete or several anatomical characteristics point toward different conclusions.
The new approach offers a more systematic way to evaluate that evidence, using patterns observed in living species to make testable predictions about animals that disappeared millions of years ago.
"Bones are all that is left to us of the vast majority of vertebrate animals that have lived on Earth," Bhullar said. "We want to know so very much about these creatures and the succession of lost worlds they inhabited, but we have so little on which to base our conclusions. From skeletal remains, people have tried to discern life habits, generally making an argument on the basis of one preferred set of features or another. Caleb's method removes the subjectivity from this process and allows the data to speak for themselves."
The study's additional co-authors are Lisa Freisem, a doctoral student at Yale's Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, and Christopher Griffin, an assistant professor of geosciences at Princeton University who previously worked as a postdoctoral fellow at Yale.
Research support was provided by the Yale Institute for Biospheric Studies, the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Crocodile Specialist Group, and the National Science Foundation.

GII 2026 places Tehran 65th among top 100 science and technology clusters
The Global Innovation Index (GII) has ranked Tehran as the world’s 65th-largest science and technology (S&T) cluster this year, according to a report released by the UN’s World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO).
Each year, the GII identifies and ranks the world’s top 100 innovation clusters. Using a bottom-up, data-driven approach that transcends administrative and political boundaries, the GII identifies geographic areas with a high concentration of inventors, scientific authors, and venture capital (VC) activity. These innovation clusters often extend across multiple municipalities or subnational regions and, in some cases, span two or more countries.
Three metrics determine the top 100: the locations of inventors listed in patent applications filed under the WIPO Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT), the affiliations of authors of published scientific articles, and the locations of companies receiving venture capital funding.
The GII 2026, under the theme “Powering entrepreneurs at the frontier of science”, examines how scientific breakthroughs become deep science startups and spinouts.
In addition to China and India, six other middle-income economies have clusters among the top 100, including Brazil (1 cluster), the Islamic Republic of Iran (1), Egypt (1), Malaysia (2), Mexico (1), and Turkey (1).
Tehran is the only cluster within Iran that falls within the top 100 innovation clusters in 2026. In 2026, Tehran had 405 PCT applications, 58,732 scientific publications, 107 venture capital deals, 0.0 percent Share of global PCT applications, 0.7 percent share of global scientific publications, and 0.0 percent share of global venture capital deals, making it the 65th largest innovation cluster and 88 innovation cluster by intensity, slipping down from 63rd and 85th, respectively in 2025.
The city’s estimated cluster population, PCT application per capita, and scientific publication capita amount to 7,852,733; 52; and 7,497 respectively, IRNA reported.
The venture capital pre-deals per capita is about 14, and the total innovation intensity share per capita is 0.097.
In patent registration, medical technology ranked first (with 19 percent share), followed by computer technology, civil engineering, and pharmaceuticals.
Top publishing organizations in Tehran are University of Tehran with 5,232 articles, Islamic Azad University with 4,081 articles, and Iran University of Science and Technology with 3,725 articles. A majority of published articles are in engineering fields.
In a recent global ranking by StartupBlink 2026, Tehran’s position has advanced by 20 spots, ranking 348 among the world’s most innovative cities.
Tehran is home to 96 startups, making up 81 percent of all startups in the country. Tehran has approximately 1 startup per 100,000 people. In 2025, the ecosystem recorded an annual growth rate of over 36 percent. The city is currently ranked as the 1st strongest startup ecosystem in Iran, having remained stable since 2025. At the regional level, Tehran ranks 11th in West Asia, having moved up 2 spots since 2025.
According to Iran Innovation Zone, the achievement is the result of strengthening innovation infrastructure and developing interactions among different sectors operating in the knowledge-based economy, Mehr news agency reported.
The report by StartupBlink has highlighted the role of Pardis Technology Park, the country’s largest technology and innovation hub, as one of the driving forces of Iran’s knowledge-based economy. The park hosts hundreds of knowledge-based and technology companies, creating business development infrastructure and providing a platform for enhancing cooperation among startups, investors, large industries, and institutions.
Moreover, hosting the International Innovation and Technology Exhibition (INOTEX) every year, Pardis Technology Park plays a key role in networking and connecting experts in the innovation ecosystem. According to the report, thanks to the capacities of Pardis Technology Parks, Iran’s startup ecosystem ranks 95 globally.
The Innovation and Prosperity Fund and MCI (Hamrah Aval – Iran’s first mobile operator) Ventures are the two other key agents that have developed Iran’s innovation ecosystem by facilitating the growth of technology and knowledge-based companies.
Iran ranks 58th globally in ‘Corporate Engagement’, an indicator that reflects the effective interactions between large industries and innovative and technological companies.
Fintech, the leading industry in Iran, ranks 72nd globally, 5th in the Middle East, indicating the country’s high capacity in the development of financial technologies. Iran Fintech Industry has 23 startups, representing 19 percent of all startups in Iran.
In the Global Startup Ecosystem Index 2026, Iran’s startup ecosystem is ranked 103 worldwide, holding steady compared to the previous year. The Iranian startup ecosystem ranks 10th in West Asia, having remained stable since 2025. It ranks right after Oman and is followed by Iraq.
The country has 118 startups, representing one percent of all startups in the Middle East. This equals approximately one startup per 100,000 people. The ecosystem grew by +54.4 percent over the past year.

Stop Translating Every Word: How to Read Ukrainian Like You Mean It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:50:00 UTC
20:50:00 KST

You open a Ukrainian news article. Three words in, you hit one you don’t know. You stop, look it up, and start again. Two lines later, it happens again. Ten minutes on, you have technically read every word, and you have no idea what the story was about.
Anyone learning Ukrainian knows this feeling. On Nov. 1, Language Lab, a Kyiv-based Ukrainian language school, is hosting a free online webinar built around a simple idea: the problem usually isn’t vocabulary or grammar. It’s the way most learners read, slowly and word by word, chasing the meaning of each term instead of the meaning of the text.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“This happens because you focus on words instead of meaning,” the workshop’s materials put it. The session sets out to change that, with a toolkit of reading strategies that most people already use without thinking in their native language.
Why reading matters
The workshop leans on the British reading scholar Christine Nuttall, who argued in 1996 that the best way to learn a language is to live among its speakers, and the next best is to “read extensively in it.”
For the many foreigners in Ukraine who hear Ukrainian daily but still struggle with a news feed, that matters. According to the workshop, regular readers build vocabulary faster, use grammar more accurately, and feel more confident. The gains don’t stay on the page: reading also feeds speaking, listening and writing.
The catch is that reading only helps if you can keep doing it. Word-by-word decoding exhausts the brain fast, and most learners give up long before the benefits arrive.
Ukrainian Speaking Club to Mark Independence Day With Free Online Session
What the webinar covers
The session, which is suitable for all Ukrainian learners, introduces different reading strategies and types of reading, from a quick skim to slow, careful study. It then shows how to apply them to very different sources: short ads and social media posts, news articles, and even fiction.
The core argument is that reading is not one skill but several. In English, you switch modes without thinking: you glance at headlines, hunt for a time in an email, settle into a novel. In Ukrainian, many learners use only the slowest mode for everything, and that is what wears them out.
The webinar also looks at how much work context can do. Knowing who is writing, to whom and why often lets a reader follow a text, or guess an unfamiliar word, without stopping to translate. Language Lab promises practical tips and real-life teaching hacks to make reading in Ukrainian simpler and more enjoyable.
Read smart, not perfectly
The takeaway is that reading is about meaning, not every word. “You don’t need to read perfectly,” the workshop materials say. “You need to read smart.”
The organizers stress that this is a workshop, not a lecture. Participants are encouraged to jump in with questions, and the session closes with 15 minutes of Q&A. It is pitched at learners who want to speed up their path to fluency in Ukrainian.
The details: Language Lab’s reading webinar runs online on Sunday, Nov. 1, at 5 p.m. Kyiv time. Registration is here. Language Lab offers Ukrainian lessons, cultural immersion events and a learners’ community, with a free trial lesson available at lngglab.com.

Ukraine had not commented on the reported strikes in Lipetsk Oblast and Perm Krai at the time of publication.
Ukraine regularly strikes military targets deep within Russia and occupied territories in an effort to diminish Moscow's ability to continue waging its war.
Ukraine's General Staff said Ukrainian forces also struck Russian military radar stations in Belgorod Oblast overnight on Oct. 25, as well as a Russian command post in occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast and a command-and-observation post in occupied Kherson Oblast.
Other targets included concentrations of Russian troops in the occupied parts of Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts, the General Staff added.
Earlier, Ukrainian monitoring channels reported a fire at the Omsky Kauchuk petrochemical plant in the Russian city of Omsk following a Ukrainian attack.
The overnight attack on Belgorod also damaged a local shopping and entertainment center, monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported.
Belgorod Mayor Valentin Demidov said one person was killed and 10 others were injured in the attack. Residential buildings and cars were also damaged, he added.

The Border Security Force (BSF) has apprehended four Pakistani fishermen who allegedly entered Indian waters for crab-catching activities and seized a fishing boat near the India-Pakistan border in Gujarat’s Kutch district.According to news agency PTI, the fishermen were apprehended from the Sir Creek area on Sunday following specific intelligence inputs, an official said. The fishermen were identified as Kadir Thaimor, Muhammad Mussa, Azgar Thaimor and Ahsan Jat, all residents of Chach Jaan Khan village in Pakistan’s Sindh province, according to information provided by the BSF.Sir Creek is a narrow, marshy tidal channel in the Rann of Kutch, along the coastal region between Gujarat and Pakistan’s Sindh province. The area is strategically sensitive because the longstanding India-Pakistan boundary dispute over the creek affects the demarcation of the maritime boundary in the Arabian Sea.The region’s shallow waters, tidal channels and extensive marshlands make navigation and border surveillance challenging. Fishing activities in the area can also lead to fishermen crossing into the other country’s waters, prompting apprehensions by security personnel.
The BSF maintains surveillance along the sensitive western border to prevent unauthorised crossings and other illegal activities. The latest apprehension follows an operation based on specific intelligence inputs, during which the four fishermen and their boat were taken into custody.

Intl. conference on Global Coalition against Scientific Apartheid set for November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25

Intl. conference on Global Coalition against Scientific Apartheid set for November
TEHRAN – The 5th International conference on Global Coalition against Scientific Apartheid is planned to be held on November 10 in Tehran to promote justice in science and technology in the new world order, and honor the scientists martyred during the US-Israeli war against the country.
Organized by the World Islamic Peace Forum and Islamic Azad University, the key objectives of the conference involve promoting scientific justice as a prerequisite for global peace and justice, examining the state of scientific justice within the current and future global order, identifying instances of scientific apartheid, analyzing the assassination of scientists and the imposition of technological sanctions, and fostering coalitions among experts and scientific institutions worldwide.
The conference is centered around five main topics, including intellectual and philosophical foundations of scientific justice and overcoming science and technology apartheid; unilateralism, scientific and technological hegemony, and the future of world order; examples of scientific and technological apartheid and countermeasures; scientific justice, fair peace and development; as well as global coalition for justice in science and technology: from discourse to action.
Sanctions contradict UNESCO’s Open Access Policy
In April, Science Minister Hossein Simaei-Sarraf condemned sanctions imposed on the country’s science sector, saying that the sanctions are in opposition to UNESCO’s Open Access Policy.
Addressing the Global Ministerial Dialogue on Science Diplomacy, which was held at UNESCO Headquarters, Paris, France, on March 25 and 26, the minister said that as per Resolution 2231 of the Security Council, imposing sanctions on scientific activities has no legal validity, IRNA reported.
The two-day event was held under the theme ‘Science Diplomacy in a Rapidly Changing World: Building Peace in the Minds of Men and Women’.
Simaei-Sarraf delineated Iran’s viewpoints and perspectives on issues such as modern science diplomacy to address the challenges of the 21st century, the role of science diplomacy in safeguarding the security of science and promoting open access in scientific research, and the role of science diplomacy in fostering fair cooperation for the development and responsible use of new and emerging technologies.
On the sidelines of the event, the official held meetings with the Deputy Director-General, Xing Qu; Assistant Director-General for Natural Science, Lidia Arthur Brito; Assistant Director-General for Education, Stefania Giannini; and Assistant Director-General for External Relations of UNESCO, Firmin Edouard Matoko.
Moreover, Simaei-Sarraf held meetings with the ministers of science of Sri Lanka and Colombia and the deputy science ministers of Iraq and Switzerland.
In a meeting with Iranian professors residing in France and Germany, Simaei-Sarraf invited them to help enhance collaborations with the country.
The official also highlighted the need to amend laws and eliminate existing gaps to be able to benefit from the scientific capacities of Iranians living abroad. It was decided that 20 prominent Iranian professors residing in Europe would travel to Iran this summer to deliver speeches and hold scientific and educational workshops in different fields such as artificial intelligence, and renewable energy.
The Global Ministerial Dialogue on science diplomacy, as part of the International Decade of Sciences for Sustainable Development, aims to advance international dialogue on creating a new global framework for science diplomacy that addresses the current needs of society.
The dialogue aims to foster a high-level commitment to science diplomacy as an instrument for promoting dialogue and peace; explore innovative science diplomacy initiatives through exchanges between ministers, scientists, diplomats, and experts to contribute to peacebuilding and human rights protection; agree on a common framework to advance shared goals through science diplomacy; and highlight ongoing initiatives and opportunities in science diplomacy.

Netanyahu rebuked for plan to use crypto to bypass economic sanctions
JERUSALEM, Oct 25 - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces re-election this week, is drawing criticism from economists and political rivals after suggesting Israel could use cryptocurrency to help shield its economy from potential international sanctions.
In an interview with Israel's Channel 10 on Friday, Netanyahu said he was preparing for a scenario in which broader sanctions were imposed on Israel.
Last month, Britain, France and Canada said they would block imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank in what was the latest in a series of actions targeting Israel's settlement policy, underscoring its growing diplomatic isolation among some of its traditional allies.
"There could be sanctions, and sanctions on banks so you need to set up a bypass economy," Netanyahu said. "You know, there are currencies that can bypass (sanctions). We are also working on that."
Asked whether he was referring to cryptocurrency, Netanyahu replied: "Very true, very true," adding that blockchain technology was another possibility.
The comments drew a rare rebuke by the Bank of Israel, which said crypto currencies cannot serve as a route to bypass sanctions and that political leaders should focus on policy that would render such measures unnecessary.
"The right course for Israel's economy is to preserve our economic relations with our main trading partners, and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy," it said.
Netanyahu on Sunday continued to defend his record, urging voters to back him and saying he and US President Donald Trump had two years left to work together to topple Iran's rulers.
PLAN DRAWS CRITICISM
On Sunday, more than 100 economists, including former Bank of Israel officials, ex-central bank governor Jacob Frenkel and several Nobel laureates, signed a letter expressing alarm over Netanyahu's proposal. They said it would lead to higher unemployment, a fall in foreign investment and the collapse of Israel's economic standing in the world.
"As we have seen in countries that have suffered similar sanctions, such as South Africa, Iran, and Russia, the living standards of Israeli citizens would plummet dramatically, and the state's ability to finance its security and defend itself against its enemies would be severely damaged," the letter read.
"Netanyahu is knowingly leading the State of Israel toward boycott and international economic isolation, and all he has to offer the Israeli economy is a puzzling solution, one accepted in criminal organizations, that will not help in the slightest."
Netanyahu's main rival in Tuesday's election, Gadi Eisenkot, called the crypto plan "madness" and said he feared that the "BibiCoin policy" would drive companies abroad and undermine national security.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said: "Netanyahu has gone off the rails ... He promises the citizens of Israel before these elections that they'll be standing in line for an hour and a half for bread, like in Russia and Iran."
Opinion polls point to a potential stalemate in the election with neither Netanyahu's ruling coalition nor an opposition alliance securing a governing majority in parliament. REUTERS

CENTCOM reportedly has plans for Iran strikes: Will Trump approve them?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:39:41 UTC
20:39:41 KST

CENTCOM reportedly has plans for Iran strikes: Will Trump approve them?
US media reporting that Pentagon has drawn up plans to renew strikes after November 3 midterm elections, but analysts question what another bombing campaign could achieve.
The US military has drawn up options for renewed attacks on Iran, according to the Washington-based website The Hill, raising the prospect of another round of major fighting in a war approaching its eighth month.
Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees US forces in the Middle East, has plans ready for follow-up strikes if authorised by the White House, the outlet reported. It also said military planners had prepared several options for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
The report focused on possible attacks after the November 3 US midterm elections. But President Donald Trump suggested on Saturday that the United States could strike as soon as “tomorrow”, while also holding out the possibility of a “big, beautiful” agreement with Tehran.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, meanwhile, accused Washington of derailing negotiations but said efforts to reach an agreement should continue. With both sides warning of further attacks, could the conflict tip back into full-scale war? Here is what we know.
What are the plans?
The latest reporting suggests military preparations are advancing, although it remains unclear which options Trump might approve or when. Earlier this month, Axios reported that the Pentagon had instructed CENTCOM to complete preparations for a possible resumption of major combat operations. Its sources said a renewed campaign could target Iranian energy facilities, infrastructure and nuclear sites.
Those preparations do not amount to an order to attack. The decision ultimately rests with Trump, whose public statements continue to leave room for both military action and negotiations.
Meanwhile, on Wednesday, The New York Times reported that the US and Israel have drawn up joint plans for an attack on Iran after the midterm elections. The reports come alongside US warnings about alleged Iranian threats to American personnel overseas. An intelligence memo sent on Friday by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran had “substantially increased efforts to target US personnel”, with lethal plots reaching “advanced stages” in the Middle East and elsewhere.
The Department of State has ordered staffing reductions at several regional embassies amid the warnings. The publicly reported memo did not identify specific targets or establish when any alleged attacks might occur.
Trump has added to the uncertainty. At a rally on Friday, he said Washington “may do another little Epic Fury”, referring to the codename of the US-Israeli military operation against Iran that began on February 28. On Saturday, he declined to disclose the timing of any possible attack while suggesting one could come as early as Sunday.
Julie Norman, associate fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera the preparations served both as short-term posturing and a possible longer-term military objective next month. “With Trump, I think he is always keeping options on the table, but I think this particular drawing up of plans is an immediate posturing deterrent, but also a very real option after the midterms,” she said.
It comes as the US is deploying a third aircraft carrier strike group, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, along with roughly 10,000 additional soldiers and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit to the Middle East by the end of November.
How has Iran responded?
Tehran has combined calls for further negotiations with warnings that renewed US attacks would bring a wider response. “We were having negotiations, the cowards [Americans] messed everything up,” Pezeshkian said in remarks broadcast on Saturday, before adding that efforts to conclude the agreement should continue.
Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf will also miss the 12th BRICS Parliamentary Forum in New Delhi, according to the Iranian Embassy in India. The embassy cited “unforeseen circumstances” without elaborating.
On Sunday, Iran’s army also said it had shot down a US-developed LUCAS drone over the southern port city of Bandar Abbas, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
The Reuters news agency has reported, quoting Iranian security officials, that Tehran has drawn up plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf in the event of a resumption of US and Israeli attacks.
The incident followed Iranian claims that seven oil tankers had caught fire or sustained damage in and around the Strait of Hormuz earlier this week, while on Wednesday, Iran also announced what it describes as a shift towards an “offensive” military doctrine, warning that countries hosting bases used in US attacks could become targets.
“Our defence doctrine was previously defensive; we used to say that if a country attacks us, we will respond. Now we say that if a country attacks us, we will both respond and launch an offensive,” Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesman Hossein Mohebi said.
The warning raises the prospect of a confrontation spreading further across the region, with energy infrastructure and countries aligned with Washington potentially exposed. “Iran is also drawing up its own target lists to include energy infrastructure and US-aligned states,” Norman said.
“So I would say both parties are certainly very prepared for another round of escalation and projecting preparedness to each other.”
“In the meantime, there is a very high risk of miscalculation by either side, a very high risk of rapid escalation.”
October has become the worst month for attacks on ships since the war began in February, with more than 120 attacks reported so far.
Would another attack serve Trump’s interests?
The timing is politically sensitive, with Trump facing pressure to avoid renewed escalation before the US midterm elections, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been pushing for an attack as his support dwindles in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s election.
It comes after Netanyahu said overthrowing Iran’s government remains Israel’s “primary objective”.
Mohamad Elmasry, a professor at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies in Qatar, said recent developments pointed towards renewed fighting rather than a diplomatic breakthrough. “There is a lot of signalling, a lot of posturing suggesting that we are headed for another round of fighting,” he told Al Jazeera.
He pointed to Hegseth’s recent visit to Israel, and Washington’s reported withdrawal of personnel from regional diplomatic and military sites. “All of that would suggest that the US and Israel are planning [another round of attacks] on Iran, either soon or very soon,” he said.
“One of the fears is this next round of fighting could actually be more dangerous, more catastrophic than the previous round.”
Norman added that while the US president may be eyeing up a strike on Iran after the midterms, “the big question for Trump from military advisers is – what would a further round of escalation bring that the other rounds didn’t?”
“What would these strategies do to force Iran to the negotiating table? And I don’t think there has been a clear answer to that.”

'Too deferential to govt': Former SC judge questions ex-CJI Chandrachud’s approach to appointments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:37:06 UTC
20:37:06 KST

Congress flags judicial independence concerns over claims in ex SC judge's memoir
NEW DELHI: Former Supreme Court judge Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul has questioned former Chief Justice of India (CJI) D Y Chandrachud's approach to judicial appointments, alleging that he was "too deferential to the government". He also expressed concern over the practice of discussing candidates with the executive before formal Collegium deliberations.In his forthcoming memoir, Without Fear or Favour, Justice Kaul recounts a Collegium meeting to fill six vacancies in the Supreme Court, during which five names had been agreed upon in advance. He alleges that Justice Chandrachud proposed a sixth candidate at the last minute and considered seeking the government's view on the appointment."The Chief Justice drew me aside into a separate room and wondered aloud whether he should telephone out to check the government's view," Kaul wrote in his book.Speaking to news portal The Wire about his memoir, Kaul said the Collegium must resist executive pressure to safeguard judicial independence.Asked whether Justice Chandrachud was trying to please the government or seeking its prior approval, Kaul said, "I don't think it was a question of pleasing the government, but what had happened was that he had discussed the names with me earlier.
"We had agreed on five names, and I thought the collegium would be quite okay with the other members of the collegium, and this (sixth) name was propped up at the last minute with me while going to the collegium meeting. I said that name is not acceptable to me and will not be acceptable."He said Justice Chandrachud wanted him to support the additional candidate, but he believed the other Collegium members would also oppose the proposal."And well, he wanted me to collaborate and go ahead with the name. I said even if I do that, the others will not. I believe, and that's what happened in the meeting. I told him this will not get through because I know the views of the other collegiate members. Maybe he had already taken some kind of an approval for the other names, including the sixth name," Kaul said.He expressed concern over the practice of discussing judicial appointments with the government before formal Collegium meetings."So this has become, unfortunately, a practice of names being discussed in some kind of a previous discussion with the government," he told senior journalist Karan Thapar."It has been happening, I think, before and after, which is what troubles me. That's why I have written that when the government introduced the NJAC (the National Judicial Appointments Commission) in 2015, we would at least have sat across the table and discussed it. It could have been fine-tuned. It could be modulated," Kaul said.Justice Kaul, who retired in December 2023, wrote that differences over how to deal with the executive strained his relationship with Justice Chandrachud, under whom he served on the Collegium from June 2022."There is a difference between consultation and what I came to regard as pre-approval, seeking the government's nod before the collegium had even formally deliberated," Kaul wrote in his memoir.Explaining why he considered Justice Chandrachud "too deferential to the government on appointment matters," Kaul said the practice could create difficulties for future Chief Justices, particularly those with shorter tenures."Well, he believed that this is how it had been happening, and I was of the view that you, with a chief justice like you, and with two years' tenure, and with your own merit and the trust, if you do this, the successors would have a problem in not following this practice because they have shorter tenures.""And the government would get used to a particular methodology before appointments to the Supreme Court were made, and that's why I endeavoured to discourage him from discussing everything beforehand," Kaul said.The former judge also raised objections to the transfer of a case concerning the reconsideration of certain aspects of a Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) judgment from a bench headed by him to another bench. He argued that cases should not be reassigned because of apprehensions about how a particular bench might decide them.Congress flags judicial independence concernsThe Congress on Sunday raised concerns over the independence of the judiciary under the Narendra Modi government, citing revelations in the forthcoming memoir. The party asserted that the institution responsible for upholding the Constitution must remain free from pressure exerted by those in power.Congress general secretary in-charge of communications Jairam Ramesh shared a media report quoting the pre-publication manuscript of Kaul's memoir, Without Fear of Favour, which reportedly states that Chief Justice of India (CJI) Justice D Y Chandrachud was "too deferential to the Government" on judicial appointments.In a post on X, Ramesh said, "A book by former Supreme Court judge Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul has raised serious questions regarding the independence of the judiciary during the tenure of the Modi government."Ramesh said Kaul had highlighted several concerning incidents, including alleged government interference in judicial appointments, attempts to secure government approval before Collegium meetings and the government's questioning of the caste of a judge belonging to a minority community.He added that issues many had previously been hesitant to discuss openly had now been documented by Kaul in measured and deliberate language."Strikingly, a former Chief Justice of India (CJI) has not denied that discussions with the government take place prior to judicial appointments. When former CJI Justice Chandrachud acknowledges that the government engages with the CJI and plays a role in the appointment process, the concerns surrounding judicial independence become even more profound," Ramesh said.
The Congress leader also flagged Kaul's account of an incident involving a case under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). According to Ramesh, Kaul revealed that after a bench presided over by him raised the possibility of reconsidering certain aspects of a court ruling in the case, the matter was reassigned to another bench without consulting him.
"This points to the extent of the government's day-to-day interference in the functioning of the Supreme Court," Ramesh said.Questioning the implications of the alleged incidents, he said, "When there is pressure to obtain government approval for judicial appointments, and when benches hearing sensitive cases are altered, one must ask -- in the interest of safeguarding democracy -- if this does not constitute pressure on the judiciary and an erosion of its independence, then what does?"Emphasising the importance of judicial independence in a democracy, Ramesh said, "The institution tasked with upholding the Constitution must remain free from the pressures of those in power. In a democracy, the independence of the judiciary is not merely an option; it is an absolute necessity," Ramesh asserted.

Uganda to impose 21-day quarantine on returning citizens with Congo travel history
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:35:53 CET
20:35:53 KST

By Elias Biryabarema
KAMPALA, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Ugandan citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to Democratic Republic of Congo will be quarantined for 21 days, Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi said on Sunday as Uganda tightened Ebola precautions despite saying it remained Ebola-free.
Uganda has been investigating a Nigerian Ebola case involving a woman who had travelled from Uganda. Officials said they were reviewing genomic sequencing, travel information, interactions and movements in coordination with Nigerian authorities and international partners.
Baryomunsi said on Sunday that all 60 contacts linked to a Kenyan Ebola case had completed their 21-day monitoring period and been discharged. The contacts were traced across points of entry and exit, hotels and transport operators linked to travellers’ movements through Uganda.
“The ministry has intensified traveller screening at Entebbe International Airport and all land border crossings. All travellers intending to enter Uganda by air, land or water must complete the passenger locator form,” he said.
Genomic analysis of Nigeria’s only confirmed Ebola case showed the virus was closely related to the strain detected in Kenya’s index case, though Nigerian authorities said there was no evidence that the Kenya case travelled to Nigeria or had a direct connection.
Uganda borders Congo, where the outbreak began, and has previously battled Ebola outbreaks.
(Reporting by Elias BiryabaremaWriting by Colleen Goko in JohannesburgEditing by David Goodman)

Factbox-Serbia election: Main players, voter concerns and what is at stake
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:35:07 CET
20:35:07 KST

By Canan Sevgili, Arda Dipova and Ivana Sekularac
Oct 25 (Reuters) - Serbia is holding parliamentary elections on Sunday, in which a popular student movement is seeking to end the rule of longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic.
Here are the main players, issues and stakes in the vote.
WHO ARE THE MAJOR PLAYERS AND WHAT DO THEY STAND FOR?
Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia: The Serbian Progressive Party (SNS)-led electoral list is campaigning on economic growth, higher wages and pensions, infrastructure investment and political stability. SNS leader Milos Vucevic has pledged 4% economic growth in 2027. Vucic, who resigned as president on September 27, is running to become prime minister.
Students Win: Emerging from protests over the November 2024 Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse that killed 16 people, the anti-corruption movement has campaigned for accountability and transparent public procurement. The Democratic Party and Kreni Promeni movement have backed it rather than fielding their own lists.
Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) – Ivica Dacic – Factor of Stability: A longstanding ally of the SNS, the pro-Russian SPS leads a coalition with Unified Serbia, the Social Democratic Party of Serbia and the Greens of Serbia. It campaigns on social justice, workers’ rights and welfare, political stability, and national interests.
European Serbia: A pro-European opposition alliance led by Marinika Tepic and Zdravko Ponos, bringing together the Party of Freedom and Justice, Serbia Centre, and the Solidarity, Self-Defence and Liberation movement. It advocates closer European integration, sanctions against Russia and democratic reforms.
WHAT ARE PARTY LISTS AND HOW DO THEY WORK?
Political parties, party coalitions, movements and other groups can submit party lists, or electoral lists comprising no more than 250 candidates.
The election commission has approved a total of 18 lists.
On election day, voters vote for one electoral list on the ballot, rather than individual candidates.
WHAT ARE THE MAIN ISSUES FOR VOTERS?
Corruption and government accountability have dominated the campaign since the Novi Sad disaster. Protesters accuse Vucic and his allies of corruption, controlling the media and mistreating demonstrators, allegations the authorities deny.
Living standards, economic development and the fairness of the electoral process are also campaign issues.
HOW WILL A VICTORY OR LOSS FOR VUCIC IMPACT SERBIA AT HOME AND ABROAD?
A victory allowing Vucic to become prime minister would extend his political leadership and could preserve Serbia’s balancing act between its ambition to join the European Union and maintain Belgrade’s close ties with Russia and China.
A defeat could pave the way for sweeping domestic reforms, including stronger institutions and measures against corruption.

EU extends sanctions against Jacques Baud
The European Union has extended the sanctions against Jacques Baud, a former colonel in the Swiss Army General Staff, who is accused of spreading pro-Russian propaganda, until October 9, 2027. He remains subject to an asset freeze and travel restrictions.
According to official EU documents reported by the French-speaking Swiss online media outlet L’Impertinent, on October 8 the Council of the European Union renewed the sanctions regime against Russia’s “destabilising activities”, which targets 80 individuals and 20 entities.
Added to this list on December 15, 2025, the 71-year-old Brussels resident is accused of his contributions to media outlets described as pro-Russian and of spreading “conspiracy theories”. The EU Council criticises him in particular for accusing Ukraine of having orchestrated its own invasion in order to join NATO.
Initially, Brussels accused him of supporting Russian actions that “undermine or threaten the stability or security of a third country (Ukraine)”. The new text now refers to actions that “undermine democracy and threaten the stability or security of a third country”. Ukraine is no longer explicitly mentioned, and the conjunction “or” has been replaced by “and”. The specific allegations remain unchanged. The EU has not provided any justification for the rewording.
The individual concerned disputes the allegations: “I have never received a single cent from Russia,” he stated in December 2025, notably in an interview with L’Impertinent. The 71-year-old claims to base his analyses on Ukrainian and American sources and disputes, in particular, the interpretation of his statements regarding the Russian invasion. In his view, these statements referred to an interview given in 2019 by Oleksiy Arestovych, who was to become an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Baud brought a case before the General Court of the EU last March seeking the annulment of his inclusion on the list.
+ Switzerland approves 20th sanctions package against Russia
A retired colonel of the General Staff, born in Geneva, Jacques Baud worked for the Swiss secret services from 1983 to 1990, where he was responsible for analysing Warsaw Pact forces. He subsequently held various posts with the UN, notably in Sudan.
Highly critical of the EU’s and Western countries’ policies on the war in Ukraine, Baud has a large online following, particularly on YouTube, where his videos have racked up several million views.
The sanctions are having a serious impact on his daily life. Baud can no longer freely access his bank accounts, particularly to access his pension. He also claims he is unable to leave Belgium.
After several months of restrictions, a humanitarian exemption had allowed him to regain access to his Belgian account from mid-March to the end of June. Since the beginning of July, he says, the funds have once again been inaccessible. A new exemption requested at the start of May was granted by the Belgian authorities at the start of October, but by the middle of the month it had still not been implemented.

Iran to add 3,800 MW of thermal power capacity to national grid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:29:29 UTC
20:29:29 KST

Iran to add 3,800 MW of thermal power capacity to national grid
TEHRAN – Iran plans to add 3,800 megawatts of new thermal power generation capacity to its national grid in the next Iranian calendar year (begins late March 2027), as the electricity sector faces financial pressures that threaten investment in infrastructure, a deputy energy minister said.
Mostafa Rajabi-Mashhadi, deputy energy minister for electricity and energy affairs, said the gap between regulated electricity tariffs and the actual cost of supply was increasing the sector’s outstanding receivables and debts while reducing its capacity to finance infrastructure development.
Without sustainable funding to offset the shortfall, the situation could further weaken investment, while covering the gap through the public budget could put additional pressure on government finances and widen the budget deficit, he said, according to IRIB.
Rajabi-Mashhadi said gradual electricity pricing reform, targeted support for vulnerable households and expansion of competitive electricity markets were among the measures needed to improve the sector’s financial sustainability and encourage new investment.
Industries to play a growing role in power generation
Of the 3,800 MW of thermal power capacity expected to come online next year, the capacity being developed by industries for their own electricity needs will be about twice that of new power units being built by the Energy Ministry, Rajabi-Mashhadi said.
The figures reflect the growing role of industrial companies in investing in electricity generation to meet domestic demand, he added.
He also highlighted the expansion of electricity trading on the Energy Exchange as a way to improve price transparency, facilitate transactions and strengthen incentives for investment and consumption management. Deepening the market could help bring electricity supply and demand into closer balance, he said.
Smart meters to support demand management
Rajabi-Mashhadi said the rollout of smart electricity meters was another key element of demand management, allowing more accurate monitoring of consumption and more effective implementation of tariff policies.
The meters also enable authorities to control the power consumption of high-use customers within established regulations, a measure that could help curb excessive demand and ease pressure on the grid during peak hours.
The Energy Ministry aims to encourage public participation in managing electricity consumption, he said. Customers who keep consumption within prescribed limits will benefit from incentives, while high-use customers are encouraged to adjust their consumption patterns and pay for electricity consumed above the prescribed level at rates reflecting its supply cost.
Power sector prepares for winter supply pressures
Rajabi-Mashhadi said fuel supplies for power plants were entering a critical period ahead of winter. Although stocks of liquid fuel at power plant storage facilities were at satisfactory levels, constraints on natural gas supplies and rising seasonal demand could make it more difficult to secure enough gas for power generation.
He said the electricity sector needed to be fully prepared for the critical 100-day winter period to ensure reliable energy supplies.
Achieving that goal would require coordination among the relevant sectors to secure fuel supplies, keep power plants operational and encourage all consumers to manage electricity and gas use, he added. The aim is to get through the period with minimal disruption to the country's energy network.

Energy Ministry implements 60 measures to secure electricity supplies during winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:29:17 UTC
20:29:17 KST

Energy Ministry implements 60 measures to secure electricity supplies during winter
TEHRAN – Iranian Energy Ministry is implementing 60 operational measures to ensure stable electricity supplies during the winter and mitigate the potential impact of fuel shortages, while power plants’ liquid fuel reserves remain at satisfactory levels, the country's electricity industry spokesman said.
Ehsan Zabihzadeh said more than 80 percent of the fuel consumed by thermal power plants comes from natural gas, with most facilities designed to operate primarily on gas. Liquid fuels serve as a backup to improve grid reliability and help offset potential gas supply constraints, he added, according to IRIB.
Gas supplies to power plants and their liquid fuel inventories are currently in a favourable position, Zabihzadeh said. Liquid fuel stocks are roughly at the same level as a year earlier, when reserves were particularly strong, and the trend this year has also been positive so far.
Some storage capacity remains to be filled, but the remaining tanks are expected to reach capacity in the coming days and weeks as winter approaches, with the help of the Oil Ministry, he said.
However, maintaining reliable electricity supplies throughout the winter will depend not only on initial preparedness but also on continued gas allocations and the timely delivery of liquid fuels, Zabihzadeh said.
Authorities have designated a roughly 100-day period, beginning in mid-December, as the main window for winter preparedness and have coordinated plans to secure power plant fuel supplies with the Oil Ministry, he added.
60 measures to manage winter constraints
Zabihzadeh said attacks attributed by Iranian officials to Israel and the United States had damaged gas supply infrastructure, reducing part of the country's gas supply capacity compared with last year, according to statements by Oil Ministry officials.
The electricity sector has therefore drawn up 60 operational measures to get through the 100-day winter period with minimal disruption. Implementation of the measures is progressing satisfactorily, he said.
The main steps include completing essential power plant maintenance on schedule, accelerating renewable energy development to increase electricity generation without fuel consumption, advancing maintenance at the country's nuclear power plant so it can return to service at the beginning of the cold season, and optimizing hydropower generation.
Improving the efficiency of thermal power generation is also a priority, Zabihzadeh said. Authorities aim to maximize the use of high-efficiency generating units and reduce diesel consumption, particularly in northern Iran, where power plants face a greater risk of fuel supply constraints.
Maintenance of the electricity grid and major energy transmission corridors is receiving greater attention than in previous years, he added, as authorities seek to minimize transmission bottlenecks that could restrict electricity supplies during winter.
Energy conservation remains a priority
Zabihzadeh said coordination among different sectors was essential to managing energy consumption and maintaining reliable electricity supplies throughout the cold season.
Government agencies and public institutions should lead by example in conserving energy, while all electricity and gas consumers should help manage demand, he said.
Reducing energy consumption can lessen the impact of potential fuel shortages, Zabihzadeh added, stressing that conservation should extend beyond winter. Even small savings can have a meaningful effect if sustained and adopted as a long-term practice.

Iran seeks to expand gas trade with GECF members

Iran seeks to expand gas trade with GECF members
TEHRAN – Iran is seeking to expand gas trade with members of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF), develop a common gas market and strengthen energy cooperation, the country's acting oil minister said ahead of the group's eighth summit in Russia.
Hamid Bovard said Iran would hold bilateral talks with oil and energy ministers from member countries on the sidelines of the summit to discuss expanding cooperation and bilateral activities.
Iran, a founding member of the GECF, would outline its positions through President Masoud Pezeshkian at the leaders' summit and through the acting oil minister at the group's ministerial meeting, Bovard said, according to Shana.
Key issues on the agenda include protecting energy infrastructure during wars and crises, expanding gas trade among exporting countries and identifying ways to increase exchanges, he said.
Bovard added that Iran would also push for the establishment of a common gas market and closer coordination among exporting countries to develop common policies on gas exports.
On relations with Russia, Bovard said the two countries had established cooperation in the energy sector, with Russian companies holding contracts to develop several Iranian oil and gas fields. Negotiations on gas exchanges between the two countries are also under way, he added.
"We hope to achieve positive results during this trip and further pave the way for strengthening cooperation and expanding energy exchanges between Iran and Russia," Bovard said.
Bovard travelled to Moscow on Sunday to accompany Pezeshkian at the eighth GECF summit and attend the forum's 28th ministerial meeting.
The ministerial meeting is scheduled for Monday, a day before the leaders' summit. An extraordinary meeting of the GECF Executive Board, chaired by Seyed Ali-Mohammad Mousavi, Iran's deputy oil minister for international affairs and commerce, and a meeting of the Ad Hoc High-Level Committee were also scheduled for Sunday.
The meetings are expected to review and finalize key documents, including the summit's final declaration.
The GECF provides a framework for dialogue and coordination among natural gas-producing and exporting countries. Its meetings address developments in gas markets, supply and demand outlooks, energy security and the role of natural gas in the global energy mix.
Other areas of focus include developing natural gas markets, monitoring trends in the liquefied natural gas (LNG) industry and assessing investment needs to meet future demand.
The forum's leaders' summit is held every two years. Previous summits took place in Doha in 2011, Moscow in 2013, Tehran in 2015, Santa Cruz de la Sierra in Bolivia in 2017, Malabo in Equatorial Guinea in 2019, Doha in 2022 and Algiers in 2024.
The GECF has 12 full members: Algeria, Bolivia, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Iran, Libya, Nigeria, Qatar, Russia, Trinidad and Tobago, the United Arab Emirates and Venezuela. Angola, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Malaysia, Mauritania, Mozambique, Peru and Senegal participate as observer countries.
According to figures cited by the forum, its members collectively hold about 70 percent of the world's proven natural gas reserves, account for 38 percent of global marketed gas production and 42 percent of global gas exports. Their share of global LNG exports is estimated at around 47 percent.

Polls opened across Brazil at 8 am local time on Sunday as voters began casting ballots in a closely contested presidential runoff between incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and conservative Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
The election pits 80-year-old Lula of the Workers' Party against 45-year-old Bolsonaro, the eldest son and political heir of former President Jair Bolsonaro.
The runoff follows a competitive first-round vote on October 4, when Bolsonaro led with 47 percent of valid votes against Lula's 45 percent. Neither candidate secured an outright majority.
The contest enters election day in a statistical dead heat, with a Datafolha poll showing both candidates tied at 50 percent of valid votes.
The election has centred on the rising cost of living, public insecurity and persistent corruption concerns affecting Brazilians' daily lives.
Lula, who governed Brazil from 2003 to 2010, returned to power after defeating Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 presidential election by less than two percentage points.
The victory marked the narrowest presidential margin in modern Brazilian history. Lula is now seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term.
Flavio Bolsonaro entered the race after his father was barred from holding public office and sentenced to 27 years in prison following investigations into a planned military coup after his 2022 defeat.
The former president's political base remains strong, with his wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, securing a seat in the Federal Senate during first-round voting.
A victory for Flavio Bolsonaro would mark a return of the right in Brazil and align the country with a broader conservative shift across the region linked to the Trump administration in the US.
More than 150 million registered voters are expected to cast their ballots electronically across Brazil's 26 states and the Federal District.
Preliminary results are expected shortly after polls close at 5 pm Brasilia time.

Jared Kushner, the Bank of Israel, and the difference between allegations and facts - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:18:09 UTC
20:18:09 KST

I know Jared Kushner. I have spoken with him personally on several occasions. I know that he worked hand in hand with Steve Witkoff to bring the Israeli hostages home from captivity in Gaza. I know that Kushner cares deeply about the future of the State of Israel. I also believe that he is one of the few people with real influence in the Trump administration who genuinely cares about the future and welfare of the Palestinian people.
I cannot speak about Kushner’s private business dealings, his financial affairs, or every aspect of his work in the Middle East. I have no firsthand knowledge of those matters, and I will not pretend otherwise.
I can speak to his involvement in efforts to help Israelis and Palestinians. I have witnessed an evolution in his thinking, and in my judgment, that evolution has been for the better. I believe he increasingly understands that Israel’s future cannot be separated from the future of the Palestinian people.
That is why I read with particular interest the extraordinary allegations published in Vanity Fair on October 22, in an article by Matthew Cole concerning Kushner’s alleged secret financial arrangements in the Middle East.
One allegation immediately caught my attention. The article claims that approximately $1 billion was transferred into an account at the Bank of Israel, supposedly connected to Kushner and, according to one source, intended for his personal benefit.
This story has a fundamental problem.
The Bank of Israel is not a commercial bank. It is Israel’s central bank. Private individuals cannot simply open accounts there.
This is not a matter of opinion. It is how the Israeli banking system operates. The Bank of Israel maintains accounts for the government, banking institutions, certain financial entities, and authorized foreign central banks and financial institutions. It does not offer private banking services to individuals, whether they are Israeli citizens, American businessmen, or presidential advisers.
Allegations of private Kushner account incompatible with bank rules
If the allegation is that Kushner personally opened or controlled a private account at the Bank of Israel, it is incompatible with the bank’s published rules.
Could money have moved through an institutional account? That is a different question and would require specific evidence. But the published allegation raises an obvious question that should have been answered before publication: Who was the legal account holder, and how could Kushner supposedly control the funds?
I do not know whether the other financial allegations in the article are true or false. But when an investigation makes an extraordinary claim involving a central bank without adequately explaining how such an arrangement could exist, it raises serious questions about the reliability of its reporting.
Extraordinary allegations require extraordinary scrutiny. They should not be accepted simply because they make sensational headlines.
My defense of Kushner is not based on political loyalty. I have disagreed with American administrations, including this one, on fundamental questions concerning Israel and Palestine. I judge people by what I know of their actions and by whether they contribute to a better future.
In Kushner’s case, I have seen someone willing to engage with difficult realities and to reconsider positions. I have seen someone who understands that diplomacy requires more than repeating established formulas. Most importantly, I believe he recognizes that a sustainable future for Israel must also offer Palestinians dignity, opportunity, and hope.
After decades of working for Israeli-Palestinian peace, I have learned to recognize the difference between people who speak about peace and people who may actually help make it possible.
Kushner increasingly an ally of those seeking peace between Israelis, Palestinians
In my personal judgment, Kushner is increasingly an ally of those of us who have devoted our lives to achieving Israeli-Palestinian peace.
That does not place him above criticism or scrutiny. No one should be above either. But criticism must be grounded in facts, and serious journalism must distinguish between evidence and speculation.
The claim about a private account at the Bank of Israel deserves a clear explanation. Until one is provided, I see no reason to accept it – and every reason to question the credibility of that part of the story.
The writer is the Middle East director of the International Communities Organization and the co-head of the Alliance for Two States.

Türkiye urges Greece to respect minority’s choice of muftis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:18:00 UTC
20:18:00 KST

AA Photo
Türkiye on Oct. 24 called on Greece to recognize Muslim religious leaders elected by the Turkish minority in Western Thrace, accusing Athens of disregarding religious freedom by appointing its own muftis in the region.
“We call on the Greek authorities to recognize the legitimate muftis elected by the minority and to refrain from attempts to impose appointed muftis,” the Turkish Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
The statement came after the Greek government appointed muftis for five-year terms in the cities of Komotini and Xanthi, following an earlier appointment to the Didymoteicho mufti office in January.
The Turkish minority in Western Thrace has elected İbrahim Şerif as mufti of Komotini and Mustafa Trampa as mufti of Xanthi.
Turkish Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmuş also urged Greece to comply with the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne, which established the framework for the protection of minority rights in the region.
“Attempting to determine a community’s religious practices and representatives through state intervention is incompatible with both the law and the fundamental principles of democracy,” Kurtulmuş said in a statement.
Western Thrace, in northeastern Greece, includes the cities of Komotini, Xanthi and Alexandroupoli and is home to a Muslim minority estimated at around 150,000 people.
The appointment of muftis has long been a point of contention between Türkiye and Greece. Ankara argues that Muslim religious leaders in the region should be elected by the members of the community they serve, citing international agreements, including the Treaty of Lausanne.
Greece, which maintained an election system for muftis until 1985, subsequently shifted to government appointments.
Athens does not officially recognize the Muslim minority in Western Thrace as a Turkish minority, instead identifying it by its religious affiliation.
