Demand for UK government action 10 months after British man’s death in Grenada
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:00:01 UTC
20:00:01 KST

A time-critical investigation into the death of a British father whose body was found in a ransacked property on the Caribbean island of Grenada has stalled because of diplomatic delays between the two countries.
Charity workers supporting the family of Andrew Frederick are demanding immediate government intervention to clear the path for a full investigation to begin almost 10 months after his death, which has been ruled a homicide by a pathologist.
The Murdered Abroad charity has called on the foreign affairs select committee to step in after Grenadian police found there was “no basis … that any homicide has occurred” and closed the case.
This was despite a report from an autopsy, done in the week he died, saying Frederick, 47, had suffered “blunt force trauma”, was tortured, including by removal of his toenail, and ruling the death a homicide.
Frederick’s body was found on 4 January. Since then, the family say they have been forced to focus on their fight for justice instead of coming to terms with their loss.
Murdered Abroad’s founder, Eve Henderson, said: “We understand there are challenges but [almost 10 months] on, this family is still being met with obfuscation. If a family this determined cannot get the FCDO [Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office] to put their diplomatic powers to good use, what hope is there for the 60 to 80 families bereaved by murder abroad each year?
“A minister must look urgently at how consular services treat these traumatised families or the foreign affairs select committee must step in,” she added.
A former Scotland Yard homicide commander who is supporting the family described Grenada’s actions as “incredible”.
“In the autopsy report … the pathologist, who is a qualified medical examiner, categorically states that he believes this is a case of homicide and that Andrew was tortured before he was killed,” David Johnston said. “And yet the police just choose to ignore that because it didn’t fit with their model. I mean, it’s incredible.”
After a sustained campaign by the family, British authorities became involved and Frederick’s body was repatriated to the UK in August, where a second autopsy was carried out, during which it was discovered his organs were missing.
The family described this discovery as “shocking and devastating”.
In a statement, they said: “We were already heartbroken that Andrew’s life was cruelly taken, but nothing could have prepared us for what we would learn afterwards. For six weeks after his death, Andrew’s body was held under the control of the Grenadian authorities. When he was later examined in the UK, parts of his neck and all of his organs, including his brain, heart, and lungs, were missing.
“That discovery has been shocking and absolutely devastating for our family; we are still struggling to process it. It has added pain upon pain and left us with deep hurt with so many unanswered questions. Despite our multiple inquiries, no one has told us where they are, what happened to them, or why we were never told. No family should ever have to ask these questions.”
Last month a UK coroner asked the Metropolitan police to conduct an investigation. Weeks later a communication from UK authorities, seen by the Guardian, said a British high commissioner had raised Frederick’s case with officials at the highest levels of government in Grenada, and indicated that authorities there had agreed to cooperate with any forthcoming formal request for the UK to assist with the investigation.
That formal request was sent weeks ago but the family say they are still waiting for Grenada “to honour their verbal commitment to the British high commissioner and approve the request to cooperate”.
“Every day for almost 10 months we have had to live without Andrew and without answers. A formal request from the UK, asking Grenada to cooperate with its investigation into Andrew’s death, still sits unsigned. It is the best chance we have of finding the truth,” the family statement said.
Johnston said the initial handling of Frederick’s case and the further delays could have a detrimental effect on the investigation.
“In a homicide investigation we have a phrase that we refer to as the golden hours, which are the first real 24 hours from the notification, or the discovery, of a homicide [which] are the most important and crucial … because evidence diminishes and can be lost if a crime scene is not properly noted and properly managed.
“In the case of the death of [Frederick] that’s exactly what happened … the police, in my view, failed to properly identify and preserve the crime scene and to treat the crime scene in the manner it should have been treated,” he said.
Johnston added that cooperation between British and Grenadian police could help to “bring some stability to that investigation”.
An FCDO spokesperson said: “We are supporting the family of a British man who died in Grenada, and are in contact with the local authorities.”
The Guardian has approached the Royal Grenada Police Force for comment but has not had a reply.
The family said: “With each passing day, our family’s heartbreak deepens. We need closure, and Grenada’s prime minister, who is also the minister of national security, can help make this possible. We appeal to him, with humanity and compassion, to sign the request without further delay.”
Additional reporting by Calistra Farrier

Arup creates arrow-shaped viewpoint for Fehmarnbelt Tunnel project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Arup creates arrow-shaped viewpoint for Fehmarnbelt Tunnel project
A zigzagging path tops the demountable Pilen viewpoint in Denmark, created by engineering firm Arup to give the public views of the construction of the vast Fehmarnbelt Tunnel.
Fehmarnbelt Tunnel is an 18-kilometre-long road-and-rail tunnel being built underwater between Rødbyhavn in Denmark and Puttgarden in Germany to improve links between continental Europe and Scandinavia.
Pilen, whose name means “the arrow” in Danish, offers views of its construction site to help the public gain an understanding of its scale.
According to Arup, its design is intended to symbolise travel, evoking an arrow or compass needle, and it points to the site where the tunnel emerges in Germany to orient users.
The ramped structure measures 217 metres in length, reflecting the size of each of the 89 individual concrete elements that will form the tunnel, which will be the longest of its kind.
“The arrow-shaped design points towards the location where the Fehmarnbelt tunnel emerges on the German side, acting as a large compass needle for visitors,” project architect Kristian Winther told Dezeen.
“At 217 metres long, the viewpoint also reflects the length of one of the tunnel elements,” Winther continued.
“We hope the viewpoint will create a closer connection between the tunnel project, the local community, and visitors, giving people an opportunity to experience the scale of the project more directly.”
Pilen was designed for contractors Femern, which is overseeing the tunnel’s construction and wanted to open up the construction site to the public.
The site was chosen for its proximity to the tunnel portal, maximising views of construction work, but also for the expansive views of the coastal landscape beyond.
Pilen’s structure is built from landfill timber and steel and designed to be demounted once the tunnel is complete.
To facilitate this, all the components, including the foundations, are engineered to be easily reused in other projects, “helping to give the materials a life beyond the viewpoint itself”, Winther said.
The main deck is formed from timber and landscaped with greenery and local vegetation, through which a fully accessible landscaped walkway zigzags as it rises 24 metres above sea level.
Fehmarnbelt tunnel is scheduled for completion in 2029. It is expected to reduce journey times between Hamburg and Copenhagen to 2.5 hours by train.
We recently reported on a 300,000 square metres land reclamation scheme in Denmark created as part of the project, which will be landscaped with ponds and planting.
Other viewpoints recently featured on Dezeen include the Titlis Tower in the Swiss Alps by Herzog & de Meuron and Lech Mountain Mirror in the Austrian Alps by Snøhetta.
Photography by Rasmus Hjortshøj

This absolutely stacked version of the MacBook Pro is one of the most powerful laptops you can buy. Rumors say that they will sport the same chip options as the current MacBook Pros, meaning we'd get an M5 Pro and M5 Max once again. So if you're mostly interested in the performance, you can save some serious cash by snagging this M5 Max deal.

Bulgaria votes for president in election dominated by Ukraine war and the economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:59:15 UTC
19:59:15 KST

The campaign has focused on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and an increase in drone attacks on commercial vessels off Bulgaria's coast in the Black Sea, as well as rising energy prices and inflation.
Bulgarians are heading to the polls to elect their president on Sunday, in a campaign that has mostly revolved around growing concerns over the economy and drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea.
The vote will be the first major test of Prime Minister Rumen Radev's Progressive Bulgaria party since it came out on top in parliamentary elections last April.
Despite a record 27 candidates, the race is expected to be decided in a runoff between incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who is backed by Radev's party and favours dialogue with Moscow while opposing military aid to Ukraine, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who is backed by pro-Western opposition parties.
Yotova is expected to win between 41% and 47% of the vote, while Gyurov is polling between 28% and 31%.
The leader of the pro-Russian far-right Vazrazhdane party, Kostadin Kostadinov, is in third place on 10-13%.
The campaign has focused heavily on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the widening hostilities in the Black Sea, where recent drone attacks on commercial vessels off Bulgaria’s coast have heightened security concerns in the European Union and NATO member country.
The strikes have raised concerns over Russia’s intentions to escalate the conflict, while also compelling the government to ask Bulgaria's partners for assistance to strengthen its maritime security.
Candidates have also looked to respond to public anxiety over rising energy prices and inflation, as many families, particularly in rural areas, struggle to make ends meet.
Two main candidates among record total of 27
Main frontrunner Yotova took over this year as president of Bulgaria when Rumen Radev stepped down to run in parliamentary elections, eventually becoming prime minister.
If successful she would become the first woman ever elected president in Bulgaria's history. A win for Yotova would be a boost for Radev, who has also called for dialogue with Moscow.
A former journalist and member of the European Parliament, Yotova was elected vice-president alongside Radev in 2016 and 2021.
Her main challenger is economist Andrey Gyurov, a former deputy governor of the central bank and caretaker prime minister in the first few months of 2026. He is supported by the pro-Western reformist opposition.
Gyurov has often expressed firm support for Ukraine, and signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his premiership.
Polling stations will close at 8 pm local time, after which initial exit polls will be announced while preliminary results are expected on Monday.
Turnout must be above 50%, and the winner needs a majority of votes. Projections have Sunday’s turnout at less than 40%, indicating a likely runoff on 1 November.

Thousands protest against Netanyahu ahead of Israeli election (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:55:26 UTC
19:55:26 KST

Thousands protest against Netanyahu ahead of Israeli election (VIDEO)
A major protest against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has taken place in Tel-Aviv just days ahead of the Israeli parliamentary election on October 27.
A square outside the Museum of Art in the country’s largest city was packed on Saturday evening, with the demonstrators holding national flags and banners, reading ‘Change will come’, ‘No more Mr. Far Right Guy’ and other slogans.
The organizers of the gathering from the October Council group put the attendance at over 100,000. The police have yet to announce official figures.
Netanyahu’s main rival in the election – Yashar party chairman and former military chief of staff, Gadi Eisenkot – and other leaders of the opposition bloc have attended the rally. The crowd cheered Eisenkot’s appearance, chanting: “Who’s coming? The next prime minister.”
The October Council was formed by families of the victims of the attack on Israel by Hamas on October 7, 2023, who demand accountability from Netanuahy’s right-wing government for the failure to prevent the incursion.
Saturday’s protest, organized with the title ‘In Three Days, Vote for a State Commission of Inquiry’, is the culmination of three years of weekly rallies, according to the group.
The State Commissions of Inquiry, which are independent panels appointed by the Supreme Court, are usually set up in Israel to investigate major failures by the authorities. However, Netanyahu refused to establish such a probe into October 7, insisting that it would be biased against his government.
Reports in the US and local media claimed that the prime minister ignored warnings of the planned attack by Hamas he had received from various sources, including Israeli intelligence and the UAE and Egypt. Netanyahu has denied those claims.
A poll by public broadcaster KAN published before the start of the election silence period on Friday, suggested that Eisenkot’s opposition bloc would get 52 out of 120 in the Israeli parliament, with Netanyahu and his supporters winning 50 seats. This means that neither is likely control the Knesset outright.
Israel responded to the October 7 incursion by Hamas, in which 1,200 people lost their lives and around 250 were taken hostage, by launching a military campaign in Gaza.
Israeli airstrikes and a ground offensive have killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children, and injured over 175,000 others in the enclave over the past three years, according to the local Health Ministry. More than 1,500 deaths happened after a US-brokered ceasefire went into effect in October 2025.

Ukrainians feel betrayed by Trump&apos;s policy toward Russia: the U.S. is effectively helping Moscow — NYT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:55:16 EET
19:55:16 KST

Ukrainians feel betrayed by Trump's policy toward Russia: the U.S. is effectively helping Moscow — NYT
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainians criticize the U.S. purchase of Russian diesel fuel and the easing of sanctions. The NYT writes about reduced aid and a rising death toll.
Ukrainians are increasingly feeling frustrated with the policies of U.S. President Donald Trump, who is attempting to restore economic relations with Russia amid its full-scale war against Ukraine. Washington’s decision to purchase Russian diesel fuel and ease sanctions against Moscow caused particular outrage. This is reported by The New York Times, according to UNN.
Details
As the publication notes, during Joe Biden’s presidency, the United States described Ukraine’s struggle as the forefront of a global confrontation for freedom and democracy. By contrast, the current White House administration is increasingly viewing the war through the prism of economic agreements with the Kremlin. Ukrainians were particularly distressed by Trump’s decision to purchase Russian diesel fuel and temporarily ease the relevant sanctions. Experts believe that such steps could provide the Russian economy with additional revenues that Moscow could use to continue the war.
The NYT emphasizes that this is happening against the backdrop of a sharp reduction in U.S. aid to Ukraine and intensified Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure. At the same time, Trump continues to demand that Kyiv halt attacks on Russian oil refineries, even though these strikes are one of Ukraine’s important instruments of economic pressure on the aggressor.
Pavlo Kazarin, a serviceman of the Unmanned Systems Forces and a journalist, said in a comment to the NYT that Washington’s current policy is destroying the reputation of the United States, which previous American administrations built over decades by supporting democracy and their allies. According to him, the U.S. administration does not realize that the goal of Russian aggression is to destroy Ukraine as an independent state.
Human rights defender, head of the NGO "Center for Civil Liberties," and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Oleksandra Matviichuk also criticized the Trump administration’s approach to peace negotiations. She stressed that Washington’s focus on territorial issues and economic agreements with Russia, without due attention to the deaths of civilians, sends a dangerous signal to the Kremlin.
According to the UN, in 2025 the number of civilians killed and injured in Ukraine increased by 31%. In the first half of 2026, this figure rose by another 37% compared with the corresponding period of the previous year.
The publication emphasizes that the growing distance between the U.S. president’s position and the reality Ukrainians face every day is causing a profound sense of betrayal.
We remind you
Somewhat earlier, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that he would try to restore the damaged relationship between Ukraine and the United States.

Over 400,000 march across France in serious challenge for Macron
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:55:00 UTC
19:55:00 KST

Clashes broke out in Paris Saturday following nationwide protests that drew more than 400,000 people over school funding and rising living costs, leading to nearly 1,000 arrests in a fresh challenge to President Emmanuel Macron.
The Paris march began peacefully, a week after widespread rioting and looting during protests across the country. But near the demonstration's endpoint in eastern Paris, masked protesters hurled objects and fireworks at police, who answered with clouds of tear gas, deafening sound grenades and jets of water cannons.
Officers with megaphones urged protesters to disperse. Some demonstrators panicked as tear-gas canisters landed in their midst, scattering with screams. Veteran protesters shouted after them: "Don’t run!"
The Interior Ministry put nationwide turnout at 410,000 – fewer than the 550,000 it said protested last weekend – while the CGT union that helped organize some of Saturday's protests estimated nearly 800,000.
The ministry’s estimate included 110,000 in Paris, where authorities confined the march to the city’s southeastern edge, away from the center. The CGT put the number of protesters in Paris at 250,000.
More than a month of unrest that started with protests in high schools for more funding and teachers is testing Macron’s authority in the final months of his presidency before voters choose his successor in May.
The stakes are high: The far-right National Rally party has accused his government of failing to protect the public and urged people to channel their anger into votes for its candidate Marine Le Pen.
On the far left, presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has backed demonstrators and criticized policing that has left some teenage protesters with life-changing injuries.
As dusk fell Saturday, violence erupted at the end of some of the 289 protests counted by the Interior Ministry nationwide. Street fires burned in the cities of Marseille and Lyon.
Police used tear gas in Lyon, Clermont–Ferrand, Strasbourg and Bordeaux and water cannons in Nice and Nantes, French media reported. In Nice, far-right extremists fought with demonstrators downtown and 11 people were arrested, regional authorities said.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said police made nearly 1,000 arrests but added that the number is expected to increase significantly as more are counted.
Nunez said beefed-up policing, with 70,000 officers backed by helicopters, armored vehicles and other support, helped prevent a repeat of widespread looting and damage to shops the previous weekend.
What began last month as a protest over staff shortages at one high school southeast of Paris spread nationwide, drawing students demanding more funding for education and workers seeking help with soaring costs for fuel and other necessities.
In Paris, Benedicte Pittion, a 46–year–old teacher, marched with her 16-year-old daughter, Garance, a high school student – in their first protest together.
"The young people who have been demonstrating have not been heard, and as a parent and as a teacher, I stand with them," Pittion said.
Garance said she'd been "really scared" after seeing the previous weekend’s violence, but felt that staying away would hand the government a victory.
Macron met high school representatives Friday. They said he had promised to overhaul university admissions, but they called for protests to continue until concrete measures are announced.
Soumaya Abed, a 58-year-old nurse wearing a red CGT union vest, complained that authorities in Paris wanted to stifle protesters by making them march on the capital's outskirts, keeping them away from the center where the Louvre and other major museums closed exceptionally.
"But it won’t stop the movement. It won’t stop students from demanding better conditions in schools," she said.
Other protesters expressed anger about record poverty and wealth inequality under Macron. Camille Chesnier, 27, said she hasn't found work despite having an engineering degree and a master’s degree.
"There are enormous numbers of people in the same situation as me but who aren’t privileged and who find themselves living on the streets and in squats and, frankly, it’s very tough," she said."
In Marseille, police put attendance at 17,000, while the CGT union estimated 100,000. In the southwestern city of Toulouse, 26,500 people joined the protests, according to authorities. Authorities had banned rallies in cities including Lyon, Nice and Montpellier.
Trade unions criticized the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.
Thousands also marched Saturday in Orleans, south of Paris, in a separate peaceful protest against the far right as Le Pen’s National Rally held a two-day congress in the city.
Gendarmes stood guard Saturday beneath the Arc de Triomphe and shopkeepers boarded up storefronts across Paris. Near the Saint-Lazare train station Saturday, Akram Ahmed, a 34–year–old contractor, was boarding up an optician’s shop.
"I got the call last night," he said. "The owner seemed desperate. He said I was saving his life."
Art Basel, one of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.
Student groups want 250,000 more places in higher education and an end to selection through Parcoursup, the national admissions system.
Their joint 10-point plan also calls for more teachers and repairs to schools and universities.
They are also seeking help with everyday costs: an extra 200 euros ($224) a month in student grants and a rent freeze in public student housing.
Energy prices in France were 21.3% higher in September than a year earlier, helping drive overall inflation to 3.1%, according to the national statistics agency, INSEE.
Paris protester Louis Ledoux-Xatard voiced frustration over inequality.
"Looking at countries like the United States, we don’t want to end up like them, where part of the population has everything and the others have nothing," he said.
"I never imagined that I’d be taking to the streets so much before my thirties."

Iran’s authorities take ‘self-sacrifice’ mobilisation campaign nationwide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:50:38 UTC
19:50:38 KST

Iran’s authorities take ‘self-sacrifice’ mobilisation campaign nationwide
The IRGC says it wants to use main squares in every capital of Iran’s 31 provinces for the Janfada campaign.
Iran’s authorities are increasing investment in a campaign to arm and train civilians who would serve in the state security apparatus against domestic and foreign threats amid growing fears that fighting with the United States and Israel could resume imminently.
The public mobilisation drive – called Janfada, or “those who sacrifice their life” – was launched in late March at the peak of the war with the US and Israel. It has now spread to large parts of the country and is aiming to attract volunteer men and women. It has a stated focus on youth but is open to all ages.
At their numerous street booths and stations, representatives of the Basij militia of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and other state bodies offer training on using weapons and other equipment to defend the government and its “revolutionary” values.
State-organised events and armed “exercises” linked with the mobilisation campaign have been held in Tehran, Isfahan, Zanjan, Shiraz, Kerman, Mashhad, Bojnord, Ahvaz and other big and small cities across many of Iran’s 31 provinces.
Ali Kowsari, Basij’s deputy for training, announced during a news conference this month that the IRGC wants to use at least 14 main squares across Tehran as training and equipment stations for Janfada volunteers. The goal is to use at least one to three squares in the capital city of every single province, he said, without divulging how many cities are currently being used as part of the campaign.
State-run nighttime events are sometimes held with rallies and motorcades during the day. A resident of Gilan province in northern Iran told Al Jazeera that people regularly see state-run stations on the streets in big and smaller cities across the province during their commutes.
“Sometimes they hold competitions to win some small prizes. They bring in live bullets, teach people how to load them into magazines, how to arm pistols and assault rifles, and how to aim and fire,” the resident said, asking to remain anonymous for security reasons.
“The organisers are mostly old men. Since the start of the war, they’ve gathered around the main square almost every night, also often playing revolutionary tunes and chanting from loudspeakers.”
In Gilan’s city of Rasht on October 15, residents objected to the noise and blocking of the street for the nighttime pro-government gathering. Videos circulating on social media showed a confrontation that escalated into a brawl although the authorities did not comment.
On Saturday, authorities cautioned residents in Alborz province’s Karaj near Tehran that they could expect explosions and loud noises from one of the Janfada exercises.
‘Revolutions are like riding a bicycle’
Last week, there was a big mobilisation campaign in northwestern Iran’s Kurdistan province, which borders Iraq.
The IRGC-linked Tasnim News Agency characterised a procession in the provincial capital, Sanandaj, as an exercise in “unity” between the Shia and Sunni Muslim populations.
But a number of foreign-based Iranian human rights groups have characterised such armed mobilisation efforts as “intimidation” campaigns that are held months after January’s nationwide protests, during which thousands of civilians, including many young people, were killed from gunshots and stab wounds.
The government has acknowledged that protests took place in more than 400 counties across all provinces but describes them as a “coup” attempt wholly orchestrated by the US and Israel to overthrow the establishment. It also rejected findings by an independent United Nations fact-finding mission that said the authorities committed crimes against humanity while cracking down on the protests.
Mehran Kamrava, a professor of government at Georgetown University in Qatar, said the US-Israeli war on Iran has “presented another opening for the more revolutionary elements of the Iranian body politic”.
“Revolutions are like riding a bicycle. To avoid a nasty fall, you must pedal hard. And this is precisely what the Janfadas and their leaders are trying to do – to remain relevant,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The Janfada’s training mobilisation also gives the more revolutionary-minded figures within the Iranian leadership a chance for choreographed displays of political and ideological loyalty to the revolution and its principles,” the professor said.
‘Siege mentality’
The government said 33 million Iranians have signed up on the campaign’s website but has provided no evidence to support this number.
It represents more than a third of the country’s population, or more than half of the over-12 population, men and women.
Earlier this year, foreign-based activists accessed the website’s source code, which showed that fewer than four million people had registered. Only a phone number was required for registration, and no national identification number was needed.
Speaking last week about the political goals of the campaign, Nematollah Bagheri, IRGC commander for the province of Lorestan, said: “The aim is to show that, just as the government supports the people, the people support the Islamic Republic and the Islamic revolution.”
Organisers said registrants could be used in future rescue operations and for social services and media and financial support. The government has also asked them to help ease the pressure of the US war, naval blockade and sanctions by consuming less fuel, electricity and other resources.
The establishment’s efforts to expand the campaign have only grown after nearly eight months of attritional war, which has killed thousands of people, made Iranians poorer and seen parts of the country’s civilian infrastructure destroyed.
Children have become a major focus for the campaign, and schools have increasingly been accommodating mobilisation. Last week, Education Minister Alireza Kazemi said the Basij militia was registering “student Janfadas” and had plans for more mobilisation and ceremonies involving children over the coming weeks.
Kamrava, the university professor, said this kind of mobilisation does not necessarily broaden the scope of the state’s legitimacy among the larger society.
“It does, however, serve to deepen the legitimacy that the state already has among its existing supporters. It reinforces belief in the revolution’s ideological and political mission and reifies the siege mentality that all revolutionaries have,” he said.

Saudi Arabia intercepts missiles and drones as fighting with Houthis rages
Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted drone and missile launched towards Riyadh and 10 missiles targeting the southern region.
Saudi Arabia has intercepted drones and missiles over its capital, Riyadh, and southern areas, the Saudi-led coalition has said, as fighting with Yemen’s Houthis continues.
Coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki said on Sunday its forces intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards the capital city that morning, as well as a drone in the Riyadh region, and a cruise missile aimed at the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, with explosions ringing out in the Saudi capital.
It later reported the interception of 10 ballistic missiles fired towards southern Saudi Arabia.
The fall of debris following the destruction of two ballistic missiles in Khamis Mushait and Ahad Rafidah caused two injuries, the Saudi Civil Defence agency said. In a post on X, it added the shrapnel also damaged three residential buildings and seven vehicles.
The attacks come as operations resumed at two terminals at Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid international airport after deadly attacks earlier this month by the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).
Operations at the airport were halted on October 10 after 13 people were killed and more than 300 others were wounded in a Houthi attack.
Late on Saturday, Riyadh airport said in a statement that international flights would resume from Terminal 2 on Sunday, while Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that the airport was still “unsafe” and a “military target” for the Iran-backed group.
“The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional and local airlines – as well as staff and travellers – against using King Khalid airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces,” he said. “The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport.”
The Iran-aligned Houthis on Saturday said they targeted three Saudi airports, including one in Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an airbase.
The Saudi civil defence agency said it also responded to falling debris in the Mecca and Medina regions on Saturday after intercepting two Houthi missiles.
The Houthis denied targeting Mecca and Medina, two of the holiest cities in Islam, calling the Saudi claim a “huge lie”.
In Yemen on Sunday, the Houthis advanced on Jabal Sabr, the strategic mountain overlooking the city of Taiz, which has become the focus of the fighting between the Houthis and Yemen’s government forces.
Houthi fighters have besieged the city and cut off the main road to Aden, which serves as the interim capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
The United Nations has warned that “time is running out” to deliver aid to the 800,000 people trapped in the city.
Yemen’s government forces, meanwhile, said they conducted more than 700 operations against Houthi targets on Saturday, claiming to have killed more than 300 fighters.
Fighting between government forces and Houthi fighters has intensified across multiple fronts in Yemen in recent weeks, causing a spiralling humanitarian crisis.
The war in Yemen escalated sharply when the Houthis seized strategic territory from forces loyal to the country’s internationally recognised government along the Red Sea coast last month.
The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, which is aligned with Yemen’s government forces, have dealt a huge blow to the kingdom, the world’s biggest exporter of crude oil, disrupting its businesses, airlines and normal life, and damaging its international image.

Vucic's mission: Can Serbia's longtime leader secure new mandate? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:42:18 UTC
19:42:18 KST

As Serbs head to the polls on Sunday in one of the most consequential elections in the country's recent history, Aleksandar Vucic is asking voters to place their confidence once again in the political leader who has dominated the Balkan country for more than a decade, overseeing a period of considerable economic development while pursuing a distinctive foreign policy that has allowed Serbia to maintain productive relations with the US, Russia, China, and Israel among them.
Vucic, who resigned as president on September 27, is seeking to return to the prime minister's office, having served as prime minister between 2014 and 2017 before winning the presidency.
This election provides an opportunity to secure a fresh public mandate following almost two years of political unrest, after student-led demonstrations that began after the collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad in November 2024, which killed 16 people and prompted widespread accusations of corruption, negligence, and a failure of public accountability.
Vucic is the head of a list called United Serbia, made up predominantly of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), a party he helped found almost two decades ago, and the Serbian Radical Party, PUPS, the Serbian People's Party, the Workers' Party, the People's Peasant Party and the United Peasant Party.
Despite the two-year-long demonstrations, Vucic enters Sunday's contest with advantages, particularly among voters who associate his leadership with the modernization of Serbia's infrastructure, alongside improvements in living standards, and the stability of a country whose recent history since the breakup of Yugoslavia has been marked by conflict and economic uncertainty.
United Serbia coalition leading student-backed list, survey shows
An Ipsos survey published on Thursday placed his United Serbia coalition at 47.4% against 40% for the student-backed list, suggesting the governing bloc retains a sizable electoral base despite the sustained campaign against it. The survey, conducted among 3,624 respondents, was commissioned by Vucic's coalition, while other opinion polls have suggested a considerably closer race or an opposition lead.
The outcome remains uncertain, although the figures do indicate somewhat the continuing appeal of a leader whose critics have repeatedly predicted that his political dominance was approaching its end - a situation one may apply to Israel as the country heads to the polls on Tuesday.
From an Israeli perspective, Vucic's continued leadership would preserve an important and valued relationship with a European country that has maintained close diplomatic and defense ties with Israel (especially since October 7), frequently taking positions at odds with those of other European governments.
During an exclusive interview with The Jerusalem Post at the Presidential Palace in Belgrade last year, Vucic spoke candidly about Serbia's decision to supply Israel with military equipment almost immediately following the October 7 massacre, despite criticism from European leaders.
“I am the only one in Europe today dealing in military ammunition with Israel,” he told this writer at the time. “And it is why I am often criticized by colleagues.”
Vucic explained that Serbia had moved quickly to assist Israel in the days following the Hamas attacks, expediting the necessary government approvals to enable the transfer of urgently needed military supplies. The relationship has since deepened, with the two countries expanding cooperation in defense technology and military production, including plans for a joint drone manufacturing facility involving Israel's Elbit Systems.
The relationship also goes beyond defense cooperation. Trade and investment have grown considerably in recent years, while the two countries have also deepened their diplomatic engagement, culminating in the establishment of a formal strategic partnership earlier this year, which Foreign Minister Marko Djuric told the Post was an “historic step forward.”
Vucic: Serbia-Israel relationship rooted in shared history, security challenges
Vucic has consistently emphasized that Serbia's relationship with Israel is rooted in a shared history and an understanding of the security challenges facing both countries, sentiments he expressed during the interview in Belgrade.
“Our ties with Jews and Israelis – this is something different from a historical perspective up to the present day,” he said. “This isn’t policy or current politics, no. This is our politics of all times, and it will always have to remain so.”
With regard to the United States, Serbia's affinity with US President Donald Trump since his reelection is seen among its population, with a 2024 Gallup International survey finding that 59% of respondents would have supported him over Kamala Harris, the highest figure recorded in Europe. Earlier this month, Trump praised the Serb-US relationship, telling Newsmax Balkans that the two countries enjoyed "very good relations."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Djuric also launched a strategic dialogue in July covering economic cooperation, security, and energy infrastructure. For Vucic, closer relations with the US are a major development given the troubled history between the two countries, particularly NATO's bombing of Serbia in 1999, while potentially helping Belgrade diversify its dependence on Russia.
Serbia has also developed an increasingly close relationship with the United Arab Emirates, where investment and trade, alongside energy cooperation, have strengthened diplomatic ties between Belgrade and Abu Dhabi.
Vucic's friendship with UAE President Sheik Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan has become an important component of that relationship, with the Serbian leader expressing solidarity with the Emirates following the outbreak of the war with Iran in February.
One can see through these relationships the diplomatic approach Vucic has pursued throughout his leadership: cultivating close ties with Israel, the US, and Arab partners while maintaining longstanding connections with Russia and China, whose investments in Serbian infrastructure and industry remain important to the country's economic development.
Sunday's election will also determine whether Vucic can successfully navigate a considerable personal political transition.
Having served as prime minister between 2014 and 2017 before winning the presidency, his resignation last month opened the way for a return to the office through which he first consolidated his leadership of Serbia. His decision does carry some political risk, particularly given the strength of the opposition movement, but it is also a reflection of Vucic's confidence that his electoral appeal remains sufficiently strong to secure another governing mandate.
For a country of approximately 6.5 million people, Serbia has established a diplomatic presence considerably greater than its demographic or economic weight might suggest, cultivating relationships with major powers and influential Middle Eastern partners while continuing to pursue its own national interests.

A life-size bronze statue of Marwan Barghouti, a senior Fatah official serving five life sentences in Israel for his involvement in the murder of five people in terrorist attacks, has been placed atop a building on High Holborn in the Camden borough of central London, alongside a giant Palestinian flag hanging from the building.
Camden Council is investigating whether the statue was installed legally and whether planning permission was required.
The investigation followed a complaint filed on Thursday by the pro-Israel British legal organization UK Lawyers for Israel (UKLFI). The following day, the council's planning enforcement department confirmed that an investigation into the property was underway and that the complaint had been referred to the relevant officer. At this stage, no determination has been made that the statue was installed unlawfully.
The statue depicts Barghouti with his handcuffed hands raised above his head, his fingers forming a V for victory, resembling the well-known photograph taken after his arrest. It stands on the roof of Palestine House, a Palestinian cultural and community center founded by Osama Qashoo, a Palestinian filmmaker and activist living in the UK.
Qashoo was among the founders of the Free Gaza Movement in 2007 and one of the organizers of the Gaza flotilla. He was aboard the Mavi Marmara when Israeli naval commandos took control of the vessel in May 2010. His name also appears in a document published by the Meir Amit Intelligence and Terrorism Information Center following the incident. Palestine House hosts cultural events, film screenings, and exhibitions.
Activists campaign for Barghouti's release from prison
Barghouti, 66, was convicted in Israel in 2004 of five murders and sentenced to five life terms plus an additional 40 years in prison. Despite his lengthy imprisonment, he continues to hold considerable political standing in Palestinian society, and his supporters have been conducting an international campaign for his release.

Previous complaints have concerned Palestinian flags displayed near the building, a giant advertisement for a beverage called Gaza Cola, and an illuminated sign bearing the slogan "Stop the Genocide." The council ordered some of the signs removed and refused to grant retrospective approval for other illuminated signage.
UKLFI seeks to remove statue due to property being in conservation area
UKLFI is challenging the installation of the Barghouti statue on planning and legal grounds, arguing that neither the statue nor its base appears in the building plans approved in July 2025. The organization emphasizes that the property is located in a conservation area and that approval for the rooftop extension was based partly on assurances that it would not be particularly prominent when viewed from street level. It is now demanding an investigation into whether the statue alters the building's appearance in a way that requires separate planning permission.
The legal organization has also sharply criticized the council's handling of the matter on public and moral grounds.
"Camden Council's failure to enforce the law in relation to this building is a disgrace," a UKLFI spokesperson said.
According to the spokesperson, the authorities' conduct encourages violations of the law and undermines public confidence, particularly when controversial messages and the glorification of an individual convicted of terrorism are involved.

Why partisan politics may be changing people's accents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:42:05 UTC
19:42:05 KST

With the midterms fast approaching, communicating just the right message has been top of mind on all sides of the political aisle.
Whether that message drives home a lack of affordability as gas, food and home prices surge or stokes fears about the rise of communism in the American heartland, Democrats and Republicans are spending a lot of time thinking about what to say.
But as a linguist who studies the impact of accents on the way people are perceived, I believe how politicians and voters say what they say might be just as important as the words they use in understanding the social consequences and linguistic changes resulting from the political divides that are growing between us.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Sounds of the South
If there is one regional American accent that has long endured on the lips of its speakers—as well as in the minds of listeners beyond the region—it’s the Southern accent. From North Carolina through Texas and pretty much all states in between, the so-called Southern drawl has long been emblematic of a distinct culture found in the South.
Yet, in the urban South, recent linguistic research finds that the drawl’s most salient features are starting to fade on the lips of young speakers. Fewer “pins” are merged with “pens,” and pronunciations such as “far” for “fire” or “say-ud” for “said” are becoming rarer.
While linguists have been busy trying to understand this trend, political scientists have been measuring how different accents perform on the campaign trail. The verdict? Southern accented candidates are generally heard as more conservative than those without a Southern accent, particularly to Democratic listeners.
Putting these findings from linguists and political scientists together, alongside a spate of studies examining correlations between voting patterns and vowels, hints, I believe, that the increasing conservative-liberal divide in American politics just might be the key to understanding what’s driving the decline of the drawl in the urban South.
Out of the mouth of the South
The traditional Southern accent has no shortage of stereotypes: From positive, friendly, country and down-home vibes to negative, backward, uneducated and lazy tropes, the accents of William Faulkner, Bill Clinton and the hillbilly Clampetts have weathered it all.
The reality, of course, is that the Southern accent is not some incorrect version of a national standard but instead a historically separate and unique dialect—or, more accurately, set of dialects.
As explored in my recent book, this dialect formed from linguistic variation that came in with colonial-era settlers from different places and stations. The incipient differences increased after the Civil War intensified hostilities and cultural differences between the North and South.
The association with “countryness” often triggered by a Southern accent grew out of this region’s agricultural past and its related cultural folkways. But what “country” has come to mean relies largely on stereotypes about what a country lifestyle involves. They include things like hunting, gun ownership and less socially progressive views—often arising from media portrayals of and beliefs about the South.
As the South has become more and more industrialized over the past half-century, these social meanings associated with the accent’s use now highlight a disconnect between its new urban vibe and its older, traditional rural one.
Voting and vowels
As rural vs. urban ideological and political divides in the U.S. have intensified, so has using symbolic means to signal this opposition.
Pickup trucks emblazoned with American flags and country music have become politicized. The white Southern accent, by virtue of its association with more rural traditional values, has also become emblematic of a conservative political identity not all modern Southerners share.
Recent linguistic research has compared voters in the South who had strong Southern accents to those with weaker ones, mainly measured through their use of a set of unique Southern vowel pronunciations, such as saying “bay-ud” for “bed” or “rawed” for “ride.”
It turns out that those holding more right-leaning positions and voting Republican in previous presidential elections used significantly more Southern vowels than those with more left-leaning positions who voted for Democrats. Three separate studies in Georgia, North Carolina and Tennessee discovered the same relationship between degree of Southern accent and political conservatism or liberalism.
The takeaway from these studies is that conservatism itself is embodied in a strong Southern accent.
New sound to the urban South?
The pronunciation of one’s vowels has become a barometer of how one’s beliefs and values fit within the old vs. new South.
Conservative ideologies and politics have become enmeshed with “country” speech and lifestyles. Young urban Southerners who don’t identify with these traits might be moving not so much away from Southern identity itself but rather specifically from this rural conservative identity it is often associated with.
Of course, other factors are also playing a role in the decline of the Southern accent in cities, such as heavy migration by non-Southerners to the region and greater interaction with people from other dialect areas via social media.
Outside the South, interestingly, recent research has found a greater embrace of Southern accent features, emerging in particular among those in rural areas where traditional lifestyles and, often, more conservative views are embraced. For instance, in a small, rural town in Ohio, speakers who identified themselves as more drawn to country lifestyles showed use of vowel features—such as saying “baa” for “bye”—more associated with the South.
So, in this circuitous and indirect way, vowels have become the latest players in partisan politics: Democratic Southerners wanting to distance themselves from the ideological and political climate associated with the rural South are moving away from its unique vowels. More “traditional” or conservative-leaning speakers continue to embrace them.
The real casualty in this particular battleground might be the obscuring of a larger culture, practice and community that the Southern accent has long represented for those who are automatically—and often erroneously —assigned a politicized identity just by the sound of their voice.
This article was first published by The Conversation. Read the original article here.

Suspect in racist Paris shooting transferred to psychiatric unit, had drugs in his system
A shooter suspected of killing one person and wounding five others on Friday in the town of Trappes, near Paris, has had his police custody suspended for a 48-hour psychiatric observation, anti-terror prosecutors said Sunday. The 39-year-old man is believed to have had racist motivations behind the gun attack as most of the victims had foreign origins.
A man suspected of a gun attack in the Paris suburbs that killed one person and wounded five has left custody and been placed in a psychiatric unit for observation, French anti-terror prosecutors said Sunday.
The 39-year-old suspect, partly identified as Kevin T., was arrested Friday in possession of a submachine gun and tear-gas grenades in his car, shortly after the victims were shot as a vehicle drove through the working-class town of Trappes and neighbouring La Verrière.
President Emmanuel Macron had branded the shooting a "racist terrorist attack", as most of the victims were from foreign backgrounds.
Read moreMacron says 'racist terrorist attack’ in Trappes marks turning point for France
The French National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office (PNAT), which is handling the case, on Saturday extended the suspect's time in detention to pursue its interrogation.
But on Sunday, the PNAT said: "After a psychiatric examination of Kevin T. carried out in the evening (of Saturday), his custody has been lifted."
It said that, in line with conclusions from a psychiatric expert, he "was transferred to the police psychiatric unit to be subjected to a psychiatric observation period likely to last 48 hours".
That observation period "should allow us to evaluate whether his state of psychiatric health is compatible with pursuing his interrogation sessions".

The person killed in Friday's shooting was a 26-year-old man of Congolese origin, Pengo Bossio Wangi.
One of those wounded was a 12-year-old girl who was hit by bullets eight times. She remains in a critical condition.

AP Photo
The heads of all eight of Slovakia's regions were reelected, according to results released yesterday.
Incumbents supported by populist Prime Minister Robert Fico's ruling coalition retained two regional leadership posts in the election on Oct. 24. The candidates of parliamentary pro-Western opposition retained four regions while independents kept the remaining two posts.
In a notable contest in the eastern Prešov region, the head of the opposition Christian Democrats, Milan Majerský, won with over 48 percent of the vote, beating a candidate nominated by the far right Republic party, who received 35%. The Republic is currently the third most popular party in Slovakia, according to polls.
A parliamentary election in Slovakia, a country of 5.4 million people and a European Union and NATO member, will take place next year.
In a separate election traditionally dominated by independent candidates, Matúš Vallo, representing the opposition, was reelected for the third time as mayor of the capital, Bratislava.

Germany news: Fire flares up at Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:36:00 UTC
19:36:00 KST

Germany news: Fire flares up at Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat
Published October 24, 2026last updated October 25, 2026
What you need to know
- A fire that has almost destroyed a retreat in the Bavarian Alps used by dictator Adolf Hitler flared up again overnight
- Most people in Germany believe the conservative-led coalition government will come to a premature end, a survey shows
- The German president is to present a prestigious environmental prize
- Low-cost carrier Ryanair has followed through with its plan to close its base at Berlin's international airport
- Chancellor Friedrich Merz has addressed the Bavarian CSU party conference as the governing coalition faces high degree of dissatisfaction
Read below for a roundup of stories making news in Germany for the weekend of October 24-25.
Fire flares up again overnight at Hitler's mountain retreat
A fire that broke out on Friday evening at the Eagle's Nest mountain retreat in southern Germany that was once used by Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler erupted again overnight to Sunday in the almost destroyed building, Bavarian police said.
A police officer said flames there burnt again at "room height" after smoldering embers provoked a flare-up in what the officer said was a common occurrence in the case of such conflagrations.
The renewed fire triggered another deployment of firefighters to the site, known as Kehlsteinhaus in German, at the top of the Obersalzberg mountain.
The site, formerly used by Hitler to receive diplomats and other foreign guests, has been a restaurant since 1952 but was closed on Friday when the fire broke out. No one was injured.
Police arrested a 33-year-old German man suspected of having lit the fire, with an initial psychiatric assessement indicating mental illness.
The building was largely destroyed by the blaze, which caused millions of euros of damage.
IN DEPTH: Audi defends decision to open plant in US
After US President Donald Trump on Saturday announced that car producer Audi would build a $4 billion (€3.77 billion) assembly plant in the state of Georgia, the company has defended its planned move against criticism that it goes against German interests.
"This decision was preceded by many months of careful planning and intense negotiations," CEO Gerbot Döllner told reporters on Sunday.
"If the American president invites you, you accept the invitation. That is what respect for the office and for the country in which we invest demands," he said, arguing that the plan could protect jobs in Germany by boosting the carmaker's global business.
The move is yet to be approved by the supervisory board of Volkswagen, which owns Audi.
You can read more here: Trump announces Audi will build $4 billion factory in US.
German Environmental Prize goes to climate-action lawyer and wastewater engineer
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has presented this year's prestigious German Environmental Prize, worth €500,000 ($560,150), to a lawyer specializing in environmental cases and an engineer who has developed high-performance filters for wastewater plants.
At a ceremony in the western city of Aachen, Steinmeier commended Hamburg-based lawyer Roda Verheyen and engineer Klaus Vossenkaul as models of environmental protection.
"They show that each and every individual can make a difference," he said.
According to the German Federal Environmental Foundation (DBU), which awards the prize, Verheyen received the honor for "getting justice done for the environment."
In his speech, Steinmeier said she had shown many people ways to fight for their interests amid human-induced climate change.
Among other things, he said, her constitutional complaint against the climate protection law in 2021 played a decisive role in the Constitutional Court's ruling that Germany should become climate-neutral by 2045.
Speaking about Vossenkaul, Steinmeier said the engineer was a prime example of "creativity and inventiveness" in the field of environmental protection.
The president said the membrane technology developed by Vossenkaul helped to make wastewater plants more economical in terms of space, energy and cost, thus protecting "our basis of life."
Most expect coalition government to fall before end of term — survey
Just one in four people in Germany (23%) believes that the coalition of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative bloc and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) will last its full term till the next federal elections at the start of 2029, a survey has shown.
Some 44% said they believed the coalition would end within the next two years, according to the YouGov survey of 2,202 eligible voters, while around 13% are even convinced that the coalition will not see out the year.
Conservative voters who support parties in the so-called Union — the alliance of Christian Democrats (CDU) and Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) — are less optimistic about the coalition's continued existence than SPD supporters.
A whole 53% of CDU/CSU voters expect a premature end to the coalition, compared with just 32% who think it will last out its term.
That compares with the 46% of SPD voters who doubt the coalition's long-term viability, with 34% trusting it will cohere until 2029.
Twenty percent gave no opinion on the issue.
The coalition has been divided over a reform of Germany's pension and welfare systems, as well as over the best way to deal with the challenge posed by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which beat the mainstream parties in recent state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Football: Bayern Munich coach Kompany to remain in hospital after collapse
Bayern Munich head coach Vincent Kompany is set to remain in hospital for several days and will be missing for a number of weeks after collapsing at the club's training center on Friday.
The 40-year-old Belgian had recently been suffering from a virus and collapsed while observing a reserve team training session.
"The good news is he's stable," said Bayern's director of sport, Max Eberl, on Saturday. "I spoke with him last night, and with his wife too. It wasn't a nice moment for any of us. He collapsed on the pitch yesterday and will spend a few more days in hospital until everything is checked over."
Eberl said that doctors are "trying to find out what it is," adding: "The tests have already yielded some results, but further results are needed to determine exactly what it is and how long it will take for him to recover."
Eberl said it will be a while before Kompany is fit to return to work. "We're not talking in terms of days, but weeks," he said. "We're all clear on that."
Kompany will miss Bayern's game away at high-flying SC Freiburg on Sunday, with assistant coach Aaron Danks set to stand in for him. He will also miss next week's Bundesliga Klassiker at home to Borussia Dortmund and the difficult trip to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League on November 3.
"It shows again that health is the most important thing in life, not football," said Eberl, stressing that Kompany will "only come back when he's fit."
Bayern will also travel to Freiburg on Sunday without captain Joshua Kimmich, whose father passed away aged 57 this week.
Goalkeeper Manuel Neuer will also miss the game due to "persistent tendonitis" in his foot, as will defender Min-jae Kim, playmaker Jamal Musiala and forward Luiz Diaz.
Ryanair closes base, cuts routes at Berlin's international airport
Low-cost Irish airline Ryanair has closed its base at Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER), and removed 12 routes there at the start of its winter timetable.
The move was announced in April and confirmed in October, with the airline having long complained about high taxes and fees at German airports.
Six of the 12 deleted routes, from BER to Palermo, Marseille, Triest, Reggio Calabria, Tallin and Pisa, can now no longer be directly reached on flights from the airport, the airline and the airport operator FBB said.
The other six — Gran Canaria, Fuerteventura, Lanzarote, Bologna, Thessaloniki and Vilnius — are served by other airlines flying from BER.
The seven Ryanair aircraft that were based at the BER airport have been reassigned to airports in European Union countries that, according to Ryanair, have got rid of aviation taxes or reduced airport charges.
Ryanair is to still fly to and from Berlin using planes based elsewhere.
The operators of BER have pointed out that despite Ryanair's move, eight more destinations can be reached from the airport than last winter, as other airlines have expanded their services at the airport.

German national facing trial over alleged attempt to join 'Islamic Sate'
Germany's prosecutor's office said that a German national has been placed in pre-trial detention for allegedly attempting to join the so-called "Islamic State" terror group, while abroad, German news agency dpa reported.
The agency cited a spokeswoman for the Federal Prosecutor's Office as saying that an arrest warrant had been executed and that a 21-year-old was extradited to Germany.
The suspect is accused of travelling to Ethiopia from Berlin in January 2025, with the purpose of joining the IS terror group in Somalia and receive training there.
Prosecutors allege that he never reached Somalia, but instead traveled to Pakistan to join Islamic State, where he was reportedly arrrested in February 2025.
The suspect stands accused of attempted membership in a terrorist organization abroad. He is also accused of preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state.
Merz highlights threat from Russia
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz highlighted the threat Germany faces from extremist parties to foreign enemies, including a "massive threat" from Russia.
"How do we safeguard our freedom and our security in Europe, in the face of growing threats from extremists within and foreign powers from without?" the chancellor said, adding that Russia was seeking "to destabilise Germany on a daily basis."
Germany is one of the biggest military and political supporters of Ukraine and has been on high alert for acts of sabotage in recent months.
That's especially since an explosive-laden drone was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport. Berlin said Moscow was behind the attempted attack.
In one of the most recent incidents, on Thursday, police in the German state of Brandenburg arrested a Ukrainian man on suspicion of spying for Russia.
No change to 'firewall' when it comes to AfD, says Merz
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz once again stood firm on any notion of ever working with Germany's far-right.
Merx restated his opposition to any change in the"firewall" policy of isolating the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) at the CSU conference in Munich.
"Anyone who feels they have to vote for these people has no place in our Union. They have no place amongst us," Merz said.
The AfD, has been topping national opinion polls although a Friday poll showed Merz's conservative bloc closing the gap.
Nevertheless, according to the poll, Merz's coalition would still fall short of a majority were an election to be held.
The poll, conducted for public broadcaster ZDF, asked voters which party they would support if a federal election were held this Sunday.
Merz confident electricity tax can be lowered
Chancellor Friedrich Merz gave an indication that the electricity tax could be lowered next year.
"If it’s possible — and I think it is — then the electricity tax must be lowered next year," Merz said Saturday at the CSU party convention in Munich.
His coalition partners have already agreed to lower the electricity tax for everyone to the European minimum as quickly as possible.
To date, the federal government has only approved reductions for industry, agriculture, and forestry and Germany's Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil (SPD) has said there is not much wiggle room, despite forecasts of higher tax revenues.
Merz calls for CDU and CSU to 'stand together'
Federal chancellor and CDU leader Friedrich Merz called on the CDU its Bavarian sister party, the CSU, to show maximum unity.
"The CDU and CSU must stand together more closely than ever," Merz said at the close of the CSU's party convention in Munich.
He said the Union is being attacked by "extremists" from the political fringes and said that the Union does not want to — and will not leave Germany in the hands of these forces.
Merz emphasized his relationship with CSU leader Markus Söder, saying that he was "the strong voice" for the CSU in Bavaria, but also at the federal level.
"We are united by a deep-seated sense of responsibility for our country," Merz said, adding that it was a shared responsibility.

Clashes erupted across France on Saturday as protesters took to the streets, a week after marches that degenerated into violence and prompted a firm security backlash from French President Emmanuel Macron, who is scrambling to restore order.

Riot police squads fired tear gas at protesters in the capital as well as in Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Lille, Toulouse, Montpellier and Nantes.
Two people were “seriously” injured, Nunez said: one man in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off, and another person in Clermont-Ferrand. He did not give details of either case.
Authorities had deployed 70,000 security personnel across the country for the new marches, called to protest the cost of living.
The violence came a week after rioting that saw public buildings vandalized, hundreds of shops looted and 2,700 people arrested, casting a pall over the country six months before an election to choose Macron’s successor.
Nunez said Saturday’s outcome was more “positive” than a week ago, with more police on the streets acting more rapidly, conducting more pre-demonstration checks and better protecting businesses.
But there was widespread anger at the government over a protest crackdown viewed as an assault on the right to protest.

Macron’s government has ordered police to prevent protesters reaching city centers, where shops are concentrated, and in Paris and some other cities, partial curfews were imposed in certain urban zones.

Oil Spills Wreak Havoc on the Bottom of the Ocean, Even a Decade Later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

This story originally appeared on Inside Climate News and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
Across hundreds of miles of the northern Gulf of Mexico, a deepwater ecosystem collapsed after the massive 2011 Deepwater Horizon oil and gas spill, and recovery is uncertain, new research concludes.
The study, published Monday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, found that animal populations—including octopus, krill, squid, and shrimp—declined by 60 to 85 percent in the three and a half years after the spill, with few signs of recovery since. Krill and lanternfish, both foundational species in the Gulf’s food web, were among the hardest hit. The findings also suggest that the die-off is causing genetic bottlenecks that could further hinder ecosystem recovery.
The researchers identified it as the “fastest and most severe faunal decline reported for Earth’s largest ecosystem type” ever documented. The widespread die-off of marine organisms may also reduce the ocean’s ability to transport carbon dioxide from the atmosphere to the deep sea. After ruling out other factors, such as water temperature and oxygen levels, the researchers identified the Deepwater Horizon blowout as “the most parsimonious explanation” for the ecosystem’s collapse.
Comprehensive natural resource damage assessments and restoration efforts involving federal, state, and tribal trustees are ongoing. In 2016, BP agreed to a $20.8 billion settlement, including up to $8.8 billion for environmental restoration.
Remote ocean depths and habitats miles below the surface may seem buffered from the impacts of human activity, the authors wrote, but their findings suggest an industrial disaster pushed part of it into a diminished state with “limited resilience to facilitate recovery.” They said their findings also show that proposed industrial deep-sea mining could damage the ecosystem before baseline conditions are assessed.
A transoceanic drilling rig, operating for BP about 50 miles southeast of the Mississippi Delta, exploded on April 20, 2010. The explosion and fire killed 11 people and triggered the largest accidental marine oil spill in history.
Oil and gas spewed uncontrollably from the broken well nearly a mile deep for 87 days, ejecting 4.9 million barrels of oil at a rate of about 400 tanker trucks per day, enough to fill up 1.2 million cars. The spill also released about 7.7 billion cubic feet of fossil gas into the deep sea at a rate of 88 million cubic feet per day, enough to supply about 820,000 US homes. State and federal agencies, including the Environmental Protection Agency, also authorized BP to apply 1.84 million gallons of chemical dispersants to try to reduce the impacts.
Some of the oil and gas dissipated and was transported out of the deep Gulf of Mexico region. Some coated barrier islands and devastated coastal wetlands and shellfish habitat, and some settled onto the ocean floor, where currents can stir it back into the water. But enough hydrocarbon and chemical-dispersant remnants stayed suspended long enough to do almost immeasurable harm.
A series of studies since the spill have shown a wide range of toxic effects on marine organisms, from impaired development and reproduction to increased mortality and lasting health problems in dolphins and whales. The new paper suggests that lingering pollutants may interfere with some species’ ability to find mates in the dark by disrupting their highly developed sense of smell.
The impacts continue to ripple through the ecosystem, said lead author Tracey Sutton, a professor of marine and environmental sciences at Nova Southeastern University in Florida. A 2024 study found an 80 percent decline in deep-diving toothed whales, he said.
“We used to have a big resident population of sperm whales right off the Mississippi River, but we haven’t seen a sperm whale in 10 years,” he said. Large predators need big, occasional dense patches of prey, and those have disappeared, he added.
Scientists have developed accurate ways to count fish. For this study, they started with a baseline from nine months of sampling in 2011 and compared it with nine subsequent surveys between 2015 and 2023. The researchers sampled deep-pelagic habitat along a large grid around the spill site from about 650 feet below the surface to about a mile down. The deep-pelagic zone accounts for about 90 percent of the Gulf’s total volume.
Across a grid of stations, scientists on slippery decks lowered and hoisted nets that open and close at different depths, with experts from different species groups to identify the catch. They sampled around noon and midnight to account for species that migrate vertically each day. Ship-mounted scientific echosounders provided an independent check, measuring sound reflected by marine life in the water column.
The research is “comprehensive and carefully composed,” marine biologist Bruce Robison, a senior scientist at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute, said via email. “There is no other study that I know of with such an incredible number of net samples,” added Robison, who did not participate in the new study.
The research focuses on species that are not commercially fished and shows for the first time that human impacts can deplete marine life even in very deep ocean water, he said.
“It is important for the public to understand just how disastrous this oil spill was,” Robison said. “The Gulf has not recovered, and it’s been over 15 years.” Robison said other activities, such as deep-sea mining, could also have severe negative consequences for deepwater pelagic ecosystems by discharging wastewater containing metals or lubricants.
Three lines of evidence—net hauls, acoustic surveys, and genetic sampling—corroborate each other, which is “unusually strong evidence to support his conclusions,” said Jeffrey Drazen, a marine ecologist at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, who did not participate in the new study.
The study examines all possible causes of the decline and shows only one aligns with the scientific evidence, he said.
“Through logical elimination,” he said, “and without actually pointing a finger, they leave no doubt that the oil spill is the cause of the decline.”

A pivotal trial of vaccines against the strain of Ebola that is driving a deadly outbreak across parts of Africa has begun in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where the epidemic originated and the vast majority of cases and deaths have occurred.
The first participant was vaccinated on Friday in Bunia, eastern Congo, with Merck & Co.’s Ervebo shot, which has been approved to guard against a different Ebola species. An experimental alternative developed specifically against Bundibugyo by Moderna Inc. and another by the University of Oxford and Serum Institute of India could also be tested in the study within weeks.
“I’m pretty confident that we have the window because the outbreak is not being brought under control,” Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations Chief Executive Officer Richard Hatchett said in an interview.
Congo recorded 9,704 confirmed cases and 4,687 deaths as of October 20, according to the World Health Organization, and is the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the country, irrespective of virus species. Infections linked to the outbreak have also been detected beyond its borders.

Lula and Bolsonaro Jr neck and neck as Brazil heads to runoff polls
Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday in a tight runoff vote that could shift Latin America's largest nation sharply rightward, bringing it closer to the United States as part of a broader conservative shift across the region.
The runoff pits leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro. Flavio scored a major upset at the start of the month by defying pollsters to lead voting in the first round.
A victory for Bolsonaro, 45, would extend a wave of right-wing victories for Latin American candidates friendly to US President Donald Trump, while a fourth mandate for Lula would be a disappointment in Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.
The election race has been dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling, which Washington denies. It has also been colored by fallout from Jair Bolsonaro's 2025 conviction for plotting a 2022 coup, with Flavio pledging to free his father if he is elected.
Trump has called the case a "witch hunt" and imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil in 2025, in a decision explicitly linked to Jair Bolsonaro's trial. While many of those were later watered down, Trump unleashed new levies against Brazil this year, citing unfair trade practices.
Lula has cast the Trump administration's proximity to the Bolsonaro clan as part of an attempt to sway the election, while labelling tariffs and other punitive measures as bullying.
On economic issues, despite falling inequality and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over an electorate grappling with high living costs and heavy household debt. Endemic gang violence also weighs on voters' minds.
Bolsonaro has sought to capitalise on cost-of-living concerns and has also promised a heavy-handed approach to fighting crime, pledging maximum-security jails and chemical castration for serious sexual offences.
Candidates are neck and neck
Polls show the candidates are practically tied going into the runoff, as Lula has closed the gap in the final days.
Historical precedent favours Bolsonaro, however, as no candidate has ever won the presidency after coming second in the first-round vote.
Bolsonaro picked up 47% of ballots cast in the first round, while Lula trailed with 45%.
The senator's first-round win sent Brazil's markets and currency soaring on expectations of pro-business reforms.
His first-round success was mirrored in congressional elections for his Liberal Party and other right-wing politicians, which could pave a legislative path for him or complicate governance for Lula.

Russia’s Missile Industry Takes a Double Hit as Ukraine Strikes Two Key Plants and Military Aircraft
