Astronomers may have discovered the first moon beyond our Solar System
- Date:
- October 24, 2026
- Source:
- ESO
- Summary:
- Astronomers have uncovered evidence of a bizarre, potentially historic discovery: the first moon ever detected beyond our Solar System. Unlike familiar moons, this mysterious object is at least as massive as Jupiter and orbits a brown dwarf, which itself circles a star. The unusual arrangement challenges traditional definitions of planets and moons, leaving scientists unsure what to call it.
- Share:
Astronomers may have found the first moon beyond our Solar System, but the mysterious object is unlike any moon we know. Observations from the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope (ESO's VLT) have uncovered evidence of an enormous moon-like body in the CD-35 2722 star system. Rather than orbiting a planet, this unusual object circles a brown dwarf, a celestial body more massive than a planet but not massive enough to become a star.
If confirmed, the discovery could mark the first detection of a natural satellite outside our Solar System, potentially changing how astronomers define moons and planets.
A Bizarre Star System Unlike Our Own
Kevin Hoy, an ESO student based in Chile and lead author of the study published in Nature, spent months examining the CD-35 2722 system. He describes its unusual arrangement as "super weird" compared with our own Solar System.
At the center of this relatively young system is CD-35 2722, a star with approximately half the Sun's mass. Orbiting the star is a brown dwarf, an object that occupies the murky boundary between planets and stars. Brown dwarfs are generally too small to sustain the hydrogen fusion that powers ordinary stars, yet they are more massive than planets.
The newly identified object orbits this brown dwarf, creating a remarkable arrangement in which a massive satellite circles an object that itself revolves around a star.
"This system is somewhat hard to define using Solar-System-based words like 'planet' and 'moon'," states Hoy, who is also affiliated with the Universidad Diego Portales and the Millennium Nucleus of Young Exoplanets and their Moons (YEMS) in Chile.
The researchers refer to the newly detected object as an exosatellite. It has at least as much mass as Jupiter, while the brown dwarf it orbits is more than 30 times as massive as Jupiter. This makes the possible moon far more massive than any natural satellite in our Solar System.
"The exosatellite is clearly massive enough to be a planet, but it does not orbit a star, though it orbits an object that orbits a star," says Hoy. "Being the third wheel in this system makes us want to call it a moon, even if it is nothing like the small, rocky moons we have in our system."
A Giant Exomoon That Challenges Cosmic Definitions
The unusual discovery highlights a fundamental problem with applying familiar astronomical labels to objects found in distant star systems.
An exosatellite is a natural satellite located beyond our Solar System, while the term exomoon generally refers to a natural satellite orbiting a planet or another celestial body outside our Solar System. However, astronomers have not established a universally accepted definition of an exomoon.
That distinction becomes especially important in the CD-35 2722 system, where the possible moon is itself massive enough to be considered a planet under some classification schemes.
Alice Zurlo, director of YEMS and a collaborator on the study, explains: "The satellite we report is a giant gaseous body orbiting a highly massive companion, itself several times the mass of Jupiter."
The arrangement is very different from the familiar structure of our Solar System, where planets orbit the Sun and moons orbit planets.
"We have a clear delineation between the planets and the Sun in the Solar System, so defining things like moons is simple. In the CD-35 2722 system, where we are blurring the lines between stars, planets, and moons, the whole thing becomes more complicated to describe," adds Zurlo, who is also an astrophysicist at Universidad Diego Portales.
Scientists Search for the First Confirmed Exomoon
Astronomers have spent years looking for moons around objects beyond our Solar System, but no candidate has yet been detected with enough certainty to establish a confirmed discovery.
That makes the latest findings particularly significant. Although scientists have identified more than 6,000 exoplanets, only a handful of possible exomoons have emerged from observations, and the evidence supporting them remains limited.
Earlier in 2026, a research team led by Quentin Kral reported possible signs of a satellite in the HD 206893 star system. Their observations, obtained with ESO's Very Large Telescope Interferometer, suggested that a moon-like companion might exist, but they did not establish a definitive detection.
The CD-35 2722 system now offers another promising opportunity, supported by measurements of how the suspected moon affects the motion of its larger companion.
How Astronomers Detected the Possible Alien Moon
To investigate CD-35 2722, Hoy, Zurlo, and their colleagues used the CRIRES+ instrument installed on ESO's Very Large Telescope.
The team applied a technique known as the radial velocity method, which was also used to discover the first exoplanet orbiting a Sun-like star.
This approach works by measuring extremely small changes in an object's motion. When two celestial bodies orbit one another, their mutual gravitational attraction causes both to move around a shared center of mass. Even a much smaller companion can produce a detectable wobble in the larger object's motion.
By examining subtle changes in the brown dwarf's motion, the researchers identified what they consider strong evidence that another massive body is orbiting it.
"As exotic as it is, this system is truly unique and represents a breakthrough: the first plausible detection of an exosatellite," says Zurlo.
A New Era in the Search for Alien Moons
Confirming moons beyond our Solar System would do more than add another category of objects to astronomical catalogs. These discoveries could help researchers understand how planetary systems form, how their components interact, and why some systems develop structures dramatically different from our own.
Future observations could also reveal whether massive satellites like the one proposed in CD-35 2722 are rare exceptions or part of a much broader population of unusual celestial objects.
ESO's upcoming Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) is expected to play a major role in that search. Equipped with an enormous 39-meter mirror and advanced scientific instruments, the telescope will give astronomers the ability to detect smaller exomoons that are currently beyond the reach of existing observatories.
As scientists begin identifying more satellites in distant planetary systems, they may discover that familiar distinctions between stars, planets, and moons are not as universal as once assumed.
What Counts as an Exomoon?
A satellite is any object that travels around another object. Satellites can be natural (like our own moon) or artificial (like a spacecraft).
An exosatellite is a satellite located outside our Solar System. The term exomoon generally describes a natural satellite orbiting a planet or another object beyond our Solar System, although astronomers have not agreed on an official definition.
The possible companion in CD-35 2722 illustrates why that definition matters. With a mass comparable to or greater than Jupiter's, it resembles a planet in size and composition, yet its orbital relationship with the brown dwarf makes it a candidate for an entirely different classification.

Israel admits forcibly displacing 2,000 Palestinians from Hebron in occupied West Bank

12:08:25 KST

Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz has acknowledged that Israeli forces forcibly displaced around 2,000 Palestinians from their homes in Hebron in the southern occupied West Bank, barring residents from returning until alleged "Hamas infrastructure" is dismantled.
Katz's remarks to public broadcaster KAN coincided with the second day of an intensive military incursion conducted alongside Shin Bet and Border Police units.
The sweep follows a Friday checkpoint attack in which two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinians were killed, and three other soldiers wounded.
The military subsequently cordoned off Hebron and neighbouring Halhul for an assault projected to last several days.
Official Palestinian news agency Wafa reported that Israeli troops took over evacuated civilian properties in the Khallat Manna and Dahiyat al-Zaytoun districts of southern Hebron to serve as military barracks.
Soldiers also ejected families from homes across other neighbourhoods to establish observation posts, following the forced displacement of hundreds of families amid raids and movement restrictions.
City lockdown
The blockade has paralysed civic life across Hebron. The local education directorate suspended classes on Sunday and Monday, while Hebron University and Al-Quds Open University moved lectures online.
Municipal authorities warned that waste is accumulating inside the city because sealed perimeter entrances prevent rubbish collection teams from reaching external disposal sites.
Near Bethlehem, Israeli forces blocked unpaved bypass routes leading to the town of Tuqu, firing tear gas and stun grenades towards Palestinian vehicles attempting to navigate alternative rough paths amid wider road closures.
The occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, has experienced escalating Israeli military incursions and settler violence since the outbreak of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.
Incursions have involved detentions, residential demolitions, the burning of mosques and vehicles, bulldozing of farmland, restriction of agricultural access, and systematic community displacement alongside illegal settlement expansion.

7.0-magnitude earthquake jolts Japan's Ogasawara Islands: JMA
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:07:03 CST
12:07:03 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- An earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 7.0 on Sunday struck waters near the Ogasawara Islands in the Pacific Ocean, south of Tokyo, with no tsunami warnings issued, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said.
The temblor occurred at around 11:10 a.m. local time at a depth of around 470 km in the waters west of the Ogasawara Archipelago, measuring 3 on the Japanese seismic intensity scale of 7 in Chichijima and Hahajima islands, said the weather agency.
The quake's epicenter was located at a latitude of 28.0 degrees north and a longitude of 139.9 degrees east.
There was no threat of a tsunami, the JMA added. ■

LONDON, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called for an open, evidence-based debate on the possibility of restoring free movement between Britain and the EU, as his government considers options for closer ties with the bloc, local media reported Saturday.
"I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this," Burnham told The Sunday Times in an interview.
The prime minister acknowledged that freedom of movement had posed significant challenges before Brexit, but argued that migration patterns had changed since Britain left the EU.
Burnham said the balance of migration had changed, stressing the need for an "honest discussion" about the differences between past and present migration patterns.
He also highlighted Britain's loss of access to EU migration information-sharing arrangements following Brexit, including Eurodac, the bloc's biometric database used to help manage asylum applications.
But Burnham ruled out recommending that Britain adopt the euro or join the Schengen Area, where internal border checks have largely been abolished.
He is scheduled to meet EU leaders at a summit in Brussels on Nov. 20 and has indicated that he would outline possible options for Britain's future relationship with the bloc at the meeting.
The 2024 election manifesto of the Labour Party, now led by Burnham, ruled out restoring free movement, rejoining the EU single market or entering a customs union.
Burnham has previously pledged to respect those commitments, suggesting that any fundamental change in Britain's relationship with the EU would be unlikely before the next general election. ■

Scientists discover a hidden flaw that challenges 40 years of superconductor science
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
02:19:07 UTC
11:19:07 KST

Scientists discover a hidden flaw that challenges 40 years of superconductor science
- Date:
- October 24, 2026
- Source:
- University of Warwick
- Summary:
- A superconducting material studied for 40 years has turned out to be far more complex than scientists believed. Advanced 3D imaging revealed a hidden patchwork of crystal structures, with unusually wide boundaries that may weaken superconductivity. The discovery challenges decades of scientific assumptions and could explain why some superconductors outperform others.
- Share:
Scientists at the University of Warwick have uncovered a surprising secret inside a superconductor that researchers have studied for 40 years. Long believed to have a uniform crystal structure, the material actually contains a complex patchwork of different atomic arrangements. Using an advanced 3D imaging technique, the team was able to see deep inside the crystal for the first time, revealing hidden features that challenge decades of scientific assumptions.
High-temperature superconductivity ranks among the most important scientific breakthroughs of the past four decades. Superconductors can carry electrical current without any resistance, eliminating the energy losses that normally occur as electricity travels through conventional materials. They also have the potential to support extraordinarily powerful magnets, making them promising for future power grids, medical scanners, and quantum computers.
The new findings, published in Physical Review Letters, come from researchers in Warwick's Department of Chemistry working with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in France. Their investigation focused on a class of copper-based superconductors known as cuprates, which can conduct electricity without resistance at unusually high (though still very cold) temperatures.
Advanced 3D Imaging Reveals a Hidden Crystal Structure
For four decades, scientists have generally built their theories of cuprate superconductivity around the assumption that these materials have the same crystal structure throughout their interiors. The new research shows that this fundamental assumption does not always hold.
To investigate, the team used scanning 3D X-ray diffraction, a sophisticated imaging method that reveals how atoms are arranged deep within a crystal. The approach is similar in principle to a medical CT scan, except that it maps atomic structures rather than tissues and organs.
This allowed the researchers to construct a detailed three-dimensional picture of the superconductor's interior, exposing structural variations that conventional techniques had not revealed.
Instead of finding a uniform crystal, they discovered a patchwork of regions containing two slightly different atomic arrangements. Even more surprising were the boundaries separating these regions, which were hundreds of times wider than expected.
These unusually broad transition zones were not simply narrow dividing lines between neighboring structures. They were extensive enough to behave almost like distinct structures themselves, potentially influencing how electricity moves through the material.
A 40-Year Assumption About Superconductors Overturned
Professor Mark Senn, who led the study at the University of Warwick's Department of Chemistry, explained why the findings could have major implications for superconductivity research.
"For forty years, the working assumption has been that these materials are the same all the way through, and nearly all the theory is built on that picture. We've shown it doesn't hold. The crystal is fundamentally patchworked and textured, with unusually wide boundary regions that likely work against superconductivity rather than just sitting alongside it.
"This might explain why some materials perform better than others and means some existing bulk measurements will need to be reinterpreted and future theoretical models built that incorporate this structural complexity."
The discovery suggests that the internal boundaries may actively interfere with superconductivity rather than simply coexist with it. If that is the case, the hidden structural differences could help explain why certain superconducting materials perform better than others.
It also means that some previous experiments, particularly those measuring the overall properties of these materials, may need to be reconsidered. Future theories will likely need to account for the complex structures inside real crystals rather than treating them as perfectly uniform.
What the Discovery Means for Future Superconductors
The researchers suspect that similar hidden structural patterns may be widespread among other cuprate superconductors. They could also occur in related materials being investigated for their ability to become superconducting under extreme pressure.
Beyond challenging existing theories, the study demonstrates the power of a new generation of imaging technology.
The advanced measurements were made possible by a recent 150 million euro upgrade to the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, which provides extremely intense X-ray beams for studying materials in extraordinary detail.
This technology now allows scientists to examine the three-dimensional interiors of many different materials with a level of precision that was previously unavailable. By revealing how hidden atomic structures affect a material's behavior, the technique could provide valuable insights across materials science.
For superconductivity research, the implications are particularly important. Understanding how internal crystal structures influence electrical performance could eventually help scientists identify ways to improve superconducting materials, bringing more advanced energy systems, powerful magnets, medical imaging devices, and quantum technologies closer to reality.

ROTTERDAM, Netherlands, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- China's Lan Xingyu reclaimed the men's rings world title after a five-year wait on Saturday, with five nations sharing the gold medals on the opening day of apparatus finals at the World Artistic Gymnastics Championships.
Lan scored 14.766 points to finish 0.433 ahead of Greece's Eleftherios Petrounias, who took silver with 14.333. Armenia's Artur Avetisyan claimed bronze with 14.233.
Competing sixth in the eight-man final, Lan combined the highest difficulty score in the field, 6.000, with an execution mark of 8.766 to secure China's first men's gold of the championships.
The 28-year-old previously won the rings title in Kitakyushu, Japan, in 2021 and took bronze at last year's championships in Jakarta.
American Frederick Richard won the men's floor exercise title with 14.633, edging Britain's defending champion Jake Jarman by just 0.033. Israel's Artem Dolgopyat finished third with 14.466.
Armenia celebrated another title through Hamlet Manukyan, who scored 15.300 on pommel horse. Italy's Gabriele Targhetta earned silver with 15.233, while Armenia's Mamikon Khachatryan completed the podium with 15.000. Japan's Daiki Hashimoto finished eighth with 13.466.
Brazil's Rebeca Andrade took the women's vault crown with 14.466, ahead of Americans Claire Pease and Skye Blakely, who scored 14.233 and 14.166 respectively.
Algeria's Kaylia Nemour won the uneven bars with 15.333, combining a difficulty score of 7.000 with 8.333 for execution. Germany's Helen Kevric secured silver with 14.833, while Blakely collected another bronze with 14.600.
Lan's victory came after China won bronze in Tuesday's men's team final, where the squad scored 249.193 behind Japan's 251.928 and Russia's 250.329. All three teams secured qualification for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
China competed without injured all-around standout Zhang Boheng. Despite recording the highest team totals on rings and parallel bars, mistakes elsewhere left the squad third overall.
The championships conclude on Sunday with finals in men's vault, parallel bars and horizontal bar, and women's balance beam and floor exercise. China's Zou Jingyuan will seek a record-extending fifth world parallel bars title. ■

Cuba extends daylight saving time to counter impact from U.S. blockade
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:18:01 CST
11:18:01 KST

HAVANA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Cuba will maintain daylight saving time until Nov. 7, 2027 to mitigate its power generation shortfall, which has been exacerbated by tighter U.S. sanctions and fuel supply restrictions, local authorities said Saturday.
The measure is expected to reduce evening peak demand by about 126 megawatts (MW), helping curb power outages, according to a joint statement by the Ministry of Energy and Mines and the Ministry of Labor and Social Security.
Of the estimated savings, 76 MW will come from reduced electricity consumption for artificial lighting and 50 MW from solar photovoltaic generation, the statement said.
To minimize disruptions to morning activities, schools and workplaces will open 30 minutes later from Nov. 1, 2026 to March 14, 2027, when standard time would normally be in effect.
Cuba has faced a severe blackout crisis for nearly two years, which worsened in January 2026 after the U.S. government threatened to impose sanctions on countries supplying fuel to the island. Havana has condemned the measure as violation of international law. ■

Why more Japanese women are choosing ‘silver divorce’ after decades of marriage

Ayumi lives alone in a spacious suburban house originally bought to raise a family, her two cats now her only full-time companions. Her two daughters have grown up and left home, and her husband of more than two decades moved out nearly a year ago as they finalise a divorce.

Midwest muso Kevin Morby is no longer America's best kept secret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Kevin Morby on famous friends, mortality and touring Little Wide Open in Australia
During the 2020 pandemic, US singer-songwriter Kevin Morby almost got stuck in Australia.
As quarantines tightened, he found himself in Melbourne before it had some of the world's toughest lockdowns.
He didn't panic. Instead, he remembers thinking:
"If I have to start a new life, this is a pretty good place to do so."
He has become acquainted with Australia's bigger cities over multiple visits.
"Feel[ing] like, 'Oh, I know where I'm at. I know this neighbourhood — I love that one restaurant! It's nice," he tells Double J's Henry Wagons.
That moment of acceptance speaks to something essential about Morby, a folk-rock journeyman who finds belonging and meaning in transit.
That philosophy feels more relevant than ever as Morby returns to tour Australia next month, supporting his latest album Little Wide Open.
Following a discography inspired by adopted homes — Laurel Canyon (2016's Singing Saw), New York (2017's City Music), Memphis (2022's This Is A Photograph) — Morby's eighth solo album heads back to the Missouri farmlands and Kansas City suburbs where he grew up.
"I have a complicated relationship to it, just as most people do with their home towns. There's a lot of love and a lot of resentment. It's all these emotions and a lot of them come out on this record."
The Midwest and musical influences
A collection of sentimental alt-country, dusky folk and lush Americana, Little Wide Open conjures rich imagery: fields of sunflowers and June bugs, late-night bars and long highways stretching into flat horizons dominated by wide open skies.
Porchside strumming and finger-picking score vivid portraits of "anywhere America" on songs with names like Cowtown and Bible Belt.
Small-town iconography and spangling riffs power 100,000, before a guitar explodes like a Fourth of July firecracker over the song's climax.
These tunes, built from tried-and-true chords and Morby's humble Dylanesque voice, romanticise the comforts of small towns but equally yearn to escape them for something larger.
For Morby, the Midwest is simple.
"I don't mean that in a derogatory sense. The lifestyles are simpler. There's a quality of life, your money goes further, things like that. But with that, there's less opportunity and less culture.
"There can be great things about the Midwest.
"I feel if you use the time and space and the boredom to your advantage, those don't have to necessarily be bad things."
You can hear the influence of Morby's "big five": Bob Dylan, Leonard Cohen, Lou Reed, Nina Simone, and Townes Van Zandt.
But also, more pluck and twang ("Country music's great. One of [music's] backbones over the past two centuries") as well as the "rootsy, heartland rock and roll" Morby was immersed in making the record.
"I bought this pick-up truck with a free subscription to satellite radio. Part of that was the Tom Petty radio station and I just got super into him. He was a big influence."
He also cites the album World Without Tears by legendary artist Lucinda Williams, who provides a drawling, cautionary spoken word on stand-out track Natural Disaster.
"I wanted this voice-of-God thing to come in. I was so thrilled when she said she'd do it."
Williams isn't Little Wide Open's only notable guest.
Famous friends
In a sign of how esteemed Morby is among his peers, the album also features Bon Iver's Justin Vernon (emulating a tornado siren on rustic opener Badlands), backing vocals from MUNA's Katie Gavin, and players from Florence + The Machine, Perfume Genius, Sylvan Esso and Hand Habits.
Then there's The National's Aaron Dessner. Fresh from producing blockbuster records for Taylor Swift and Ed Sheeran, Dessner recorded Little Wide Open at his studio in upstate New York.
"He made the songs feel big and dense in their ways without distracting the story or the vocal," Morby explains.
"He really kept my vocal front and centre. It felt like I was standing a little bit naked on these recordings, but I think it benefited the album in the end.
"Besides that, he's just an unbelievable musician. And really believed in these songs through moments where maybe I wasn't believing in them … 'Kevin, you gotta let these songs breathe.'"
Dessner's fingerprints are all over Junebug, with its gossamer guitars and piano decorated by oboe and harp. But those flourishes never overshadow Morby.
"Sometimes the myth grows bigger than the dream" he sings on the swooning title track, where banjo, slide guitar and fiddle comfortably sprawl past the eight-minute mark.
Getting older (and better)
Little Wide Open is also charged by Morby "looking down the barrel of 40," and the sense of life moving too fast.
"Am I a has-been? Am I a husband?" he sings ruefully amid the otherwise upbeat Javelin. Nearly cut for being too vulnerable, the lyric was prompted by impending parenthood.
Morby recently welcomed his first child alongside his musician-partner Katie Crutchfield, better known as alt-country favourite Waxahatchee.
"We fell in love on tour. We're these creative sounding boards for one other. I really trust Katie's ear and her thoughts. It's real easy to walk in the other room and say, 'Hey, is this lyric good?'"
While she doesn't feature on Little Wide Open, "Katie is very much in the DNA. It's a lot of love songs," Morby says.
"It's a funny thing being in a public relationship because people are going to know who you're singing about."
Because Morby's music is presented with such easy-going charm, you can easily miss the serious subject matter of his lyrics, which contemplate existential questions about life, time and mortality.
"It's a darker song [but] for the longest time, I wanted to call the record I Ride Passenger," Morby says of a tune loosely inspired by a fan who died in a car crash on his way to see him perform.
The central lyric? "If time is a violent driver, then we ride passenger."
Die Young is a warm, mid-tempo reflection on aging, and surviving the fragile existence of a touring musician.
That idea is revisited on the plaintive closer, Field Guide for The Butterflies, which uses insects splattered on windshields as a metaphor for troubadours compelled to reach and share deeper truths despite the risks of lonely lives spent on the road.
But "it's not suicide if I die out chasing thrills" Morby confides in the album's closing moments. "Just me trying to grow wings."
It's a moving finish to a record where Morby ponders where he's been, what happens next and what it all means.
Kevin Morby's tour begins in Eltham on Thursday, November 12, before shows in Bellingen, Brisbane, Mt Glorious, Sydney, Brunswick Heads, Castlemaine and Melbourne.

Midwest muso Kevin Morby is no longer America's best kept secret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Kevin Morby on famous friends, mortality and touring Little Wide Open in Australia
During the 2020 pandemic, US singer-songwriter Kevin Morby almost got stuck in Australia.
As quarantines tightened, he found himself in Melbourne before it had some of the world's toughest lockdowns.
He didn't panic. Instead, he remembers thinking:
"If I have to start a new life, this is a pretty good place to do so."
He has become acquainted with Australia's bigger cities over multiple visits.
"Feel[ing] like, 'Oh, I know where I'm at. I know this neighbourhood — I love that one restaurant! It's nice," he tells Double J's Henry Wagons.
That moment of acceptance speaks to something essential about Morby, a folk-rock journeyman who finds belonging and meaning in transit.
That philosophy feels more relevant than ever as Morby returns to tour Australia next month, supporting his latest album Little Wide Open.
Following a discography inspired by adopted homes — Laurel Canyon (2016's Singing Saw), New York (2017's City Music), Memphis (2022's This Is A Photograph) — Morby's eighth solo album heads back to the Missouri farmlands and Kansas City suburbs where he grew up.
"I have a complicated relationship to it, just as most people do with their home towns. There's a lot of love and a lot of resentment. It's all these emotions and a lot of them come out on this record."
The Midwest and musical influences
A collection of sentimental alt-country, dusky folk and lush Americana, Little Wide Open conjures rich imagery: fields of sunflowers and June bugs, late-night bars and long highways stretching into flat horizons dominated by wide open skies.
Porchside strumming and finger-picking score vivid portraits of "anywhere America" on songs with names like Cowtown and Bible Belt.
Small-town iconography and spangling riffs power 100,000, before a guitar explodes like a Fourth of July firecracker over the song's climax.
These tunes, built from tried-and-true chords and Morby's humble Dylanesque voice, romanticise the comforts of small towns but equally yearn to escape them for something larger.
For Morby, the Midwest is simple.
"I don't mean that in a derogatory sense. The lifestyles are simpler. There's a quality of life, your money goes further, things like that. But with that, there's less opportunity and less culture.
"There can be great things about the Midwest.
"I feel if you use the time and space and the boredom to your advantage, those don't have to necessarily be bad things."
You can hear the influence of Morby's "big five": Bob Dylan, Leonard Cohen, Lou Reed, Nina Simone, and Townes Van Zandt.

BELGRADE, October 25. /TASS/. Early elections to the National Assembly (unicameral parliament) will be held in Serbia.

Polling stations will open at 7:00 a.m. local time (6:00 a.m. GMT) and close at 8:00 p.m. (7:00 p.m. GMT). According to the REC, more than 16,000 observers, including 622 foreign observers, will monitor the voting process.

Hong Kong needs a civil service fit for a changed world
Beyond administrative expertise, civil servants must now master technology, cross-departmental cooperation and strategic flexibility
Hong Kong’s civil service has long enjoyed a reputation for efficiency, professionalism and probity. It has also been a pillar of stability, particularly during the transition from British to Chinese rule.
Outside the general and administrative grades, many civil servants spend much of their careers in relatively specialised areas of responsibility. This allows them to develop deep expertise and makes them dependable regulators and administrators. However, it can also make it harder to adapt when new challenges cut across established departmental boundaries.
Hong Kong was once a British outpost built on trade. Government played a relatively limited role in economic development, while free trade, market forces and the city’s strategic position at the crossroads of East and West helped it prosper.

COLOMBO, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- The Sri Lankan Navy and Coast Guard on Saturday seized more than 561 kilograms of methamphetamine and heroin during a joint operation on the country's southern coast, the navy said.
The operation was conducted at Naotunna beach in Thalalla, Matara, following information received by the Coast Guard.
Search teams recovered 21 sacks and travel bags containing suspected narcotics, alongside a dinghy believed to have been used to smuggle the consignment.
Examinations conducted with assistance from the Police Narcotics Bureau confirmed more than 240 kilograms of methamphetamine in 200 packages and over 320 kilograms of heroin in 275 packages, the navy said.
Deputy Defense Minister Aruna Jayasekara said joint Navy and Coast Guard operations over the past year had seized drugs with an estimated street value of 97 billion Sri Lankan rupees (about 292 million U.S. dollars).
He said coordinated operations involving the armed forces, police and local and foreign intelligence agencies would continue to prevent narcotics from entering the country.
Sri Lanka launched its national anti-narcotics drive "A Nation United" on Oct. 30 last year. Official data indicated that more than 303,000 suspects were arrested as of Oct. 18. ■

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
01:15:01 UTC

RIO DE JANEIRO, October 25. /TASS/. The second, decisive round of the general election will take place in Brazil. Voters will decide who will serve as head of state for the next four years: incumbent President and Workers’ Party leader Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva or the candidate from the right-wing opposition, senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
Voting procedure
Voting in Brazil will take place from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. local time (11:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. GMT). More than 158.7 million Brazilian citizens are eligible to vote. Voting is mandatory for all literate Brazilians between the ages of 18 and 69.
Key candidates
Incumbent President Lula da Silva is seeking re-election for what would be the final term of his political career. He is building his campaign around strengthening Brazil’s international standing and expanding export opportunities, particularly with countries in the Global South and the BRICS. His domestic policy agenda includes tax reform, government funding for defense and technology initiatives, and actively developing hydrocarbon reserves.
Meanwhile, Flavio Bolsonaro is focusing his campaign on strongly condemning the government’s policies and drawing public attention to the excessive tax burden and rampant street crime. The right-wing opposition candidate has rallied the conservative electorate and powerful agricultural interests behind him. In foreign policy, he favors the US market and aims to restore bilateral relations to the level seen during the administrations of Jair Bolsonaro and Donald Trump.
First-round results, political landscape
The October 4 vote showed an advantage for conservative forces and fell short of the incumbent president’s expectations, falling short of the incumbent president’s expectations of a first-round victory. According to the results, Flavio Bolsonaro took the lead with 47.03% of the vote. Lula da Silva is in second place with 45.16%. The margin between the candidates was less than two percentage points. Given an electorate of 150 million, this is equal to nearly two to three million votes.
On the eve of the second round, the son of the former Brazilian leader is considered the frontrunner. Flavio Bolsonaro managed to seize the political initiative by successfully mobilizing voters in economically developed regions and the agricultural business sector.
Lula da Silva’s campaign shifted to a defensive strategy between the rounds, finding itself playing catch-up. The government passed emergency social measures, including debt relief for four million self-employed individuals and an unexpected increase in benefits for the poor.

Serbia votes as students seek to unseat Vucic in snap election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
01:05:39 UTC
10:05:39 KST

Serbia votes in historic election as students seek to end Vucic's long grip on power
BELGRADE, Oct 25 - Serbian voters turned out in force on Sunday as a mass student protest movement sought to unseat longtime populist leader Aleksandar Vucic in the biggest challenge to his rule for more than a decade.
The snap parliamentary elections, called by Vucic in September, come after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of 16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024. The students have since gained widespread support.
Unusually long lines snaked from polling stations in cities and towns across the country. Pollsters and monitors CeSID and Ipsos put turnout at 27.3% by 11 a.m. (1000 GMT), nearly double the 15.1% at the same time in the previous election in 2023. Even Vucic waited in line for nearly two hours to vote. First indications of results are expected around two hours after polls close at 8 p.m. (1900 GMT).
A student victory would be a profound political shift in the Balkan country of some 6 million people, reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary's Viktor Orban in April. It could also offer a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest, in some cases violently, against poor education standards and a lack of prospects.
"It is very important for all people to come and vote if they want to change something and I think it is a time for change," said lawyer Marija Cvjeticanin at a Belgrade polling station.
Vucic, who resigned from his second term as president to run again for prime minister, is a strong incumbent. Many voters thank him for pulling Serbia from economic obscurity and orchestrating a period of sustained modernisation including new highways, railways, schools and hospitals.
OPINION POLLS PREDICT TIGHT RACE
Vucic has pledged higher pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare. Internationally, he has sought closer ties with China, a major investor, and remained close to Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas. At the same time, he still says he wants to join the European Union, Serbia's largest trading partner, but the bloc has become increasingly frustrated with a lack of reform.
"I voted for our children, our young people...our children deserve peace and work, only Vucic can bring that," said Hatidza, a Roma woman.
The students' domestic agenda aims to root out graft and improve schooling, but they have been quieter on their international ambitions. Their list of 250 largely unknown candidates includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, although it is not clear who would be prime minister should they win.
"I hope that today will pass in a democratic atmosphere, in peace, and that we will legitimately elect a new government in Serbia," Srdanovic said after casting his vote in Novi Sad, adding that the scenes suggested there would be a record voter turnout in the country's recent history.
After casting his vote, Vucic said he would respect the result.
"If we lose we will acknowledge the will of the electorate, if we win no one will take it (from us)," he said.
Opinion polls ahead of the vote predicted a tight race. The head of the Election Commission, Vladimir Dimitrijevic, said voting had so far passed without incident, but monitoring bodies CeSID and CRTA pointed to incidents related to the electoral roll and secrecy of voting.
STUDENT PROTESTS INCREASE PRESSURE ON VUCIC
The student-led street protests sparked by the station disaster quickly became the biggest in a generation, calling for Vucic to step down. Rights groups and activists say repression has worsened in the period since.
"For decades the people have been waiting for this time, something to bring hope that we can live freely and by the rules of democracy," said actor Jelena Stupljanin, 48, at a Belgrade polling station.
Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) have repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. He says the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss.
"This has been one of the most difficult but the most emotional campaigns," Vucic told his supporters on Thursday. "We stood against those who wanted to destroy Serbia." REUTERS

School bullying cases in Hong Kong rise 32% to nearly 500 a year
Youth group attributes increase to heightened mental health awareness and students struggling to distinguish jokes from bullying
Hong Kong schools handled an average of 496 bullying cases each academic year from 2022 to 2025 – a 32 per cent jump compared with the previous three years, according to the Education Bureau.
A youth group attributed the increase to greater reporting driven by heightened mental health awareness, but also students struggling to distinguish playful jokes from bullying.
According to the bureau, public primary and secondary schools recorded an average of 496 bullying cases each year between 2022 and 2025, up 32 per cent from the 377 recorded annually from 2019 to 2022.
The bureau told the Legislative Council in 2023 that the number of cases involving school bullying, including cyberbullying, from the 2019-20 to 2021-22 school years was 411, 306 and 413 respectively. The average number for these three school years was 377.

Federal police chief links threats against MPs directly to political debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
00:57:01 UTC
09:57:01 KST

AFP chief Krissy Barrett warns political discourse is driving threats to MPs
In short:
AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett says there is a correlation between "particular political discourse" and threats to parliamentarians.
She would not provide an example but says there was a "direct connection" when pressed to consider examples like some of One Nation's YouTube content.
What's next?
Commissioner Barrett says the AFP will keep advising MPs but they will have to make their own decisions about safety.
The head of the Australian Federal Police says there is a direct correlation between inflammatory political discourse and threats against parliamentarians.
AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett said police regularly saw harassment of MPs increase following periods of heated debate.
"It does have a direct correlation to what we see in terms of threats and abuse, and sometimes it's very immediate," she told Insiders.
Commissioner Barrett said police did not want to curtail free speech or intervene in legitimate political debate, but there was a role for law enforcement when rhetoric escalated into violent threats.
"I would challenge any Australian to read some of these threats and some of the abuse that is reported to us from federal parliamentarians and for anyone to argue that that is free speech or political discourse," she said.
Asked whether One Nation's cartoons depicting politicians being hit by cars were the type of political discourse she was referring to, Commissioner Barrett said they could be.
"We do see examples where there are particular announcements or things like you've just described. There is a reaction amongst the community," she said.
"Words matter, and we do see the flow-on impact from that."
Politicians across the divide have raised concerns about their personal security after independent MP Helen Haines was hit by a car in an attack outside her Wangaratta electorate office last week.
The member for Indi remains in a serious but stable condition in hospital and has had both her legs amputated.
Brendan Nugent, 43, has been arrested and charged in relation to the attack.
Commissioner Barrett said investigators were focused on establishing a motive but cautioned that process could take weeks, even months.
"Sometimes it is difficult to determine a clear motive," she said.
"There is media reporting around his mental health, around some of the social media footprint that is out there in terms of different issues that he may or may not be aligned with.
"We need to work through all of that to determine whether it is directly linked to her role as a federal parliamentarian."
MPs must make own decisions about safety, chief says
Commissioner Barrett said police would continue briefing federal parliamentarians and their staff on security arrangements, but said MPs would need to make their own decisions about their personal safety.
The comments come as some federal members have spoken about fears for their safety, while describing mixed experiences with the security support available to them.
She defended the resources devoted to protecting parliamentarians, arguing the focus should be on how those capabilities are deployed rather than the size of the budget.
"It's about having the flexibility to evolve our capabilities, invest in technology and respond to changing threats," she said.
"At the end of the day we're here to give advice, but I would say it's up to the individual parliamentarian … to make those decisions."
Commissioner Barrett said personal duress alarms were among a range of measures being considered, but stressed that calling Triple Zero was still the most effective option in an emergency.
"I think there is a place for duress alarms, but we need parliamentarians to understand what a duress alarm does and doesn't do."
MPs consider language as parliament returns
Shadow cabinet minister Ted O'Brien said politicians of all stripes would return to Canberra on Monday reflecting on the tone of political debate.
"I think [the attack] demands the nation does pause and think about how we can do things better, and how we can debate better," he said.
"Robust debate is fundamental to our system, but personal nastiness is not. We've got to make sure we can address this."
Labor frontbencher Catherine King flagged there might be a reassessment of security arrangements at Parliament House, while acknowledging parliamentarians were already "very well looked after" by the AFP.
"Obviously, when an incident … as horrible as this happened to Helen, they'll go back and look at all of the security measures that are in place," she told News 24.
"All our thoughts, I know as we head into parliament, will be with Helen not being there with us."

A host of state and federal politicians attended the opening ceremony, including Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition leader Angus Taylor.
Albanese said it was a "great day for the nation" as Australia welcomed its first new major airport in more than 50 years.
"This is not Sydney's second airport. This is not even Western Sydney's best airport, new airport. This is Australia's best airport, without question in the way that it will function going forward."
Taylor said he was "proud to see history made in Western Sydney" as the facility opened in his electorate.
"It's a great achievement for this country ... not just because of the flights but because of the jobs and opportunities it creates," he said.
'Transformational' for Sydney
The airport has capacity to cater for up to 10 million passengers a year. It's aiming to eventually become Australia’s primary gateway and cater to more than 80 million passengers annually.
It's located at Luddenham near Badgerys Creek, about 45km from Sydney's CBD.
Simon Hickey, chief executive of the airport, said it was a "surreal" moment to see it finally open.
"When I was a boy, Sydney's population was around 2 million. Today it's edging closer to about 6 million," he said at the opening ceremony.
"And the home of that rapid growth is here, the vibrant cultural heartland of Western Sydney."
Many leaders have long believed Australia's most populous city deserved a round-the-clock, second airport for both cargo and passengers.
Hickey said the infrastructure project was the most "transformational" since the Sydney Harbour Bridge, which was completed nearly a century ago.
"Hundreds of people helped build it, and millions of journeys have since taken place across it. But importantly, it changed the way Sydney travelled, and worked, and played."
"So too will be the case for Western Sydney International."
"It brings the world closer to western Sydney and opportunity closer to home, creating new meaningful jobs for generations to come.
"Young people growing up in the west can now look to the sky and see their future is bright and right here, in their own backyard."
Construction on the airport began in 2018 after the Abbott government formally signed off on the Badgerys Creek site in 2014.
Earth workers moved more than 25 million cubic metres of soil and rock to prepare the site before builders delivered the project on time and on budget in 2025.
It will be Sydney's first 24-hour airport. It is not subject to an overnight curfew between 11pm and 6am like the Kingsfird Smith Airport.
Transport links playing catch-up
Local leaders and western Sydney businesses now hope the airport will transform the region into an economic powerhouse.
Liverpool City Council mayor Ned Mannoun said greater Sydney's future was "only limited by imagination".
His Penrith counterpart Todd Carney agreed, but said state and federal governments would have to support growth with significant investment in roads, amenities and critical infrastructure.
Unlike Kingsford Smith Airport, which is connected to Sydney's rail network, Western Sydney International Airport will initially rely on road connections and bus services while major transport infrastructure is completed.
A Sydney Metro line linking the airport with a train station in the Western Sydney suburb of St Marys is under construction and expected to open next year.
Until then, passengers can connect to St Marys via a free airport shuttle bus, or travel by express coach, public bus, taxi, rideshare or private vehicle.
Those in private business said many were ready to jump on opportunities, but were also waiting for those critical connections.
Paul Fletcher, who served as federal infrastructure minister through much of the 2010s, said Australians would have to watch the master plan "play out over coming decades".
"This is a 10, 20, 30, 50, 100-year project," he told the Australian Associated Press.
So far, seven passenger carriers have committed to servicing the new airport: Qantas, Jetstar, Qatar Airways, Air New Zealand, Singapore Airlines, Fiji Airways and Vietjet Air.

Israel needs sanctions-proof economy – Netanyahu
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said his country must prepare to adapt its economy to global sanctions, citing declining international support and a potential end to US financial and military aid.
Public opinion toward Israel has grown increasingly negative amid the wars in Gaza and Iran. In the US, a recent Chicago Council on Global Affairs report recorded the country’s lowest favorability rating since its polling began in 1978, with a majority supporting reducing or ending military aid.
Last month, the UK announced a ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband describing settlers as “terrorists” supported by Netanyahu’s government and accusing them of ethnically cleansing Palestinians. The same day, 11 other countries, including France, Spain, and Canada, joined Britain in a statement supporting the two-state solution and announcing plans to impose or consider restrictions on trade with the settlements.
“We must understand that there could be sanctions, including banking sanctions,” Netanyahu said in an interview which aired on Israel’s Channel 10 on Friday.
“We need to prepare an alternative economy capable of functioning by circumventing these sanctions,” he added, noting that blockchain technology, which underpins cryptocurrencies, was among the options under consideration and that he had already requested an implementation plan.
The Israeli prime minister also expressed concern over a potential shift in Washington’s position, saying that “it’s only a matter of time” before US military aid is completely “over.”
“If you think we’re going to continue receiving what I secured twice, and that’s tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defense budget, prepare yourselves and get used to the fact that it won’t happen because America has changed,” he said.
Under an agreement signed in 2016, Washington committed to providing $38 billion in military aid through 2028. Netanyahu previously said he wanted to phase out the financial component of US military assistance within ten years.
Former prime minister and opposition figure Yair Lapid seized on the remarks, saying that “Netanyahu now admits, in his own words, that if his government is returned to power, American military aid will end and Israel will face sanctions that will devastate our economy, trigger uncontrolled price surges, and cause irreparable damage.”
The comments come days before Israel’s first national election since the October 7 Hamas attacks, with accountability for security failures, the cost of living, ultra-Orthodox military service, and the country’s international standing among the issues facing voters. Neither Netanyahu’s allies nor the opposition have a clear path to a parliamentary majority.

Six Flags will add seatbelts to some roller coasters after rider’s death
Emmett Lindner
- Six Flags will add seat belts to select roller coasters after Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, died on Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia. The ride is closed while state and police investigate.
- The company said independent engineers and inspectors are reviewing all rides. John Reilly said Six Flags will take action to “further strengthen” safety standards.
- Nitro and Raging Bull will also get seat belts. The move follows lawsuits over X2 at Six Flags Magic Mountain and wider scrutiny of ride safety.
AI generated
CHARLOTTE, North Carolina – Six Flags will add seatbelts to select roller coasters across its parks, the company said on Oct 23, weeks after the death of a man who fell from a ride at one of its properties.
This comes as it is contending with recent lawsuits over safety concerns.
Six Flags Entertainment president John Reilly said in a statement that it hired independent engineers and inspectors to conduct safety reviews of all rides and attractions as the additional safety measures were put in place.
“We are committed to carefully evaluating their findings and taking appropriate action to further strengthen standards and safety,” he said.
Earlier in October, Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was thrown from his seat and declared dead after riding Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia in Austell, Georgia, the state’s tallest roller coaster. That ride is temporarily closed and will include seatbelts when it reopens.
Goliath was previously equipped with the commonly used lap-bar “clamshell” restraints, which swing down to lock above riders’ laps.
The Cobb County Police Department is investigating the death, but there is no single federal agency responsible for enforcing safety standards for rides like Goliath, which passed its most recent state inspection on March 16.
The other attractions to get safety additions are Nitro at Six Flags Great Adventure in Jackson, New Jersey, and Raging Bull at Six Flags Great America in Gurnee, Illinois, which is north of Chicago, a company spokesperson said on Oct 24.
Aside from Goliath, eight rides at five other parks are temporarily closed, Reilly added.
Ride safety at Six Flags parks has come under intense scrutiny over the past several weeks, even before Kariem’s death.
In September, three people sued the amusement park company and the ride’s manufacturer after suffering what they said were catastrophic brain injuries from riding the X2 coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California.
The lawsuits accuse Six Flags and a manufacturer of X2’s parts of operating a defectively designed ride and failing to adequately warn passengers about the risk of serious brain injuries.
That month, Six Flags Magic Mountain said the X2 would permanently close.
Before those lawsuits, Reilly said during an August call with analysts that the company incurred higher repair and maintenance expenses at certain parks as it reduced downtime, adding: “We will not compromise on safety.”
In its second-quarter financial filings released in August, Six Flags reported that its net revenue was US$865 million (S$1.1 billion), a decrease of US$65 million from the same time in 2025. Attendance for the quarter was just above 13 million visits, a decrease from more than 14 million for the same period in 2025.
There are currently more than 220 coasters operating across all Six Flags parks, Reilly said. NYTIMES

Bulgaria votes for president in wake of deadly Black Sea drone strikes
SOFIA, Oct 25 - Bulgarians vote in presidential elections on Sunday as Russia's war in Ukraine spreads to the waters off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast.
Polls place acting President Iliana Iotova, 61, and ex-caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, as leaders in a race of 27 candidates.
While the presidency is largely ceremonial, Sunday's vote has taken on added significance after a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast that likely killed some two-dozen international seafarers.
The strikes, which sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine, prompted the government to seek allied assistance to bolster maritime security.
Bulgaria has stopped short of directly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks, but Prime Minister Rumen Radev said their outcome "benefits the Russian Federation".
Both leading presidential candidates condemned the strikes, but they differ over the broader war.
Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, is supported by pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed support for Ukraine. He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier.
"I want Bulgaria to have a voice of its own in Europe. A reliable NATO ally that defends its interests through preparedness, strong diplomacy and a clear position," he said at a rally on Thursday.
Iotova, formerly vice president, became acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter the parliamentary race, which he won on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket. Radev supports Iotova and they both call for a diplomatic end to the war.
A victory for Iotova would make her Bulgaria's first elected female president.
"My opponents argue that there must be a war of attrition." she told a rally on Thursday. "The truth is, we are all the ones who are most exhausted."
Polls by Alpha Research give Iotova 41% of the vote and Gyurov 28%. If no candidate wins a majority, a runoff vote will be held on November 1.
Voting starts at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT) and polls close at 8 p.m. REUTERS

India slams Pakistan over minority rights
Puri underlined that protecting minority rights was primarily the sovereign responsibility of individual states, guided by the principle of sovereign equality.He said India's civilisational tradition of diversity was reflected in its constitutional safeguards for religious and linguistic minorities.
He also highlighted the substantial contributions made by minorities to India's national development, including at the highest levels of government and key institutions.
The latest confrontation followed India's strong rebuke to Pakistan at the UN on October 23 over its treatment of religious minorities. New Delhi accused Islamabad of failing to protect vulnerable communities while attempting to lecture India on religious freedom, burial rights and minority protections.During an interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Religion or Belief, India's First Secretary at the UN mission, Bhavika Mangalanandan, challenged the report's approach to religious discrimination during the Covid-19 pandemic and its advocacy concerning funeral rights for terrorists.Mangalanandan argued that the report appeared to place disproportionate emphasis on discriminatory practices and shortcomings in countries in the Global South while overlooking similar tragedies in developed nations.
India asserts climate justice and judicial independence
Separately, India also defended its approach to climate change at the UN General Assembly, stressing the importance of equity, climate justice and sustainable development.Deputy secretary Barkha Tamrakar delivered India's statement before the Third Committee on the report of the Special Rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, titled “An urgent and existential threat: the role of justice systems in addressing the climate crisis.”Tamrakar described climate change as a serious global challenge with consequences for development, livelihoods and human rights. She said India's response was guided by equity, climate justice, sustainable development and the principle of Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC).
She highlighted the Constitution, environmental legislation, the National Green Tribunal and an independent judiciary as key safeguards supporting environmental protection in India.Tamrakar also noted that the Supreme Court had recognised the fundamental rights to life and equality as essential protections against the adverse effects of climate change.On judicial independence, she pointed to transparent, institutionally supervised training programmes, including those conducted by the National Judicial Academy, as measures to strengthen impartiality and safeguard the independence of the judiciary.

He loves digging into legal maxims and political trivia. On off days, when not turning pages or learning русский, he lives in the reverie of “what ifs” and “how abouts.”

The conflict has become an increasingly destabilising front in the United States-Israeli offensive against Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.
On Oct 25, Saudi civil defence authorities issued emergency alerts for Riyadh, Abha and Khamis Mushait, before announcing minutes later that the danger had passed.
The coalition said two drones and a ballistic missile were launched towards Riyadh, and a cruise missile towards the southern city of Khamis Mushait.
It later said it had intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired towards southern Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis had earlier on Oct 25 renewed their warning against using Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, hours after the facility announced it would designate two terminals for flights following a suspension earlier in October.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the airport remained a “military target” and that operations targeting the airport will continue, warning all airlines, airport staff and travellers against using it.
Late on Oct 24, King Khalid Airport said Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights and Terminal 2 for international flights operated by national carriers starting on Oct 25.
Airport operations were halted on Oct 10 following an attack on the airport, claimed by the Houthis, that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300 others, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. The suspension of operations was extended two days later.
The Houthis have been firing ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi airports, ports and oil installations.
Saudi Arabia has recently stepped up its military involvement in Yemen, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a government counter-offensive after the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast in September.
The renewed fighting in Yemen has shattered a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022.
Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen’s civil war in 2015 at the head of a coalition supporting the internationally recognised government after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa a year earlier. REUTERS

4-MIN READ4-MIN

Kolette Limin Singapore
Singapore is turning to major technology firms to strengthen its cyber defences, even as it presses them for greater transparency over security breaches – a balancing act facing regional governments as they seek to harness artificial intelligence while guarding against the risks it introduces.
Those risks were highlighted by an AI agent linked to OpenAI that gained unauthorised access to files on an Australian government website earlier this year, raising questions over how quickly companies disclose security incidents as AI systems become more capable and autonomous.
At a summit earlier this month, Singapore launched a refreshed cybersecurity strategy that would see it progressively deploy AI across its cyber defence operations and work with industry partners to accelerate adoption, as it seeks to bolster protection for its critical infrastructure.
The city state would take a “pragmatic” approach to AI adoption, allowing it to choose between the “best available” models, K. Shanmugam, coordinating minister for national security, said during a speech at Singapore International Cyber Week on October 13.
“We will not need to develop our own AI models for every use case. What we really need is the capability to evaluate the best available models and to adapt them to our own needs.”

The group urged foreign governments and international institutions to intervene using all mechanisms available under international law to halt the forcible displacement of Palestinian civilians, collective punishment, and extensive unlawful destruction, stressing: "Israeli leaders are openly declaring their intentions, and actions on the ground have already begun."
The warning followed a shooting incident near Hebron on Friday that resulted in the deaths of two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinians, with three other soldiers injured.
Subsequently, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced measures to forcibly displace residents and carry out extensive demolitions.
"We will apply in the cities the successful offensive model we implemented in the refugee camps," Netanyahu said.
B’Tselem noted that this exact model has already displaced more than 33,000 Palestinians across the northern occupied West Bank.
Siege and demolitions
Israeli military forces cordoned off Hebron and neighbouring Halhul for a second consecutive day, forcing dozens of Palestinians from their homes, raiding residences, and demolishing a residential building alongside other properties.
The Israeli Civil Administration has concurrently commenced razing Palestinian structures in the Farsh al-Hawa neighbourhood.
Simultaneously, extremist Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich announced the establishment of four new illegal settlement farming outposts across the South Hebron Hills.
B’Tselem warned that these coordinated measures could constitute war crimes that mirror Israel's devastating attacks during its multi-year genocide in Gaza.
The organisation characterised the campaign as part of a wider policy intended to dismantle Palestinian community life while expanding illegal settlements and entrenching permanent Israeli occupation.
"The world cannot stand by as Israel continues its assault on Palestinians, waiting for yet more neighbourhoods to be emptied and erased before intervening," the rights group added.

Abuse survivors approve $800 million settlement with Archdiocese of New York
WASHINGTON, Oct 24 - Survivors of clergy sexual abuse have agreed to an $800 million settlement with the Archdiocese of New York, lawyers said on Saturday, to resolve claims brought by approximately 1,300 people.
• The Catholic Archdiocese of New York agreed to the payment in May, one of the largest payouts in a wave of lawsuits over clergy sex abuse in the US.
• Jeff Anderson & Associates, which represents 300 abuse survivors, called it "a powerful moment in the pursuit of justice."
• The settlement is second only to an $880 million deal reached by the Archdiocese of Los Angeles in 2024.
• The Catholic Church has paid billions of dollars in settlements across the US in the past several years, after New York and other states enacted laws that temporarily enabled victims of child sexual abuse to file lawsuits over decades-old crimes.
• In addition to the $800 million settlement, the archdiocese agreed to release documents pertaining to sexual offenders in the Church.
• The settlement also allows survivors to litigate against the Church's insurers for additional payouts, but avoids a bankruptcy by the archdiocese. REUTERS

Bodies of ambushed Salvadoran soldiers found in Haiti, New York Times reports
PORT-AU-PRINCE, Oct 24 - Bodies believed to be those of four Salvadoran soldiers missing since an ambush by armed gangs in Haiti have been found outside the capital, Port-au-Prince, the New York Times reported on Saturday, citing two people close to the security mission.
The newspaper said the remains were recovered on Saturday and were badly burned, meaning autopsies would be needed to confirm their identities. It said the bodies were handed over at the international airport to a Salvadoran military team that had flown into Haiti on Friday.
The international security mission declined to comment. Reuters could not immediately confirm the report.
The four Salvadorans went missing on Sunday after they jumped from a burning armored vehicle that came under attack on the outskirts of Port-au-Prince while they were returning from a market to their base, Salvadoran officials said earlier this week. The ambush was the first major attack on the Gang Suppression Force, a United Nations-authorized multinational mission, since it began operations in Haiti this year.
President Nayib Bukele said on Wednesday that gangs were holding the four men and that El Salvador had launched a military operation to bring them back unharmed. Additional Salvadoran troops were later deployed to support search and security operations.
No group has publicly claimed responsibility for the attack. Local media have linked the ambush to gangs operating in the area, including powerful armed groups Chen Mechan and 400 Mawozo.
A year into its mandate, the GSF has about 2,000 troops on the ground, well below its authorized ceiling of 5,500. An earlier Kenyan-led security effort struggled with chronic shortages of money, equipment and personnel.
Haiti's gangs have expanded sharply since the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moise, taking control of large parts of Port-au-Prince and displacing 1.4 million to 1.5 million people. REUTERS

The result left WA with a 0-3 record, all but ending its title hopes just three games into the season.
NSW moved into second spot with a 3-1 record.
But it remains to be seen how much longer its will have Konstas in its Shield and one-day ranks given his rich vein of form.
The 21-year-old burst onto the international scene in December 2024 when he made a memorable Boxing Day Test debut against India, scoring 60 in his maiden knock.
Konstas failed to pass 25 in his next nine Test innings, with his most recent appearance in the baggy green coming in July last year against the West Indies.
The talented opener has worked hard on his game over the past 15 months, and it was on full display on Saturday as he cracked 15 fours and four sixes in a masterful display.
And with Australia still crying out for an opener to make his mark ahead of a busy Test schedule, it seems just a matter of time before Konstas is donning the baggy green again.
Whiteman was brave in WA's run chase, but he simply lacked the support needed.
Jack Nisbet snared 3-47 for NSW, including the key scalp of Whiteman in the 46th over, while Bryce Jackson chipped in with 2-58.
One rare highlight for WA came earlier in the day when Agar leapt high into the air to pull off a stunning one-handed catch at backward point to remove Ben Dwarshuis for 20.

Violence flares in Paris after largely peaceful protests
Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators marched in France on Oct 24, with largely peaceful rallies giving way to clashes in Paris and Marseille as night fell despite a huge security operation aimed at preventing a repeat of last week’s unrest.
The Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in protests nationwide, though unions said the true figure was twice as high.
The main demonstration took place in Paris, where around 110,000 people marched on the south-eastern fringes of the capital, denouncing rising living costs and growing inequality.
The atmosphere deteriorated sharply after the rally ended. Riot police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse a group of around 500 hooded youths who hurled stones at officers, a security official said.
Trump votes early in Florida for US midterm elections
US President Donald Trump on Oct 24 voted early in his home state of Florida for the Nov 3 midterm elections, in which his Republican Party is battling to maintain control of Congress.
Trump and his wife, Melania, cast their ballots ahead of an appearance by the president at a campaign rally in the southern US state of Georgia.
Trump said he voted party line, or exclusively for members of his Republican Party.
Obama blasts Trump’s ‘chaos and cruelty’ at Ohio rally

“The operation team conducted a search and rescue using specialised equipment, hoes and spades to facilitate excavation. The victim was successfully extricated and pronounced dead by Ministry of Health personnel at 12.33pm,” the statement read.

Feature: Taste of China's Wuyi Mountain at Switzerland's Grindelwald-First
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
06:06:38 CST
07:06:38 KST

Participants attend an unveiling ceremony marking the sister-peaks partnership between Yunv Peak, a landmark of China's Wuyi Mountain, and Switzerland's Grindelwald-First mountain in the canton of Bern, Switzerland, Oct. 23, 2026. (Xinhua/Lian Yi)
GENEVA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- A display board showcasing China's Wuyi Mountain was unveiled at Switzerland's Grindelwald-First mountain on Friday in simultaneous ceremonies linked by video, marking the destinations' sister-peaks partnership between Yunv Peak, a landmark of Wuyi Mountain, and the Swiss Alpine destination.
At an altitude of more than 2,100 meters, Grindelwald-First mountain was dusted with drifting snow as Alpine peaks emerged from the mist before fading from view. On the newly unveiled board, Yunv Peak was reflected in a clear stream, with bamboo rafts gliding below. The display brought together the landscapes of China and Switzerland, as guests in both countries witnessed the ceremonies via video link.
Oliver Hammel, chief executive of Jungfrau Railways, which operates Grindelwald-First mountain's tourism facilities, said he hoped the display would inspire more international visitors to explore Wuyi Mountain.
"We receive guests from all over the world," he told Xinhua. He expressed hope that visitors would scan the board's QR code to learn more about Wuyi Mountain and eventually travel there themselves.
Presented in Chinese and English, the board highlights cooperation in sustainable tourism and cultural exchange. It also showcases Wuyi Mountain's UNESCO World Heritage status, which recognizes its cultural and natural significance, as well as activities such as hiking, bamboo rafting and visits to tea plantations.
Yunv Peak, also known as Jade Maiden Peak, and Grindelwald-First form the fourth pair of sister peaks linking China and Switzerland. Previous partnerships have linked Yulong Snow Mountain with the Matterhorn, Mount Huangshan with the Jungfrau, and Mount Emei with Mount Rigi.
Fujian Wuyishan Culture and Tourism Group and Jungfrau Railways signed the agreement in November 2025 to promote tourism and cultural exchanges between the destinations.
Located in Switzerland's Jungfrau Region, Grindelwald-First attracts visitors with its spectacular Alpine scenery and diverse outdoor activities. Wuyi Mountain, meanwhile, is renowned for its Danxia landforms, characterized by striking red sandstone cliffs and peaks, as well as its tea culture, rich biodiversity and cultural heritage.
Hammel noted that two of the Swiss peaks involved in the partnerships -- the Jungfrau and Grindelwald-First -- are in the Jungfrau Region.
"The Chinese market, Chinese guests, and exchange with China are important for us," Hammel said, adding that he looked forward to welcoming more Chinese tourists.
In his ceremony address, Hammel also said the two destinations could share experience in sustainable tourism and conservation, helping preserve their landscapes for future generations.
Cui Ke, counselor at the Chinese Embassy and director of the China Cultural Center in Bern, addressed the ceremony on behalf of Chinese Ambassador Qian Minjian. He described the unveiling as another example of cooperation between the two countries in culture and tourism.
Cui expressed hope that the display would serve as more than a photo opportunity, encouraging visitors to discover both destinations and fostering closer ties between the two countries.
Speaking at the outdoor ceremony in Wuyi Mountain, Li Yan, deputy mayor of Wuyishan City, called for closer cooperation in mountain tourism. She said she hoped more Swiss visitors would discover Wuyi Mountain and more Chinese travelers would experience the Swiss Alps.
For Swiss participant Roger Strahm, Wuyi Mountain is already on his travel wish list.
"I am keen to visit Wuyi Mountain to explore its beautiful landscapes and experience China's rich tea culture and profound historical heritage," said Strahm. "I hope that there will be more opportunities for exchanges between the two destinations, allowing more Swiss friends to discover Wuyi Mountain, appreciate its beauty, and fall in love with all that it has to offer." ■

Protests sweep Italian cities, clashes reported
China
Unknown Publisher

Police stand guard near Circo Massimo for an anti-war march in Rome, Italy, Oct. 24, 2026.
