Commentary
Will Maga die in red Ohio? Controversial ad tests Trump’s staying power in midterm elections
- Ohio’s governor race has become a test of Trump-style politics, with Vivek Ramaswamy's ad featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Amy Acton casting her daughter as untrustworthy and a “liar”.
- The Ramaswamy ad using family trauma sparked anger and sympathy, but Trump defended the ad while JD Vance called critics “whining”.
- Polls are tight in a usually Republican state, with voters split over costs, taxes and character, and the result may show whether Trump’s style still wins.
AI generated
WOODSVILLE, Ohio – The world perhaps doesn’t care too much about who runs an American Rust Belt state, if we are to be painfully honest.
But it is hard to look away when the race to become governor of Ohio morphs into the most crucial stress test for President Donald Trump’s brand of shoot-from-the-hip politics.
Will Trump’s combative style – demonising an opponent and never saying sorry even in the face of certifiable fact and breaching the norms of human decency – survive beyond his term? Can a candidate win by borrowing his methods? What kinds of leaders will American voters elevate after seeing two years of Trump’s second term? What, now, is the political temperament of the world’s most influential democracy?
Ohio will offer an answer to all those questions on Nov 3, when Vivek Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire, attempts a Trump-like transition from a MAGA celebrity to an elected executive.
For most of 2026, the race favoured the Ohio-born Ramaswamy whose Tamil-speaking parents emigrated from the southern Indian state of Kerala. The 41-year-old, who studied biology at Harvard and law at Yale, had already made a splash on the national stage with his 2024 presidential run.
His gubernatorial run seemed a shoo-in at first, given Ohio’s hospitality to Republicans and an endorsement by Trump, who won the state in all three of his Republican Party presidential campaigns.
Meanwhile, the Democrats, who have won only one of the state’s past nine gubernatorial elections, have thrown in their lot with Amy Acton, 60, a physician who has never worked as a doctor but won notice for her handling of the state’s response to Covid-19 as a former state health director. A New York Times opinion piece in May 2020 called her “the leader we wish we all had”.
Under Acton’s guidance, Ohio became the first state in the US to order a statewide closure of all public schools. Her policies were widely praised by liberals and panned by conservatives who found the lockdown and mask mandates to be too intrusive and alarmist. She resigned soon after, under pressure to roll back the Covid-19 restrictions.
As months went by, the opinion polls began to show Acton catching up with Ramaswamy against a backdrop of inflation and growing dissatisfaction with Trump.
When the contest tightened, the vitriol rose. She called him a con artist, an out-of-touch billionaire surveying the state from a private jet.
He called her tenure as health director a failure. Her “only qualification for this job is a short-lived stint as the health director when she shut down the economy of this state, and then when the legislature forced her to actually follow real data, she quit on the job”, he said.
But all that paled beside a bombshell ad by the Ramaswamy campaign that began airing on Oct 22. From bitterness over public records, it crossed the line to private trauma.
The ad featured Acton’s elderly mother casting her daughter as untrustworthy and a “liar”. What it left out was that the mother lost custody of Acton at the age of 12 after Acton accused her stepfather of sexual assault. He fled the state before he could be tried and Acton’s mother stood by him.
The ad won Acton, who had publicly disclosed the abuse in 2019, a wave of public sympathy.
It also elicited an intervention from Trump, who leaned in to praise the mother’s “courage” and told Ramaswamy to carry on broadcasting the ad. “What she was really doing was saving Ohio from making a truly horrible choice,” he wrote on Truth Social.
“The Press is trying to convince everyone that this ad is bad, because it’s so good! Who wouldn’t use such an Ad? I would, it’s called, ‘hitting pay dirt’,” he wrote.
Vice-President J.D. Vance, seen as a contender in the 2028 presidential election, said he was “disgusted”. Not by the ad but by fellow Republicans who were “whining” about it.
Confidence beneath the rafters
A day before the storm broke, I spoke to Ramaswamy briefly at a campaign stop in Woodsfield, a once prosperous Appalachian town in south-eastern Ohio, its compact historic downtown surrounded by wooded hills and farmlands.
The townhall-style meeting was held in a cosy barn with wooden rafters. Ramaswamy spoke from a small wooden stage, his voice modulating with emphasis, rather like a businessman making a pitch than a politician given to rhetoric.
He told me his voters were missing in the opinion polls.
“Midterm environments are always tough for the party that’s in power. That’s always true, whether it’s Democrat or Republican. I am confident we will win this election because Ohio polls have consistently undercounted Republicans,” Ramaswamy said.
“That’s just a fact. In this room, if I asked how many have been polled, probably no hands would go up. I ask them how many are going to vote, all of them are going to vote.”
He pointed to the elections in 2024, 2022, 2020 and 2018 as evidence. “That has been the pattern in Ohio,” he said. “I am confident we will prevail because of people like those who are in this room.”
Nathaniel Swigger, associate professor at the Ohio State University who studies public opinion, political psychology and campaigns, told The Straits Times that there was no particular reason to think the polls are wrong.
“Many Republicans will use the ‘Republicans don’t answer polls’ line to claim that they are always undercounted, but that’s not really true,” he said.
Response rates across all groups, including independents, are pretty bad and pollsters use weighted sample results to try and make up for that.
“If the polls are wrong – a big if – then they are just as likely to be wrong in ways that overrate voter support for Ramaswamy,” Swigger said.
“For example, social desirability bias may prevent voters from expressing true opinions if they think others will judge those views as racist or sexist.
“Maybe some people say they’ll vote for Acton because they don’t want to admit they would never vote for a woman.
“Or maybe some people say they’ll vote for Ramaswamy because they don’t want to admit they would never vote for an Indian-American or non-Christian candidate.
“Without controlled experiments to specifically test that, it’s hard to say what that bias might be ahead of an election,” he said.
The uncertainty is striking because Ohio’s recent political history has been stable. This has been ruby-red Republican for a decade, having voted for Trump, Trump and Trump again in the last three presidential elections after spurning Hillary Clinton, Joe Biden and Kamala Harris. Of its 88 counties, only six voted for the Democrats in 2024.
Ohio Republicans are trying to hold on to the control over all three branches of the state government they’ve had since 2011.
Of 15 congressmen that Ohio elected to the US House of Representatives, 10 are Republican. Both senators from Ohio are Republican as well. The last time a Democrat won the governor’s race in Ohio was in 2006.
Yet, most polls now paint Ohio as a volatile, purple territory. “Anything could happen” is the response I heard over and over as I travelled.
In Monroe County, county commissioner Mick Schumacher, describing a transformation of what was predominantly Democrat territory until it voted Trump the first time in 2016, said: “And then we broke a national record per capita for people that flip from D to R.”
That flip has not erased practical concerns. Schumacher cautiously welcomed Ramaswamy’s promise to cut property taxes. “Now, I’m a county commissioner and we depend on that property tax to run the emergency services and county government. So I was not in favour of it until we know what there is that’s going to replace it,” he said.
He also said he had heard that the plan was to raise sales tax to make up the difference, but that could devastate a border town like Woodsfield.
“We border West Virginia; a lot of our people can shop there. So it will decimate the border towns. People in Columbus, maybe they won’t be affected,” Schumacher said.
For Jimmy Williams, a Monroe County Republican Party official, polls that showed Acton in the lead were a pressure tactic.
“The Democrats’ playbook is to talk and try to sound like they’re winning and trying to discourage the Republicans from getting out the vote. But they don’t realise, we’re energised,” he said.
What do the candidates stand for?
Away from the campaign events, it was easier to find voters who are firmly opposed to Acton but still needed persuading about Ramaswamy, a Hindu in a state where over 60 per cent of the predominantly white population identify as Christian.
A florist’s assistant in Youngstown, a largely Democratic area, who asked not to be named for fear of hurting the shop’s business, said the Acton campaign is running limp, “kind of like Joe Biden’s campaign”.
“You don’t see her; you just see ads on TV. And if anybody wants to get close to her, she’s got bodyguards that don’t let you get near. She doesn’t answer questions. We don’t even really know what she’s for. She’s just there,” she said.
She was more tentative on Ramaswamy. “Vivek seems smart. I am going to give him a closer look,” she added.
An air force veteran expressed surprise that an Oct 12 Trump rally in Youngstown had pulled in a sizeable crowd.
“This area is very Democratic,” said Chad, who gave only his first name. “So if he got 70 per cent seats filled, he did well,” he said.
He regarded Trump’s defence of the controversial ad featuring Acton’s mother as “marginal”.
“Some things Trump does and says I don’t agree with, but I think he does what he thinks is right for the country. And at least I know where he stands. I’d rather have a politician do that than one that lies in my face, which is what we normally get,” he said.
It was an argument I’ve heard often: an approval of Trump despite reservations about his conduct.
Democrats believe that rising costs and unease about government corruption have cracked the door open.
At the Ohio Democratic Party’s headquarters in state capital Columbus – an inconspicuous building with no boards, banners or signs to mark it – spokeswoman Marisa Nahem maintained that Acton was ahead.
“Ohioans are excited about Dr Acton’s campaign because they know she’s the only candidate in this race who will tackle rising costs, stand up to the corporate special interests and billionaires trying to buy Ohio, and put working families first,” she said.
“We are seeing incredible energy among Ohioans, with raw Democratic vote totals in primaries higher in most counties when compared to 2022,” she said, adding that there was lower Republican primary participation and stronger Democrat early voting.
A promise to lower costs and tackle Republican corruption was a message that crossed party lines, she said.
“It is a mission that isn’t just popular, it’s unifying among Ohioans of all political backgrounds,” she added.
The quiet on the campaign trail
For all the competing claims of loyalty and energy, the race’s intensity was not always apparent on the streets: Along the routes I visited, few yard signs advertised a contest that polling showed was closely fought.
There were the occasional posters for local judges or sheriffs or other county officials. Officials from both parties claimed that the fear of intimidation from the other side had discouraged yard signs this cycle.
When I said I saw only a few Ramaswamy signs and more of Acton’s, Williams in Monroe County brushed it off.
“Was that Acton sign just setting out along the road? When I’m driving around, it doesn’t bother me if they’re along the road. It bothers me if they’re in someone’s truck, but I don’t see that,” he said.
Gathering hard data on yard signs is problematic so it’s hard to say for sure, said Swigger, who teaches at Ohio State University. But he, too, had noticed fewer in his neighbourhood.
“My guess is that it is a combination of conflict avoidance and exhaustion,” he said.
“It’s no secret that American politics, and Ohio politics, has become angrier and many people are probably reluctant to put up signs or put bumper stickers on their cars because they are avoiding a touchy subject.”
But that itself had a message, he said.
“I think the lack of yard signs can be taken as a sign that many, many voters are dissatisfied with the US political system,” he said.
That leaves Ohio with a contest where the currents are hard to read. Is it hidden Republican strength or Democratic opportunity?
Trump’s name will not be on the ballot but this is still his race.

Rs 10 lakh cover for 45 paise: Counter rail ticket buyers get insurance option
Unknown

05:44:19 KST

At present, the optional travel insurance facility is available only for reserved tickets bought online.
NEW DELHI: From Tuesday (Oct 27), all railway passengers buying reserved tickets from reservation counters can opt for travel insurance. At present, optional travel insurance facility is available only for reserved tickets bought online.The insurance premium is only 45 paise per passenger, including taxes, with coverage of Rs 10 lakh in case of death and permanent total disability in a train accident.The scheme has provision for payment of Rs 7.5 lakh for permanent partial disability and up to Rs 2 lakh for hospitalisation expenses arising from injuries, as well as Rs 10,000 towards transportation of mortal remains of deceased passengers. The Railway Board has directed all its zones to implement the facility.It said, “Where a passenger opts for insurance, the applicable premium shall be collected along with the ticket fare through digital means only. Staff shall ensure that where the person is opting for insurance, payment is done through digital means.”Reservation staff will inform passengers about the availability of the optional insurance facility and facilitate the exercise of their choice.The board said reservation staff will ensure that the mobile number (mandatory) along with other requisite passenger particulars are captured accurately so as to facilitate transmission of relevant details to the insurance firm for issuance of the policy.
Passengers opting for insurance shall be informed that the policy details will be communicated to their registered mobile number.It covers specified railway accidents and untoward incidents, including train collisions, derailments, violent attacks, robbery, arson and accidental falls from trains. Coverage extends to diverted routes and alternative transport arranged by the railways in certain cases of train diversion or short termination.
Normal second class or general class passengers are not covered under the insurance policy. It is also not applicable to children below the age of 5 years for whom tickets are issued without a berth or seat. But it is applicable to children in 5-11 age group who have reservation with berth or without berth.

[FEATURED]
ALEXEY DANILIN CONCEIVES ‘hope’ CERAMIC TABLE LAMP for MAYTONI
Designed by Alexey Danilin for German lighting brand Maytoni, Hope is a table lamp composed almost entirely of natural ceramic. Conceived for mass production within technical and budgetary parameters, the design replaces conventional fabric or metal shades with a split ceramic envelope, allowing approximately 90% of the fixture’s mass to remain recyclable at the end of its lifecycle.
LED MODULES PROJECT REFLECTED LIGHT THROUGH SLIT OF SPLIT VOLUMES
For the lamp’s sculptural silhouette, designer Alexey Danilin draws inspiration from classical Roman statuary and traditional pottery forms, pairing curved, arching geometries with contemporary product design. Internally, integrated LED boards are oriented to direct illumination outward through the central gap separating the two ceramic halves, utilizing surface reflection to soften light output. A central vertical stem fastens the two ceramic elements, capped by a small metal sphere at the top. This structural component doubles as a functional touch-sensitive switch and dimmer, offered in various metal finishes to integrate with diverse interior palettes.

An Istanbul court ordered prosecutors to investigate Turkish nationals allegedly involved in the mistreatment of participants in a Gaza-bound aid flotilla while they were held in Israel during the first hearing of a case against 35 defendants, including the Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The Istanbul 11th High Criminal Court ruled that individuals identified by complainants as Turkish citizens who participated in alleged abuses against them in Israeli custody should be identified and referred to prosecutors for necessary legal action.
The court also ordered that existing arrest warrants and Interpol Red Notice requests against all 35 defendants remain in effect.
The case concerns Israel's armed interception of the Gaza-bound flotilla, which was carrying humanitarian aid to Gaza.
Flotilla participants describe alleged mistreatment
During the hearing, one complainant said he had joined the flotilla as a doctor to deliver medical supplies to Palestinians in Gaza.
He said Israeli soldiers confiscated five or six boxes of medical supplies from their vessel and that participants were subjected to mistreatment at Israel's Ashdod port.
He said he wished to pursue his complaint against the defendants.
Another complainant said she had been subjected to two strip searches and had an altercation with Israeli soldiers after refusing to remove her headscarf.
"They recorded me wearing the clothes they gave me instead of my headscarf and mocked me," she told the court.
She said one of the soldiers who detained her had told her he was from Türkiye's central province of Yozgat.
"They took our personal belongings, and I have not been able to recover any of them. Our privacy was seriously violated. I am filing a complaint," she said.
A Turkish lawmaker also testified, saying she and approximately 80 other participants were held in a poorly ventilated room after being detained.
She said that an Israeli soldier insulted Islam while they were reading the Quran.
Un said detainees were not allowed to sleep and were subjected to verbal abuse and psychological mistreatment.
"We were not even allowed to close our eyes where we were held. Sleeping was forbidden," she said.

Lawyers call for broader investigation into Gaza
Riza Saka, president of the bar association, described the proceedings as historic and called for further international evidence to be included in the case.
Saka referred to provisional measures ordered by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in proceedings concerning allegations of genocide in Gaza.
He requested copies of relevant ICJ documents and a UN report concerning allegations of genocide in Gaza.
He also referred to the arrest warrants and Red Notice requests issued against Netanyahu and the other defendants.
Lawyer Yasin Samli argued that the case involved allegations of genocide, crimes against humanity and attacks against civilians.
Samli said lawyers had submitted eight volumes of evidence, including five concerning alleged crimes against women and children in Gaza.
Court seeks separate indictment over alleged crimes against Gaza civilians

The panel said investigations into genocide and crimes against humanity could be conducted upon a request from Türkiye's justice minister.
Taking into account the principle that courts are bound by the factual allegations set out in an indictment, the panel ordered a formal request to prosecutors concerning a possible new indictment.
The request calls for alleged crimes against civilians in Gaza, separate from the actions involving the flotilla, to be described in concrete terms and linked to supporting evidence.
The court said evidence submitted by legal organisations should be considered in that process.
Court orders asset inquiries, requests ICC documents
The panel also ordered inquiries into whether any of the 35 defendants hold movable or immovable assets in Türkiye.
It directed that a request be sent through the Justice Ministry for documents from proceedings involving the defendants before the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The court additionally ordered that a UN report submitted concerning allegations of genocide in Gaza be requested through the Justice Ministry.
The panel accepted applications to participate in the proceedings from complainants and several legal and human rights organisations.
The hearing was adjourned until 30 March 2027.

No EC nod needed for voter to sue candidate over false information: Supreme Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
20:03:20 UTC
05:03:20 KST

The Supreme Court said that Section 125-A was inserted in the RoP Act in 2002.
NEW DELHI: A voter can now not only cast a vote in an election but can also drag an election candidate to court and initiate criminal proceedings for lying and furnishing a false declaration as Supreme Court has ruled that a complaint filed by a private person alleging an offence under Section 125-A of Representation of People Act (filing false affidavit) is maintainable and the Election Commission’s nod was not needed.Explaining the interplay between Section 125-A of Representation of People Act and Section 195(1) of the CrPC which says that no court shall take cognisance of any offences punishable under sections 172 to 188, including the offence of furnishing false information to a public servant, the top court held that Section 125A of RoP Act does not come within the ambit of Section 195 of CrPC and a court can take cognisance of a private complaint. The court’s ruling will further empower the electorate against candidates who lied in their affidavits.A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu quashed the Karnataka HC order which had held that “right given to the voter is only to file an election petition, and not to register a private complaint of crime which is the duty of the Election Commission, if it wants to do so”.SC said that Section 125-A was inserted in the RoP Act in 2002, while Section 195 of CrPC was amended in 2006, and that the omission of the legislature to include Section 125-A of the RoP Act in Section 195 of CrPC was deliberate and no court would be barred from taking cognisance of an alleged offence under Section 125-A of the RoP Act, even on the complaint lodged by a private person.
“Should we read into Section 195 of CrPC a prohibition in respect of Section 125-A of the RoP Act also, apart from those expressly included? If indeed it were the intention of the legislature that cognisance of any offence relating to furnishing of false information by a candidate in an affidavit with intent of being elected in an election (referred to in Section 125-A of the RoP Act) could only be taken if the complainant were a public servant, the same could have been provided by an amendment of Section 195, CrPC since Section 125-A of the RoP Act is of fairly recent origin.”SC also refused to give credence to the EC’s press note that it can take cognisance of such complaints and refer such matters to the relevant investigating authorities on a case-to-case basis. “...Even though the ECI is supreme in its own sphere and has, indeed, issued guidelines/press notes based on its understanding of the statutory provisions, interpretation of statutes is primarily the task of the courts and such guidelines/press notes do not bind us,” the court said.
It said that Karnataka HC erred in holding that a private complaint cannot be filed for an offence under Section 125A of RoP Act which is punishable up to six months of jail term. The HC had interpreted the provision solely upon reading the letter issued by the Election Commission of India on the issue which was rejected by the apex court.Allaying the apprehension that allowing the lodging of a criminal complaint by a private person would be misused and frivolous cases would be filed by political rivals, SC said, “If at all a complaint is lodged to harass an elected candidate or frivolous allegations are levelled therein, the laws of the country duly empower the competent magistrates to pass such order(s) as they deem fit and proper commensurate with the facts and circumstances of each case.”

====================================================================================================

Expecting to lose economic standing hurts well-being more than expecting to gain helps it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
20:00:56 UTC
05:00:56 KST

Believing that your socioeconomic position could decline in the future may itself reduce well-being by increasing anxiety about social status, according to research published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin. Expectations of moving up the ladder, by contrast, had weaker and less consistent effects.
Social mobility describes movement up or down the socioeconomic ladder, which can involve changes in income, employment and social standing. Much of the previous research has focused on the promise of upward mobility. But the prospect of moving in the opposite direction may be especially important at a time when some people in wealthy countries expect to experience lower living standards than previous generations.
The researchers focused on status anxiety, or worry about one’s position in the socioeconomic hierarchy. This can include concerns about losing status, failing to advance or being left behind compared with other people. Because anticipated downward mobility represents the possibility of losing resources and social standing, the researchers proposed that it could increase status anxiety and consequently reduce well-being.
Led by Davide Melita of the University of Granada in Spain, the researchers conducted four studies involving 2,819 people in Spain and the United States. The first two were surveys, while the final two were experiments designed to determine whether changing people’s expectations about their socioeconomic future could actually affect status anxiety.
Study 1 surveyed 216 full-time U.S. workers (average age 39; 49% women) about their beliefs regarding mobility in American society as a whole, such as whether most people now earn less than the previous generation. Those who believed downward mobility was more common reported greater status anxiety, which was in turn associated with lower life satisfaction, poorer perceived health and more depressive symptoms. Beliefs about upward mobility were not linked to status anxiety.
Study 2 surveyed 1,536 people in Spain (51% women), recruited to resemble the national population, using single questions about whether participants expected their own socioeconomic status to improve or worsen. Expecting one’s own status to worsen was associated with greater status anxiety and lower life satisfaction. Unexpectedly, expecting one’s status to improve was also associated with greater status anxiety, although it was directly linked to higher life satisfaction as well. The authors suggest that strong expectations of change in either direction may bring uncertainty about the future.
The researchers then tested the relationship experimentally. In Study 3, 472 Spanish university students (average age 22; 70% women) imagined starting a new life in a fictional society called Bimboola. Everyone began in the middle-income group, but participants were randomly told they had good chances of moving up, staying in the same group or moving down, while the level of inequality in the society was held constant.
Participants told they were likely to move down reported more status anxiety than those told they were likely to stay put, although the difference was small. In exploratory analyses, that increased anxiety in turn predicted lower satisfaction with their imagined life in Bimboola. Being told they were likely to move up, however, did not affect status anxiety.
Study 4 repeated the experiment with 595 employed Americans recruited online, and here the manipulation had much stronger effects on participants’ expectations. Prospects of moving down increased status anxiety, while prospects of moving up reduced it, and these changes in anxiety carried through to life satisfaction in Bimboola in opposite directions. The negative effect of anticipated decline was larger than the positive effect of anticipated advancement.
Across the four studies, the pattern for downward mobility was notably consistent: believing that one’s socioeconomic position could worsen was associated with greater status anxiety and, through that anxiety, lower well-being. By contrast, the results for upward mobility varied between studies, and only the U.S. experiment found that prospects of moving up reduced status anxiety and indirectly increased life satisfaction.
Melita and colleagues summarized, “our findings suggest that both upward and downward beliefs influence well-being through status anxiety, but the effects of downward mobility beliefs are stronger and more consistent.” The authors argue that policies aimed at improving well-being should not only expand opportunities for upward mobility but also protect vulnerable groups from economic downturns, for example by strengthening social safety nets.
Some limitations should be noted. The first two studies were correlational, and Study 2 measured mobility expectations with single questions. The experiments involved an imaginary society rather than actual unemployment, income loss or downward mobility, and they measured satisfaction with life in that imaginary society rather than participants’ real lives.
The researchers also noted that cultural circumstances could influence people’s reactions to the scenarios. The Spanish experiment involved young adults in a country with high youth unemployment, who may be skeptical about upward mobility, while Americans tend to overestimate how much mobility exists.
The study, “Prospects of Downward Mobility Cause Status Anxiety and Life Dissatisfaction,” was authored by Davide Melita, Matthias S. Gobel, Juan Matamoros-Lima, Rosa Rodríguez-Bailón and Guillermo B. Willis.

Sullivan actually intended to vote for the incumbent senator.
Trump told reporters on Friday that he directed the Justice Department to file the lawsuit: "I'm the one that said 'do it.'"
The move drew swift bipartisan backlash, including from Alaska's Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski, who said on social media, "The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit."
Two Sullivans
The legal battle centers on Daniel J. Sullivan, a non-incumbent challenger sharing a near-identical name with incumbent GOP Senator Daniel S. Sullivan. Alaska election officials initially removed the challenger from the ballot after a complaint from the state Republican Party, but state courts ordered his inclusion on the ballot.
In June, the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed that decision and directed election officials to clearly distinguish the two men.
The ballot now lists Sen. Sullivan as the "incumbent" and Republican, while the other Sullivan has no party registration.
The Justice Department filed its lawsuit on Oct. 22, seeking an order to prevent Alaska from certifying the Senate election if the incumbent loses.
The proposed intervenors say the department's approach would force Alaska voters to choose between electing the president's preferred candidate and risking the state being barred from certifying its election results.
Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee argue that the lawsuit directly threatens their interests because it could prevent Peltola from taking office even if she wins the election under Alaska's ranked-choice system.
They also question whether Alaska state officials will mount a sufficiently vigorous defense, given that the state's Division of Elections previously tried to exclude Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot before a state court overturned the move.
The DSCC and Alaskans for Mary are asking the court to grant them defendant-intervenor status so they can formally file motions to dismiss the lawsuit.
Severe hazards
The Democrats argue that while the DOJ has cited the National Voter Registration Act as the legal basis for its lawsuit, the statute contains no provision authorizing the federal government to dictate candidate eligibility or ballot layout, which are state matters under the Constitution.
Legal experts have echoed those concerns, noting that relying on the NVRA's general preamble language to halt state election certification lacks precedent.
The League of Women Voters of Alaska and Common Cause filed separately, warning that the DOJ's demand to investigate voter intent presents severe constitutional hazards.
The filings note that the DOJ has offered no mechanism to determine whether voters who selected Daniel J. Sullivan intended to vote for the incumbent.
Blocking certification, the groups argue, would disenfranchise Alaskans by denying them representation and injecting chaos into the election outcome.
Both organizations are asking the court for permission to join the case as defendants. The Democratic groups say they intend to seek dismissal if the court grants their motion.

'Set and forget': Is Australia's healthcare system failing us?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
19:45:37 UTC
04:45:37 KST

As Australians process the aftermath of the alleged attack on independent Indi MP Helen Haines, attention has again turned to whether gaps in the health system may have contributed to the circumstances surrounding the incident.
The alleged attacker, who is accused of ramming Haines with a car near her electorate office, reportedly has a rare neurological condition, idiopathic transverse myelitis, and has previously received treatment for mental health issues. He is also facing charges related to cultivating and possessing cannabis.
It comes after Queensland man Joel Cauchi, who had been diagnosed with recurrent schizophrenia, fatally stabbed six people at Westfield Bondi Junction in 2024 before being shot dead by police.
Earlier this year, two patients who escaped from Cumberland Hospital, a major mental health facility in NSW, allegedly committed separate crimes that resulted in the deaths of three people within days of each other.
Health economist Luke Slawomirski of The Australia Institute says the overwhelming majority of people with mental illness are not violent, but there are questions around whether they are receiving the care and support they need, and whether earlier and more consistent care could avert some crises.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"We have built a health system that is very good at delivering expensive medical interventions but much less effective at keeping people well," he tells SBS News.
"Mental health is perhaps one of the clearest examples of this imbalance."
This month, internal documents released by the NSW government under a parliamentary order revealed a shortfall of nearly $600 million in funding for the state's public mental health services. Doctors across Victoria's healthcare system also planned to strike over understaffing and unsafe working conditions.
Experts say change is needed to improve the healthcare system, including mental health services, especially for those in regional and rural areas.
Haines previously championed the need for reform in her own electorate, saying in a statement in March last year: "Indi does not have enough doctors, nurses, psychologists and allied health workers to care for our community and the result is people waiting too long, spending too much and travelling too far to access necessary healthcare."
Are gaps in health care fuelling support for One Nation?
Disenchantment with Australia's healthcare system may also be contributing to political volatility.
The electorate of Indi in Victoria's north-east extends to the border with NSW and neighbours the electorate of Farrer, where One Nation won its first lower house seat earlier this year.
Support for One Nation, which wants substantial cuts to immigration, has grown significantly and polling indicates it may rival the Coalition as the party of opposition.
Research group Redbridge has found healthcare is frequently among the top two issues for One Nation voters.
During the Farrer by-election, the standard of care provided by the hospitals serving communities on the NSW/Victorian border, managed by Albury Wodonga Health, was one of the top issues raised.
Redbridge research and reputation director Simon Welsh says some One Nation voters nominate immigration as one of their top concerns, but the majority rank cost of living and health among their highest priorities.
He says many believe a two-tiered health system is emerging in Australia, with certain services only available to those with money.
As part of research for the Australian Resilience Index, Redbridge found the average One Nation seat had five hospitals located within 15km, but the average Labor or Coalition seat had 38 hospitals.
"When you look at what we call 'health resilience', the lineup between the areas with the lowest health resilience and the areas with the highest One Nation vote is significant," Welsh says.
Health resilience was assessed by looking at factors such as access to health care and mental health support, rates of alcohol and smoking consumption, and data on exercise and diet.
The 'lost tribe' of medical graduates
Australian Medical Association (AMA) vice president Julian Rait agrees Australia's system has become very inequitable, especially for rural and regional Australians.
He believes there's been a lack of investment in public hospital outpatient services — which provide care to patients who are not formally admitted to hospital overnight — as well as the health workforce.
There's a nationwide shortage of practitioners of all sorts, including allied health professionals, and that has led to deficiencies [even] in the outer suburbs of major cities, or some of our smaller capital cities like Darwin or Hobart.
"We're seeing a deficiency of sufficient GPs and also specialist services as well."
Rait says the AMA has been calling for a national workforce strategy, and the reintroduction of Health Workforce Australia (HWA), an agency that used to oversee clinical training arrangements and planning for the sector, but which was abolished by the Abbott government in 2014.
The AMA also wants targeted strategies to boost the rural and regional workforce, including local hubs for specialist training.
While medical school places have expanded, Rait says many students struggle to find training positions after they graduate, limiting their ability to practice independently as GPs or other specialists.
"We've got large increasing numbers of people that have got medical qualifications but can't actually train in any speciality," Rait says, noting that positions are limited by a lack of state government funding.
We call them a 'lost tribe', [those] who finish their medical degrees but have nowhere to go in terms of their training pathways.
"It's a depressing situation for those people, but also it's a lost opportunity to try and address the shortages that are in rural and regional areas of our country."
Regional healthcare inequalities
Catholic Health Australia director of health policy Katharine Bassett says Australia has one of the best health systems in the world but access is an issue. She agrees on the need for a national, independent approach to planning the care workforce in Australia.
Workers move constantly between hospitals, aged care, disability and community services, as well as between states, but nobody is looking at the workforce as a whole.
The Australia Institute also supports the reinstatement of the HWA, and Slawomirski says it would be valuable to have a coordinated whole-of-system view of how many specialists and GPs are trained, and where they end up working.
He says the system should also make it easier for overseas-trained doctors to practice in Australia and make work in public hospital outpatient departments more attractive to specialists.
Fees charged by specialists should be scrutinised to assess whether they are justifiable, Slawomirski says, and potential Medicare incentives for rural and regional areas could help improve access.
More transparent information about the costs of seeing a specialist, expected treatment outcomes, and alternatives should also be considered.
While Slawomirski doesn't think those living in the regions will ever have the same outcomes in terms of mortality as those living in the cities, he says the differences at the moment are "really appalling", noting that the rates of premature deaths in some remote or regional areas were two or three times those in metropolitan areas.
"It's just unacceptable," he says.
Challenges to mental health treatment
Bassett says Australia performs well when it comes to acute mental health care through the public system, and community services for those with lower-level needs, but it struggles to maintain services for those whose needs fall in between.
"Where we struggle is the middle — people who are too unwell to be managed by a GP or a community program but don't need an emergency admission," she says.
Private hospitals carry a lot of that care in Australia, but only for people with private health insurance, and many people don’t have it or can't afford it.
Bassett also stresses the importance of other factors that can influence outcomes.
"Whether someone stays well often depends on having a stable home, an education, a job and feel[ing] supported by people around them," she says.
Despite this, housing, education, employment, health and disability support are run and funded as separate systems.
"Joining services up is the real challenge."
Overall, Bassett believes too much health policy is "set and forget".
"We need to be comfortable putting a policy in place, evaluating it honestly, and admitting when we haven't got it right. Circumstances change, and policy has to change with them."

Mass protests have swept across Europe over the weekend, with demonstrators clashing with riot police amid widespread anger over soaring living costs and government policies.
The unrest has largely been inspired by the protests in France, which began in September. Spearheaded by students, they were originally aimed at rising education costs, a lack of teachers, and the poor condition of educational facilities. They eventually morphed into widespread violence and now carry a broader anti-government undertone.
France remains the hotbed of the protests, with at least 410,000 people hitting the streets nationwide on Saturday, including some 110,000 in Paris, according to Interior Ministry figures. The CGT union, one of the key organizers of the demonstrations, put the estimate nearly twice as high, at about 800,000.
The French authorities have implemented strict security measures in an effort to avoid a repeat of widespread rioting over the past weekend. In Paris, the demonstrators were banned from gathering at several central locations, ending up confined to the city’s southeastern edge.
The protests nevertheless turned violent in multiple locations, including Paris, where clashes between police and rowdy demonstrators were observed after the march concluded. Violence has been reported in Clermont-Ferrand, Lyon, Marseille, Strasbourg, Nice, Nantes, and other cities, where law enforcement used riot control measures to repel protesters.

Accused paedophile barrister asked Cambodian woman to help find 'virgins'

Case of accused paedophile barrister Mark Dennis prompts former charity insiders to speak out
In January, prominent barrister Mark Dennis was arrested at Sydney Airport and charged with possessing child abuse material. Weeks later, before entering a formal plea, he was found dead in his home.
An ABC investigation has uncovered Dennis's longstanding relationship with celebrated children's charity Sunrise Cambodia, where he was chairman from 2018 to 2020.
The revelations have prompted an examination of Sunrise's child protection history, raising questions about the culture of orphanages across the country.
Warning: This article contains references to child sexual abuse and suicide.
When Akara* was working at the Cambodian orphanage Sunrise, she noticed the charity's chairman, Australian barrister Mark Dennis SC, always liked spending time with "pretty girls" when he visited.
"He was always playing with the girls," she said. "He liked girls."
Her relationship with Dennis was professional, so she was surprised to receive a text message from him a few years after leaving Sunrise.
Mark Dennis: If I send a full video will you delete it after watching?
Akara didn't answer the question directly, but he persisted.
Mark Dennis: Ok I send and you can watch tonight — hope you enjoy 😂😂😂💦💦💦🍆🍆
Less than two hours later, he sent a link to a Dropbox file– the thumbnail showing an unmade bed. It was a video of him having sex with a Cambodian person.
Mark Dennis: Did you enjoy watching?
Mark Dennis: ?
Mark Dennis: You like it?
He called her. She did not answer. He kept asking.
Akara stayed positive but said she did not want any more videos.
Then, Dennis changed tack.
Mark Dennis: Do you know any Cambodian girl who speaks English and wants to find a husband?
How old? And be English speaking?
Mark Dennis: Young is good 😂
Mark Dennis: I prefer virgin of course 😂🥰

Mark Dennis: Any time you can help me in any way let me know — happy to reward you 😂😂😇😇

Mark Dennis: Ok you can come and watch me if you want 😂😂

Mark Dennis: I pay you $300 watch one hour 😂😂

The chat ended with Akara sending a dog-barking emoji — one final effort to make him stop.
The ABC has reviewed the metadata to verify the text messages were sent from the same number Dennis used for his legal work.
Akara said she had no idea why Dennis sent the messages and did not report them to Sunrise or police.
"I feel horrible," she told the ABC. "I'm still thinking 'why, why, why'. It's disgusting."
In January, Dennis was charged with possessing and transmitting child abuse material, but he was found dead in his home before facing trial.
The ABC has revealed Australian and Cambodian national police are still jointly investigating Dennis's network, including his links to Sunrise, in a cross-border investigation codenamed Operation Queenstown.
Dennis sponsored a handful of children at Sunrise over many years, regularly visited these and other children in the orphanage, and maintained close relationships with some children he met through Sunrise once they left as adults.
Former Sunrise employees have alleged inappropriate behaviour by Dennis, including sexual harassment of an employee, excessive touching of teenage girls and entering children's dormitories.
None of these allegations were reported to Sunrise. A spokesperson for Sunrise said police had informed the charity that no current or former Sunrise child had been identified as one of Dennis's victims.
"We take child protection extremely seriously. Sunrise operates under Cambodian, Australian and international child protection standards, is independently audited, and any concern raised by a child or graduate is followed up thoroughly."
Now, documents obtained by Background Briefing and ABC Investigations reveal that Sunrise was made aware of allegations of misconduct, including against two former Sunrise employees and one current employee.
The claims include one historical allegation of rape by a former employee against a Sunrise girl, after being given a "final warning" for sexual misconduct years earlier.
Sunrise declined to comment on what action was taken in response to this for privacy reasons but added that some allegations that had been made to the ABC did not align with its records.
The revelations have prompted former Sunrise staff to come forward with historical concerns about the celebrated charity's policies and culture, and wider reflection across the industry about how all charities balance fundraising with child safety.
Maggie Eno, a co-founder of Cambodian children's charity M'Lop Tapang, speaking generally, said the ABC's investigation raised awareness across all charities about unsafe practices, which "goes on a lot sadly", and questioned the future of orphanages in Cambodia.
"We're not post-Khmer Rouge anymore, where there really genuinely was so many orphans. The need is not there. The need is for family-based care, community-based care," she said.
Social worker Rob Madsen, who worked as Sunrise's operations manager from 2008-2012, said there needed to be an independent investigation run by Cambodian experts into Dennis's role at Sunrise.
"There's been a significant intrusion by an alleged offender," he said. "There needs to be an arms-length investigation. If there are potential victims, those victims must be identified and provided support."
A 'revolving door' of visitors
Madsen was excited to join Sunrise Cambodia in 2008, a high-profile Australian charity celebrated for helping disadvantaged children.
He had spent the previous 15 years working with government agencies and non-government organisations in child protection, and his skills were embraced by the charity's founder Geraldine Cox.
"You have strengths to bring to Sunrise that have never been offered before, and I know the children will benefit from what you have to give," Cox wrote to Madsen.
However, upon starting as operations manager, Madsen was quickly disturbed by some of what he saw.
He said a busload of tourists came to see the children, who performed dance shows, in what he described as a "revolving door" of visitors and sponsors who felt entitled to take children outside the orphanage.
"I was shocked," Madsen said. "Australians have come to Cambodia for the sole purpose of harming children, sexually abusing a child."
Madsen introduced new rules for visitors, staff and sponsors — designed to limit and supervise adult interactions with children, and record and investigate any allegations of wrongdoing.
Sunrise said it used standard guidelines provided by the Cambodian government prior to Madsen's arrival but acknowledged "more extensive" policies were developed at that time.
Madsen's framework was tested in December 2008, when an Australian sponsor emailed Cox about an interaction with a young girl who told her a Sunrise employee was a "bad man" because of something that happened in the bedroom.
"I am very concerned that he may be a paedophile or at least acting improperly … I will leave the matter in your capable hands," the sponsor wrote.
"As a primary teacher with 20 years' experience, I feel I know when children are telling the truth."
The following day, Cox responded that she was having "this looked into privately".
"But find it difficult to believe that [staff member] is guilty of anything along the lines of your message. He is a dedicated father [Sunrise term for employee] of 43 girls and has been with us for over 10 years."
In response, Madsen initially wrote to Cox saying that he thought the sponsor was "clearly overstepping her perceived role as sponsor".
He suggested the staff member not be left alone with children "so as he is not placed in a position of further accusation".
Then, Madsen said he did eventually put the staff member on watch, and when the same person was accused of sending pornographic material to a young teacher the following year, he was sacked.
Asked about this account in a series of questions, Sunrise did not respond.
Bus driver accused of rape
Not long after, Sunrise faced a bigger crisis when a 16-year-old girl alleged she had been raped by the charity's long-term bus driver.
According to reports compiled two months after the alleged incident, the bus driver dropped the children at school but asked one girl to stay behind, then drove to a quiet plot of land, and allegedly raped her.
The girl fell pregnant and underwent an abortion. She reported what happened to Sunrise and the police. The bus driver was terminated by Sunrise but disappeared to evade police arrest, according to the documents.
This same bus driver had a history of multiple allegations of sexual misconduct towards children at Sunrise, detailed in the documents.
An incident report, written by Madsen, said the bus driver was given a "final warning" in 2004 for "abnormal sexualised behaviour" towards children, including "flirting and watching girls undress in the toilet".
"I cannot hide my feeling of anger and frustration over this, and the fact that such behaviour was not taken more seriously at the time."
Madsen wrote the staff member should have been "instantly dismissed", and he was worried the "mild action … may very well come back to bite".
He also warned Sunrise was at risk of "being exposed in the media" and said there had been "clearly a number of serious gaps" with previous management of this staff member.
"I am confident though, that we are now doing all we can to ensure the best possible protection of our children."
Sunrise said historical allegations the ABC asked it to comment on did not reflect the "substantial safeguarding measures, oversight mechanisms, and continuous improvements that Sunrise has implemented to protect children and promote their wellbeing".
Boy 'rewarded' despite abuse
Sunrise reported another case — of sexual assault by a child — to authorities, but a subsequent decision raised questions about its attitude towards offenders.
For decades, Sunrise sent Cambodian students on exchanges to private schools in Australia.
The opportunities were highly sought-after among the children, and only a handful of students were selected through a competitive process.
In 2010, a teenager was chosen to study at a prestigious boys' college in Australia despite the boy admitting to "penetrative, forced sex with a female child" in Cambodia two years earlier.
"The police were informed of the abuse," Madsen wrote to the board. "A brief record kept in the file at [Sunrise]."
However, Madsen said the boy did not undergo a psychological assessment before being selected and warned that choosing the boy sent the wrong signal to other children.
"We, by our actions, also give other children a clear message that in life, we can indeed do wrong — break rules of life and law, and in fact be rewarded without consequence."
Sunrise did not respond to specific questions about Madsen's email or the case.
Employee accused of lacking professional boundaries
Sunrise staff members have not just raised historical concerns.
The ABC has obtained a resignation letter written by a senior employee in 2020 raising concerns about another Sunrise employee, who remains employed by Sunrise at the time of publication.
In the letter, the resigning employee told Cox and other managers that this employee should not stay in his current position because "his behaviour is against child protection policy".
"He takes children to his house and he sleep in the same bed," the senior employee wrote. "And he likes to bring the children that he likes outside."
The allegation was that this man had unprofessional boundaries with children.
The ABC has spoken with two additional sources who also made claims against the same employee but did not report these to management.
Sunrise said an investigation into the 2020 letter found the bed-sharing claim was unsubstantiated but confirmed the employee had taken children to his home on multiple occasions with other people and had "shown favouritism in taking children on outings".
"[The employee] was warned about this behaviour by Sunrise management at the time," a spokesperson said. "Sunrise therefore does not accept any suggestion that the concerns about [employee] were simply disregarded."
Sunrise also released a statement on behalf of the employee, saying he "strongly rejects any suggestion of inappropriate conduct".
'He misses his mother'
Sunrise was founded by Cox in the 1990s on land gifted to her by then-Cambodian prime minister Hun Sen as an orphanage for children with nowhere to go.
Cox has spoken publicly about how her infertility morphed into a maternal instinct for the children under her care.
"I feel about these children as though they are my own," she said in the documentary My Khmer Heart. "It's very difficult for me to make people understand that these are my children."
However, many of the children living at Sunrise — like other orphanages in Cambodia — have living biological families.
Madsen said he was surprised by the number of children in Sunrise who were not orphans, but had living parents or relatives.
This became apparent during his first Khmer New Year on the job, when the orphanage cleared out as children returned to stay with their families.
"That was the first light globe moment to me," he said. "And the question that came to me is, 'What's going on? They've got family?'"
Madsen hired case workers to track down family members.
The team discovered a "harrowing" case of a young girl who was incorrectly classified as an orphan. Her mother was found, but died suddenly before they could be reconnected.
"She didn't get the chance to be reunited in any sense with her mum. She went to [her] mum's funeral," Madsen said.
UNICEF has long warned about how institutional care could harm child development. Madsen said it was also cheaper to support families to send children to school while living at home, and pushed for more families to be reunited.
Sunrise acknowledged paperwork was often incomplete or missing, but said this was often out of their control, and they did their best to reunite families.
"This is the reality of life in Cambodia," Cox said.
Sunrise said helping children return to live with family, known as reintegration, has always been a priority, and that many children live in the centre due to abandonment, family violence or other factors that make it unsafe to return home.
Reports obtained by the ABC show poverty alone has also been a reason that children lived in Sunrise in the 2010s, with reports detailing parents struggling with harsh living conditions or low-paid jobs in garment factories and food markets.
"She [mother] wants to live together with the child, but she is afraid that the child cannot have a bright future if the child lives with her," one stated.
The reports also detail experiences of some Sunrise children who suffered emotionally from family separation.
"She sometimes misses her mother until she cries at night," one report stated. "He misses his mother and wants to visit his mother," another said.
Yi Soksan, who worked at Sunrise in management roles from 2010 to 2018, said Cox accepted reintegration was necessary but felt this was sometimes difficult because she had formed emotional bonds with the children.
"We don't want to hurt her [Cox], but sometimes we have no choice," he said. "She doesn't want kids back to the family."
In an email sent shortly before he left in a management restructure in 2012, Madsen said some children were made to "jump through hoops" to leave Sunrise.
"Unless there is a serious risk of abuse or neglect, I see no reason why Sunrise Children's Villages should deny the rights of this family to live together.
"To deny such rights will certainly open Sunrise to some serious criticism."
Cox said families had always been reconnected when it was safe.
"What you describe as the feelings of former staff members may well come down to nothing more than a difference of opinion as to approach and emphasis, as can happen in any workplace."
Sunrise said residential care was no longer its core program and children who continued to live there were referred by the Cambodian government or facing "imminent danger".
It said it complied with all Cambodian government regulations and had passed its last three audits with 100 per cent compliance.
"Reintegration must be carried out with great care, as once custody is handed over, we can no longer intervene," it said.
Children wrote letters to sponsors
Sunrise said its child protection policies "have evolved significantly … as have international standards and practices across the NGO sector" and has sought to draw a distinction between current and prior leadership.
But in the past, Sunrise, like many other charities, promoted connections between sponsors and children to drive donations.
Meeting minutes from 2018, sent to directors including Dennis, show efforts to raise funds by increasing communication from children to donors through emails, photos and drawings.
Around Christmas and birthdays, children were asked to write letters "thanking them" for presents and asking for more money.
Sponsors also received annual reports with photographs of individual children, along with personal details, such as their weight, age, height and the "best thing you did last year".
"He always behaves like girls," one sponsor report stated about a child in 2019. "He always makes up his body very similar to the girls in girl dressing."
Other reports included a 10-year-old girl's history of sexual abuse, and another child's experience of domestic violence.
Responding to questions about whether this breached the children's privacy and created an unhealthy dynamic between sponsors and children, a Sunrise spokesperson said this practice was "immediately stopped and new child privacy policies were applied" under current leadership.
"Child histories are now strictly confidential, even among staff and children. However, children are of [course] free to speak about their own background."
M'Lop Tapang co-founder Maggie Eno said fundraising was difficult, but there should be "zero contact" between children and sponsors.
"They're not friends. They're not uncles or aunties. They are strangers to that child," she said. "They have a power dynamic over that child, and they don't have the right to be playing with that child."
She said the charity sector in Cambodia had come a long way in the past two decades, but she was surprised that child sponsorship was still being used.
"It's just inconceivable that a sponsor and a child would even know each other," she said. "In 2026, I just can't really fathom the idea that that still goes on, to be honest."
Former Sunrise director Peter Winkler, who said he had not been involved since 2015, said children "should never be used as attractions for fundraising or tourism".
"My understanding is that SCV [Sunrise] has not kept up with the times."
Winkler, who now advocates to end residential care in Cambodia, said the Dennis case should be handled transparently and had broader lessons for all donors.
"Australian-funded charities working overseas are, in many ways, a reflection of Australian values, and we have an obligation to undertake due diligence."
*Name has been changed.

Athens stage performance honors Minab school victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
19:03:30 UTC
04:03:30 KST

Athens stage performance honors Minab school victims
TEHRAN- A theatrical performance commemorating the schoolchildren killed in the US-Israeli attack on Shajareh Tayyebeh School in Minab has been staged in Athens, Greece, as part of a cultural program highlighting the human consequences of the tragedy.
“Reading Sara’s Memories from Minab,” written and directed by Greek theater artist Andreas Zafeiris, was presented at the Brecht Stage of the 2510 Cultural Center in cooperation with Iran’s Cultural Attaché Office and Embassy in Greece on Thursday.
The play draws on the memories of Sara, a girl who survived the attack on the school in southern Iran. Through the perspective of a child, it portrays everyday life, fear, loss and the lasting consequences of the assault, bringing the experiences of those affected into focus.
The program also featured documentaries about the attack on the Minab school, as well as a screening of the short film “MINAB 168.”
Following the theatrical performance and film screenings, writers and media activists took part in a discussion titled “The Role of Art in Resistance and the Fight against Oppression and Injustice.”
Mohammadreza Bahmani, Iran’s cultural attaché in Greece, referred to the killing of thousands of children in Gaza, Palestine, Yemen, Lebanon and Iran over the past three years. He described protecting children and defending human dignity as responsibilities that transcend political and geographical boundaries.
Bahmani also emphasized the role of art in exposing injustice, conveying the voices of victims and preventing such tragedies from fading from collective memory. He expressed appreciation for the Greek artistic group’s efforts to commemorate the children martyred in Minab.
Palestinian writer and translator Nawzat Hadid spoke about the role of art in preserving collective memory and the historical identity of the Palestinian people. She described artistic expression as a means of documenting displacement, conveying experiences of resistance and representing the suffering of individuals whose lives can otherwise disappear behind statistics and reports.
Greek journalist, writer and director Thomas Sideris highlighted the responsibility of the media in covering wars and humanitarian crises. Drawing on his professional experience, he said journalists should go beyond reducing victims to numbers and communicate their actual lives and experiences to audiences.
Konstantina Karouti, a representative of the “Until Victory / MINAB 168” campaign, stressed the importance of preserving the memory of the 168 children who lost their lives and turning public sympathy into social action. She described art and cultural activities as ways to challenge indifference, racism and the normalization of violence.
Zafeiris said theater could bring audiences closer to victims’ experiences and encourage them to listen to their stories. He emphasized that taking time to hear about other people’s lives could help transform passive spectators into responsible participants.
The program also included video messages from Minab artist and eyewitness Jafar Qassemi, Lebanese journalist Marwa Othman and Australian researcher Tim Anderson.
An art exhibition titled “MINAB 168” was another feature of the event, paying tribute to the children killed in the attack.
According to the organizers, proceeds from the program will go toward rebuilding Shajareh Tayyebeh School. The play is scheduled to return to the stage on October 29 at the Brecht Stage in Athens.

Majid Entezami to perform his memorable pieces in Tehran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
19:02:57 UTC

Majid Entezami to perform his memorable pieces in Tehran
TEHRAN – Maestro Majid Entezami will conduct a 150-piece orchestra on October 29 at the Espinas Palace Hotel in Tehran, at a concert featuring the memorable works he has made for Iranian films and TV series.
The works to be performed in the concert include “Kolah Pahlavi,” “From Karkheh to Rhein,” “The Glass Agency,” “The Scent of Joseph’s Shirt,” “The Insane Flew Away,” “Kani Manga,” “Men of Anjelos,” “Duel,” “Once Upon a Time, Cinema,” “The Eagles,” “Zaal and Simorgh,” “The Train,” “The Wolves,” and “The Symphony of the Epic of Khorramshahr,” Honaronline reported.
In 2023, the veteran composer and conductor Entezami staged the concert “Along with Memories,” in which he presented a selection of his works accompanied by Iran’s National Orchestra at Tehran’s Vahdat Hall. His presence on the stage, which happened after an 11-year hiatus, was met with remarkable audience reception, and the concert was extended for multiple runs.
Also an oboist, Entezami, 78, has composed music for over 80 movies, 10 television series, and 10 suite symphonies. He holds the record for winning the most Crystal Simorgh awards in the Best Original Score category at the Fajr International Film Festival.
He studied at State University of West Berlin under the supervision of Karl Steins and Lothar Koch in 1968. He performed successful concerts with the Berlin University Symphony Orchestra in Lyon, Nancy, and Marseille from 1969 to 1972.
In 1973, Entezami came to Iran by the invitation of the Tehran Symphony Orchestra and performed a successful Mozart concert as oboe soloist, conducted by Helge Dorsch. Then he returned to Germany as a member of the Berlin Symphony Orchestra and the West Deutsche Philharmonie.
In 1974, he became a member of the Tehran Symphony Orchestra as well as a teacher at the Tehran Conservatory and the music department of the University of Tehran. He performed two oboe recitals with Lucette Martirossian on piano and harpsichord and Ivan Pristas on bassoon in 1976 and a concert with the Les Jeunesses Musicales de l’Iran orchestra conducted by Ali Rahbari and Valodia Tarkhanian as viola d’amore soloist.
Despite being the son of famous Iranian actor Ezzatollah Entezami, Majid's entrance into the cinema industry was his own.
He has a profound understanding of the picture and has always tried to tell the untold essence of the story. He also has experience with a variety of styles, which has given his portfolio variety, from comedies to epic war movies.
The music of Entezami is orchestral and based on Western classical music, but with Iranian instruments and unusual rhythms which give his works an eastern feel.
Every theme and musical color heard in Entezami's work has a rational explanation in the story. He believes that music tells a part of the story that is not already told in the picture. Some of his works seem to be narrative, almost like part of the script, but he maintains that no director has ever asked him for such characteristics.

Iran slams US-Israeli attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities, condemns double standards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
19:01:24 UTC
04:01:24 KST

Iran slams US-Israeli attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities, condemns double standards
TEHRAN– Iran’s ambassador to the United Nations has condemned US and Israeli attacks on Iran’s peaceful nuclear facilities, accusing Western countries and international nuclear authorities of applying double standards and politicizing global non-proliferation efforts.
Addressing the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York on Friday, Gholamhossein Darzi, Iran’s ambassador and deputy permanent representative to the United Nations, reaffirmed Iran’s inalienable right under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) to develop nuclear energy for peaceful purposes, including uranium enrichment.
Darzi said the United States was challenging the rights of NPT member states by questioning their entitlement to pursue the full nuclear fuel cycle. He argued that denying countries access to uranium enrichment technology while claiming to support peaceful nuclear energy was incompatible with Article IV of the treaty.
“No State can unilaterally rewrite the Treaty or impose its own political veto on the legitimate rights of other States Parties,” he said, warning against the use of non-proliferation concerns as a means of exerting political pressure on sovereign nations.
The Iranian envoy said the United States and Israel had launched two wars of aggression against Iran in 2025 and 2026, targeting its peaceful nuclear facilities under International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) safeguards. He described the attacks as violations of international law, the UN Charter, the IAEA Statute, relevant IAEA General Conference resolutions and UN Security Council Resolution 487 (1981).
According to Darzi, the attacks caused extensive destruction and claimed thousands of lives, including that of Iran’s Leader, whose religious decree, or fatwa, rejects nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction.
Iran criticizes international response
Darzi strongly criticized the IAEA’s governing bodies, its director general and the UN Security Council for failing to condemn the attacks on safeguarded nuclear facilities. He said the absence of a clear response had exposed the selective application of international non-proliferation standards.
“Instead, pressure is directed against the victim while the aggressors escape accountability,” he said.
The envoy contrasted the treatment of Iran, an NPT member since 1970, with that of Israel, which he described as the only nuclear-armed state in the region and whose nuclear facilities are not subject to comprehensive IAEA safeguards.
He argued that continued political and military pressure on Iran, alongside 'impunity for Israel,' undermined the credibility of the international non-proliferation regime. He also criticized the withholding of technical cooperation that, in his view, deprived Iran of the benefits of peaceful nuclear development that the IAEA is mandated to promote.
Safety conditions remain central to inspections
Addressing calls for the resumption of inspections, Darzi said Iran had neither abandoned nor formally suspended its safeguards obligations. However, he stressed that the military attacks had fundamentally changed the physical and security conditions under which verification activities could take place.
He noted that the IAEA’s own reports acknowledged that verification activities had ceased and inspectors had been withdrawn for safety reasons. Such concerns, he said, could not be disregarded when demands were made for their return.
“No country can reasonably be expected to provide access amid military operations and persistent threats without adequate safety guarantees,” Darzi said, adding that responsibility for creating these conditions rested with the countries that carried out the attacks.
He concluded that Iran remained prepared to cooperate with the IAEA to the extent permitted by prevailing circumstances, but emphasized that such cooperation must not compromise the safety of the Iranian people, nuclear facilities or agency inspectors.
Darzi also insisted that the IAEA’s reporting must remain professional, objective and free from political influence, arguing that the agency’s credibility depended on technical integrity and impartiality.
