How One Danish Entrepreneur Is Bringing Ukrainian Art to the World
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:37:00 UTC
23:37:00 KST

For many international audiences, Ukraine remains synonymous with war. But beyond the headlines, artists continue to paint landscapes, portraits, and scenes of everyday life, preserving the country’s identity and documenting what Ukrainians are fighting to protect.
Danish entrepreneur Caspar Ejsing founded artfromukraine, an online gallery selling works by Ukrainian artists to international buyers. The platform allocates 70% of each sale to the artist, 25% to operating costs, and 5% to the Hospitallers Medical Battalion, whose volunteer medics evacuate wounded soldiers from the front.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Recently featured by UNITED24 Media and Spend With Ukraine, the project aims to expand the international market for Ukrainian art and introduce audiences to a side of the country that often goes unseen.
In an interview with Kyiv Post, Ejsing explains how his experience in Ukraine shaped the initiative, why art can change perceptions of a country at war, and how he plans to build a sustainable platform for Ukrainian artists.
Kyiv Post: What do international audiences still fail to understand about Ukrainian society?
Caspar Ejsing: I find this question hard to answer on behalf of others, because my own view of Ukraine is very different from that of most people in Denmark. I have seen the side of Ukraine that rarely makes the news: the warmth of its people, its culture, and the way life goes on in cities like Kyiv. That is why I fell in love with the country.
Peskov Says Kremlin Open to EU Envoy if Focused on Genuine Peace
For many people abroad, Ukraine has become synonymous with war. When they think of Ukrainians, they often picture soldiers on the front line or elderly women in damaged villages. Those images are real and important, but they are only part of the picture.
What is often missing is a modern, creative, and highly educated society, with artists, musicians, young professionals, and entrepreneurs who continue to build their lives and their country under attack.
In Denmark, I think understanding is better than in many places. We have a strong Ukrainian community in Copenhagen, including around Ukraine House, and many Danes now have Ukrainian colleagues, neighbors, and friends – myself included.
On the wider international stage, especially in the US, I think the picture is still much narrower. That is exactly where art can make a difference.
How did your time in Ukraine shape your understanding of Ukrainian art, and why did you decide to build a business around it?
I spent most of my time in Kyiv, a city full of culture – not only visual art, but also music and countless grassroots initiatives. What struck me was how Ukrainians use art and culture to express themselves, including their feelings about the war.
Art has always been a personal interest of mine. I have spent a lot of time drawing myself and attended art schools here in Denmark, so the connection came naturally.
Artfromukraine had already started when the real turning point came. I was invited by Professor Leonid Pavlenko to visit the National Academy of Fine Arts and Architecture in Kyiv. Seeing the studios and the quality of the work, I realized that it deserved a much bigger international audience. That was the moment I decided to take the project seriously.
The gallery is possible because of cspaar, a Danish IT company, which develops and operates the platform. Without cspaar, artfromukraine would not exist.
What do these works reveal about Ukraine that war reporting cannot capture?
War reporting naturally focuses on the front line: which towns are taken, which are lost, and how the lines move back and forth. That is necessary, but it reduces Ukraine to a battlefield.
The paintings show what Ukrainians are fighting for. a landscape, a street in Kyiv, a portrait of a friend – these are the places, the people, and the everyday life the war is trying to destroy.
They show a country with its own identity, traditions, and beauty, making it much harder to see Ukraine as just a headline.
At the same time, we do not avoid the war. On our channels, we regularly remind our audiences in Denmark, the UK, and the US that the war is ongoing and devastating, and that Ukraine still needs support.
Art opens the door. Once people care about the culture, they also care about the country.
How do you balance the commercial side of the gallery with supporting Ukraine, and what impact has the initiative made so far?
The model is built in from the start: 70% of every sale goes directly to the artist, 25% covers operating costs such as shipping and export documentation, and 5% goes to the Hospitallers Medical Battalion. The donation is not decided case by case. It is part of every sale.
Our costs are low because the platform is developed and operated by cspaar. This means the gallery does not need large margins to survive, and the artist always receives the majority of the price.
Artfromukraine is still at an early stage. So far, the biggest impact has been visibility: we have onboarded Ukrainian artists, and the project has been covered by UNITED24 Media and Spend With Ukraine.
That matters because it puts Ukrainian artists in front of international buyers who would otherwise never have seen their work.
How do you plan to grow artfromukraine and strengthen the international market for Ukrainian art?
We plan to grow slowly and steadily. In the short term, the focus is on onboarding more artists and building a stronger network in Ukraine. We are also working on establishing a Ukrainian company, which will make payments and cooperation with Ukrainian partners much easier.
In the longer term, I want to run the project together with Ukrainian partners, whether they are co-investors, development partners, or marketing companies.
The goal is for artfromukraine to become a trusted place for international buyers to discover Ukrainian art, and a reliable source of income for the artists we work with.

Over 50 air defence towers reportedly built around Putin's Valdai residence
Another 16 air defence towers have been built around Russian leader Vladimir Putin's Valdai residence. The total number of air defence positions in the area has now exceeded 50.
Source: Radio Liberty's Russian Service, citing an analysis of satellite imagery conducted jointly with OSINT analyst jembobineuse
Details: The new towers were built mainly south of the residence, within a 50 km radius. They form an outer air defence ring facing Ukraine.

Background: In mid-April, it became known that seven new towers armed with Pantsir air defence systems had been built around Putin's Valdai residence during March, bringing the total to 27.

A Palestinian was also hospitalized with a gunshot wound to the foot after Israeli forces opened fire in the Al-Faluja area west of Jabalia refugee camp.
In southern Gaza, two Palestinians were killed and three others injured in an Israeli strike in al-Mawasi, west of Khan Younis, according to medical sources.
The sources also reported that a woman sustained moderate injuries from Israeli gunfire in Khan Younis.
Israeli artillery also shelled areas east and south of the city, while gunboats fired bullets and shells toward its coast, witnesses told Anadolu.
In central Gaza, a 33-year-old man was killed in an Israeli strike east of Deir al-Balah.
At dawn Sunday, Israeli forces carried out two demolitions of homes and buildings in areas under their control in the Al-Tuffah neighborhood of eastern Gaza City, causing two large explosions, local sources said.
Despite a ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, the Israeli army has killed 1,551 Palestinians and injured 5,573 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, Israel's war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000, while causing widespread destruction to about 90% of the territory's civilian infrastructure.

Time is running out for Germany to pay Polish WWII victims the compensation they deserve [Opinion]
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:10:55 UTC
23:10:55 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
By Philipp Fritz, Warsaw correspondent for Die Welt (which first published this article in German here)
Negotiations on compensation for the still-living victims of the German occupation of Poland have been going on for years. There are some 30,000 to 50,000 such survivors, but their number dwindles every week. Berlin should act now.
No “humanitarian gesture” has emerged. “The draft budget currently reflects the fact that no decision has been made,” said Josef Hinterseher, a German foreign office spokesman, at a press conference in late September.
He thereby confirmed what many observers had suspected: survivors of concentration camps, ghettos and death marches, former forced workers and participants in the Warsaw Uprising who are still living in Poland will not receive any compensation, one-off payment or monthly pension from the German government.
The German chancellor has announced that his country will offer support to surviving Polish victims of WW2 and will help strengthen Poland’s eastern border.
However, in both cases he did not provide details of what these measures will involve in practice https://t.co/gKX6142Alo
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2024
Just a few sentences later, Hinterseher moved onto the next subject – the fact that two Russian oligarchs were to be removed from the EU’s sanctions list. Or at least, that Berlin had not been successful in opposing this decision.
The fact that these two issues were dealt with publicly one after the other shows that the German government is quicker to reach a decision that makes Putin’s supporters’ lives easier than it is with victims of the Nazi terror. It is a declaration of moral bankruptcy.
Warsaw and Berlin have been negotiating compensation for the last remaining victims of the German occupation of Poland for years. There are between 30,000 and 50,000 of them – aged over 90, often living alone and in poor health. Their numbers are dwindling every week.
The fact that talks are taking place in Berlin ministries but without any decision being taken is met with sadness and fury in Poland.
Increasingly, Poles are getting the impression that, even if the Germans manage to put up memorials, they cannot offer survivors tangible help when it is asked for. It is a common view that in Berlin the descendants of the perpetrators are simply waiting for the victims to die so that this pesky issue will sort itself out.
Should that happen, those left behind will not forget, and the Germans will hardly be able to forgive themselves.
Warsaw is no longer demanding war reparations from Berlin. In December 2023, Donald Tusk’s government switched to talking about “making amends”.
Polish foreign minister @sikorskiradek has called on Germany to “think creatively” about compensating Poland for WWII.
On a visit to Berlin, he also said that the new government would "end the cold war" waged by the former ruling PiS party against Germany https://t.co/kZ62nUuqqO
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 31, 2024
This is not just splitting hairs. In so doing, Tusk put the ball in the German government’s court, giving it the chance to take action and, through a gesture recognising suffering and providing a relatively small sum of money, to offer people tangible help and do a service to the German-Polish relationship.
Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz is reported to have offered Tusk a one-off payment in 2024, but Poland’s prime minister turned the sum down as insufficient. Instead, Polish diplomats are demanding monthly pensions.
In any case, we are talking about a few hundred million euro: a relatively small amount compared to the equivalent of €1.3 trillion that Poland’s former ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party once demanded from Germany, and also in comparison to many other budget items – and yet still there is nothing about compensation in the budget planning.
Poland is seeking $1.3 trillion in war reparations from Germany, but Berlin says the issue was legally settled long ago.
Legal scholar @MPiatkowski1 examines the arguments of both sides, explains the legal context, and looks at what could come next https://t.co/xsKAY2TukS
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2022
Rumour has it that, in return for compensation, German foreign ministry officials are asking for a kind of Polish guarantee that in future there will be no more demands for reparations, or at least that at least the German gesture will receive good press in Poland.
If that is true, it would be thoroughly indecent, bringing to mind an image of a perpetrator trying to buy his victim’s silence. This reflects a belief in objectification, an ugly bureaucratic mentality stemming from a system in which “work” in a ghetto counts towards statutory pension contributions, but no one can bring themselves to pay compensation.
This issue can be resolved at the very top. Chancellor Friedrich Merz would have to work with the relevant ministries – the foreign office and finance ministry – to provide for compensation for the victims in the budget. This would be a belated but major and morally right gesture. If politics is too slow – time really is of the essence – then civil society should take it upon itself to show where it stands.
Donations for the still living victims of the German tyranny or a fund from which survivors would receive monthly payments can be created from within society. Business can also get involved. German corporations which were guilty of, for instance, exploiting forced labourers in occupied Poland, or those that emerged from them, such as BASF, Siemens, Volkswagen, BMW and Deutsche Bank, could contribute.
Poland covers almost all the costs of maintaining former Nazi-German camps on its territory. It has spent more on this than Germany has paid in compensation to Polish war victims
It's time for Germany to fund preservation of the sites, argues @W_Kononczuk https://t.co/08nf4c2jMz
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 25, 2026
Right now, since its state elections in September, Germany gives the impression of a country whose compass for right and wrong is broken.
As of 6 October, the state parliament of Sachsen-Anhalt has as its vice-president Hans-Thomas Tillschneider of the AfD, a man who wrote on X that “the Poles have been getting on my nerves for a long time now”. In Berlin, not only did the left-wing Die Linke celebrate their electoral success with Israel haters and antisemites, they even tolerate them in their ranks. It is shameful.
But now Germany, and particularly its government, has the opportunity to show that the rhetoric of responsibility for the victims is not merely empty words. That, contrary to a mood that does not support it, they are doing what is morally right. Time is running out, Germany – it’s your last chance.
